en: The Collected Edition of the *Xuan-yi Shiyi-ji* (Supplementary Record of the Profound Meaning) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, Volume I, Part I.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Zhili of Shuangming, including preface and record;
recorded with annotations beneath the *Xuan-yi* by the Śramaṇa Mingde of Shuangjing.
Question: In the past, Dharma Master Baoyun once compiled a commentary and sub-commentary on the *Xuanbian*;

in recent years, the Acharya of Mount Gu also clarified its subtle purport through his notes and records. Why, then, have you now undertaken this compilation again? Answer: During Baoyun’s lectures, disciples recorded the teachings as they went along;
however, some meanings were incomplete or missing, and he had not yet had the opportunity to supplement or correct them. Thus, I have undertaken this work.

Fortunately, I have returned to the quietude of Mount Gu; yet, many matters have led to the obscuration of the text, and in the interim, the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) has been destroyed and removed.

This is truly unbearable, and I therefore now take up my pen to recover the remaining meanings left by my former teacher and to retrieve the texts discarded by later generations, so that the two paths of teaching and practice shall not remain obstructed. May this suffice to inform both beginners and the learned.
Preface on the day of the full moon in the fourth month of the first year of the Tiānshèng era, the year of Guǐhài.

△ Regarding the preliminary explanation of the *Xuányì* (Profound Meaning), the main outline is divided into two parts: First, explaining the title; Second, [explaining the text]. First, the title of the scripture’s meaning.
The title of the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning) of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* contains six characters: the upper four are the object of explanation, while the lower two are the means of explanation.

The means of explanation is universal, for Master Zhizhe established five meanings when explaining all sutras; thus, by using the object of explanation, one distinguishes this work from other sections. Entering the text:
Because the four characters of the sutra title are explained extensively, the two characters "capable of explaining" (*nengshi*) are not pre-narrated here.

"Mystery" (*xuan*) means that which is profound and subtle, difficult to perceive; "meaning" (*yi*) refers to the depth of the principle and its underlying rationale. Regarding these profound and subtle meanings, there are five layers:

first, the names that can express the teaching throughout the beginning and end of the sutra, and the essence (*ti*) invoked by those names; this is the essence itself, the primary principle (*zong*).

The Great Master investigated and extracted these five meanings—namely, the accomplishment of power and function, these four words, the teaching, the pervasive and the specific, and their respective characteristics—to explain this single title.
He did so desiring that students first understand the intent of the sutra before examining the text, thereby enabling them to cultivate wisdom and practice with every word.
This is the special occasion at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), where, through the arousal of tranquility, he has expounded this in accordance with the Buddha’s mind.
Therefore, those who rely on obscure evidence and those who merely follow the literal text cannot be discussed as being on the same level as one who grasps the profound intent.
How could such subtle and profound meaning be a mere empty name? △ Second, the title of the Teacher who expounds it.
Spoken by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai; recorded by his disciple Guanding.
"Tiantai" refers to the place where he dwelt in truth; "Zhizhe" is the title bestowed by the Sovereign of the Sui dynasty; "Great Master" (Dashi) indicates that he was a model for all living beings;

"spoke" (shuo) distinguishes him from other teachers; and "wrote with pen" (zhuobian) refers to his composition of these records. If one wishes to fully understand his life and deeds from beginning to end, [they are contained herein].
The *Biézhuàn* (Separate Biography) is now omitted for brevity. △ Second, the explanation of the text has two parts: first, the explanation of the preface;
second, the general indication of the essence of the Dharma. This *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is profound and immeasurable.
This [term "this"] is a word designating [the subject]. "Suvarṇaprabhāsa" (Golden Light) is the dharma-body revealed; it is the profound, immeasurable essence and virtue of illumination.
One should know that these three characters of the distinct title of this sutra refer to the Dharma itself and not to a metaphor.
How is this known? Because the sutra describes the Tathāgata wandering within the immeasurable and profound *dharmatā*, the sphere of action of all Buddhas. Thus...
Abiding in this samādhi, one proclaims: "This is the King of all Sūtras, the Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
Is this not a direct pointing to the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) in which one dwells, naming it "Suvarṇaprabhāsa"? It does not say that the *dharmatā* is like gold and light;
rather, regarding the various metaphors established in the subsequent text, one interpretation holds that the masters of old explained "Suvarṇaprabhāsa" as referring to worldly objects and images.

For example, although various masters employ metaphors to illustrate the profound Dharma attained by the Tathāgata, they do not actually understand that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are perfectly interfused;
rather, they provide restricted interpretations according to specific names. Consequently, they are unable to use metaphors to encompass all phenomena.

The Great Master, wishing to demonstrate that within the ocean of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* there is no phenomenon not fully present and no phenomenon not perfectly interfused, follows the various masters [in their use of metaphors].
The three characters "Jin Guang Ming" (Golden Light) serve as a complete analogy for the Buddha’s sphere of activity. Briefly, there are ten kinds of triads of dharmas;
extensively, all dharma-gates are mutually integrated, each being inconceivable. This [previous method] was limited because it compared [the Buddha] to other things through incomplete analogies;

therefore, this [current section] extensively reveals the perfect fulfillment of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Nevertheless, although this follows the perspective of others by means of analogy, [it nonetheless manifests the ultimate reality].

To clarify the Dharma according to the title of the sutra: since this is the Dharma itself and not a mere metaphor, [the author] subsequently establishes two types of interpretation—based on the text and based on the essence—to refute that [previous] view which infers the meaning through a remote analogy. Relying instead upon the sutra and focusing directly on the Dharma is what constitutes true intimacy.
This is because the Great Master deeply understood the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), which is venerable and precious; thus, the essence itself is named "Gold," being both quiescent and eternal.
Illuminating its own essence is called "Light" (*prabhā*); benefiting all things through great compassion is designated by its own essence as "Glory" (*tejas*).
Thus, one knows that the *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) fully possesses the true meaning of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, which is ultimately accomplished.

Since all names and phrases apart from this *dharmatā* lack real meaning, the three dharma-gates of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* are such that taking one is to take all three, and the entirety of these three is [this single essence].
It is neither three nor one, yet it is both one and three; neither vertical nor horizontal, it transcends thought and deliberation—this is the secret treasury, the realm where the Buddhas dwell.
Furthermore, it should be understood that that which reveals the essence of the Dharma through the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* is the essence of the five chapters;
for this sutra takes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as its title and takes the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as its essence.

Taking *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as the essence, taking *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as the principle, and taking *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* as the pedagogical form—these three terms may also be correlated individually with the five chapters:
taking "Gold" (*suvarṇa*) as the substance, "Light" (*prabhā*) as the principle, and "Radiance" (*sūrya*) as the function;
these three together constitute the title. By distinguishing these three names, they form the pedagogical form. Since the substance of the Dharma is thus, its essence...

The virtue of "conformity" is profoundly deep because this light's virtue exhausts the bottom of the *dharmatā*. The virtue of "immeasurability" is that of "clarity" because it reaches the limits of the *dharmatā*.
The virtue of "non-duality" of these two is that of "gold," because the ultimate *dharmatā* has the sense of being supremely noble.
Furthermore, all three meanings may be considered profoundly deep, immeasurable, and non-dual; this concludes the fifth chapter.
Virtue is never otherwise than this. △ Second, the specific elucidation of the intent of the teaching. Above, the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of the five chapters was shown in general;
now, the intent for initiating the teaching is specifically clarified. First, the narration of the intent for preaching the sutra, which is the Tathāgata’s manifestation of the five chapters.
Second, the narration of the intent for proclaiming and transmitting [the teaching], which is Chih-i’s circulation of the five chapters. The first [section] is further divided into two parts. First:
To sever speech according to principle is because the ultimate truth can only be wondrously realized and is difficult to describe through names;

yet, when responding to conditions, it may be spoken—this being based on great compassion, speaking where there is no speaking, and such speaking necessarily benefits others. This initial section is further divided into two parts:
first, regarding the self, it is argued that from the supreme fruit above down to the common ordinary person below, none can cause the subtle truth to have words for it.
Furthermore, this is divided into three parts. First, it clarifies that no analogy can fully express the person who has attained the fruit.
Even the great realm of empty space cannot serve as a metaphor for its height and vastness; how much less could the weight of mountains or drops from the ocean ever reach its limits?
The four Buddhas spoke in verse: "Mountains, weights, ocean drops, particles of earth-dust, and the realm of space—none of these can compare to the lifespan of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni.
Among these four metaphors, space is the greatest, for the other three—mountains and so forth—depend upon space to exist.
Although space is vast, it is an object manifested by the deluded mind; because one is confused about reality, it arises, but when one awakens to the nature of reality, it ceases.
The eye is a sensory faculty, and the mind is limited by its objects of perception; how could these ever suffice as metaphors for the inconceivable *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*? Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"The void arises within the Great Awakening, like a single bubble emerging from the ocean. How could one compare a single bubble to the great ocean?

Even the void cannot serve as a metaphor—how much less can the other three? The question asks: The Sūtra states that even the void and so forth cannot be compared to the World-Honored One. Why is this?
Regarding the lifespan attained, how can it now be said that it is not comparable to the Great Awakened One or the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*?

If the nature of awakening were slight, or if the three meanings—such as gold and so forth—were lacking, it would not be called "Great. The meaning of the World-Honored One’s lifespan corresponds to "clarity";

if the golden light were not complete, it would not be eternal life. It is not that one dharma is deficient or that three dharmas are excessive; there is no difference between the Buddhas of the past and the present.
The essence and its function are non-dual; were it otherwise, it would not be the meaning of the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) sūtras.

The four Buddha-World-Honored Ones could not have matched this through metaphors, for it reveals that the principle transcends words. △ Second, clarifying that those at the stage of the cause cannot exhaust the source:

Above, it was shown that although the fruit-Buddhas are ultimately perfected, because the Dharma is fundamentally quiescent, even metaphors cannot manifest it. Now, we examine those at the stage of the cause who have not yet [reached this state].
Because it reaches the very source of nature, deliberation cannot reach it; this constitutes the first of two parts, wherein the [opponent's] wisdom and severance are refuted by means of analogy:
"The sun’s orb blazes so brightly that it is not something an infant can gaze upon; how could the masts and battlements of a great ship be grasped by one newly born?"

The blazing brilliance of the sun’s orb is a metaphor for the wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*) of *prajñā*; the infant’s eye is a metaphor for the insight of the contemplations of emptiness and the provisional.
Since such [discriminative] wisdom contradicts fundamental wisdom, it is not the Buddha-eye; therefore, one cannot gaze upon the blazing sun of wisdom-virtue.

The multi-storied tower of a great ship is a metaphor for the liberation-virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*); the newly delivered woman is a metaphor for the compassion arising from conditions (*dharmapratyaya-karuṇā*). Since these differ from the [unconditioned], [they are not the ultimate].
Because conditioned phenomena lack wondrous power, they cannot sustain the battlement of the virtue of cessation (*nirodha-guṇa*).

This is a critique of the compassion and wisdom of the bodhisattvas of the three previous vehicles from the perspective of the three knowledges and three liberations of the perfect fruit (*pariniṣpanna-phala*).

If a bodhisattva of the Perfect Teaching cultivates [the path] as being identical to their nature, then from the very beginning they do not deviate from these two virtues. Nevertheless, although there is an understanding of this identity, if one views the cause in light of the fruit—
Wisdom has degrees of clarity and obscurity, and its powers have strengths and weaknesses; therefore, depending on the person, the wisdom regarding the fruit may be refined or not.
One must understand that the abandonment of ignorance is called "light" and these two virtues are non-dual, which is the Dharmakāya.
It is further named "gold. Although the two [preceding] metaphors are used for exclusion, they do not yet exhaust the source of the three dharmas. △
Second, it is determined by means of the Dharma through cause and effect.
The sphere of action of all Buddhas transcends the spheres of action of all Bodhisattvas and is pure.

While both partial and perfect Bodhisattvas are able to subdue and sever [afflictions] according to their respective practices, all such practices are termed "pure"; now, it is the ultimate perfection.

Because the dharma-nature of the fruition transcends all things, it is said to "surpass" them. Even those who have attained ultimate realization regarding the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* cannot adequately describe it;
how much less can those who have not fathomed its source? △ Third, clarifying why ordinary beings and followers of the Small Vehicle are utterly deluded, in two parts: first, the Small Vehicle.
How much more so, then, can the mind and speech of those of the Two Vehicles be conceived or described?

Even for the partial and perfect bodhisattvas who have given rise to the vast and great mind and possess the wisdom of partial realization, they are still unable to fully express or establish words regarding the wondrous and absolute principle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*;
how much less so for those of the Two Vehicles, who extinguish their minds to save themselves alone, like the deaf.
Just as a mute person can neither contemplate nor speak of the sphere of action of the Buddhas. △ Second, the ordinary person:
An ordinary person vainly desires to speak of it, yet speaking harms its reality; they vainly desire not to speak, yet silence leads to its loss.
Neither approach is possible: if one wishes to speak, even speaking is impossible; if one wishes to remain silent, even silence is impossible.
Although the noble ones of the Three Vehicles differ slightly, their great cause does not equal their fruit;

yet they are able to cultivate and realize the principle and wisdom of the three truths, which even transcends words and thought—how much more so the ocean of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*! As for those of the mundane and non-Buddhist paths, it is not their lot to begin with;

thus, to follow words gives rise to views, and speaking would therefore harm the reality. Since they cling to the idea that there are no words, remaining silent would lead to failure. If one were to possess...

Regarding speech, there are single words, compound phrases, and complete sentences; regarding silence, there are likewise one wordless instance for each of the three groups beyond the fourfold propositions.
Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīya school’s "self" in the fifth "inexpressible basket" (*avyākṛta-piṭaka*)—all of these are the views on speech and silence held by heterodox outsiders.
As for those who are merely indifferent or those who study the Buddha's teachings, [they should consider this] alone...
The mind of principle is neither speech nor silence; regarding these two states, one increases views and grows in attachment.

Although this is not the *puruṣa* (spiritual self), it fully constitutes the grasping of a person. Thus, the four teachings and four gates all give rise to views based on speech; yet, even within those four, they give rise to views of wordlessness.
Therefore, the *Awakening of Faith* clarifies that the five types of grasping at a person are all attachments to the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is now explained.
The reason for this rejection lies precisely in such a person; therefore, it is said that both speech and silence are equally "unacceptable.

Thus, when discussing in full detail the speech and silence of ordinary beings who give rise to views, the thoughts of the two vehicles who have attained partial realization, and the intellectual eloquence of Bodhisattvas whose wisdom is not yet ultimate—all these are unable to express the perfectly complete nature.
Even ascending to the fruit-stage Buddha, one must exhaustively investigate the pure mind and speech.

That even after exhaustive explanation, it cannot be illustrated by analogy, is intended to reveal that the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is fundamentally secret, transcending the characteristics of verbal expression and the characteristics of mental objects, so as to cause the practitioner to lose words and forget thoughts. △ Second, citing texts as proof, in two parts:
first, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Therefore, in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, a brahmin says: "One does not attain this bodhi by means of internal contemplation;
one does not attain this bodhi by means of external contemplation; nor does one attain this bodhi by means of both internal and external contemplation."
That sutra and its commentary clarify that although the brahmin Śreṇika was originally a heterodox outsider, his faculties had already matured;
when the Buddhas requested him, saying, "May you not rise from this seat until you have attained the eye," the Buddha opened the way for him to realize the stage of Srotāpanna.
The Buddha then questioned him regarding the wisdom by which he realized the principle: "Did you attain this wisdom through internal contemplation? He replied, "No."
If one asks whether such wisdom is attained through external appearance, internal reality, or both, the answer to all is "no. This refers to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*);
only when conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) is entirely severed does one attain the stream-entry (*srotāpanna*). If even this minor wisdom is thus, how much more so the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*?
△ Second, the Great Sutra.

The Sūtra states: "All are inconceivable and ineffable; moreover, arising from arising is ineffable, non-arising from arising is ineffable, arising from non-arising is ineffable, and non-arising from non-arising is ineffable."

The initial passage generally subsumes all discourse on "thought" (*manasikāra*); furthermore, the subsequent section specifically forgets the four types of discourse. Our school uses this to subsume the four teachings.

As for the path of "thought," it is truly that which generates and gives rise to the dharmas produced; thus, it is called "generating generation" (*sheng-sheng*), which refers to the Tripitaka Teaching.
The generation of illusory existence is precisely non-generation; this is called "generation of non-generation" (*sheng-bu-sheng*), which refers to the Shared Teaching.

The Teaching Vehicle (Śrāvaka-yāna) is called "non-abiding" and "non-arising," establishing the ten realms as "arising" while naming it "non-arising arising"; this is the Distinct Teaching (Pratyekabuddha-yāna). The Perfect Teaching (Ekayāna) is named "non-arising non-arising.
This means that the Principle is fundamentally non-arising, and since phenomena are identical to the Principle, phenomena are also non-arising; thus it is named "non-arising non-arising.
Furthermore, because the nature is fundamentally non-arising, practicing in accordance with that nature means that both nature and practice are non-arising; thus there are two [aspects].
4. It is "non-arising" because the essence of delusion does not arise; it is "non-arising" because the function of wisdom is forgotten.
Because both are non-arising, there is no cause to be cultivated; because both are non-arising, there is no fruit to be attained.

Because both are non-arising, the various relative phenomena of self and other, response and stimulus, and so forth, are all non-dual in their fundamental quiescence. Thus, "non-arising" is stated twice.

The statement that all [teachings] are "inexpressible" (avaktavya) has two intended meanings. First, regarding the specific categories (*prabheda*), the principles of the four teachings can only be realized through wisdom;
they cannot be expressed in words. As Śāriputra said: "Within liberation, there is no verbal expression"—this refers to the Tripiṭaka.
Second, the three types of practitioners alike attain the severance of all afflictions through the path of wordlessness—this refers to the Shared Teaching (*pāṛmitā-naya*). It is wordless.

The youth is neither ordinary nor holy, neither existent nor empty; thus, his silence distinguishes him. All phenomena are quiescent and cannot be proclaimed—this is their perfection (*pariniṣpanna*).
If one transcends these categories, the wondrous principle of perfection cannot be demonstrated through the four modes of speech;
it is difficult even to speak of its perfection, let alone through the three teachings. In this way, all of these manifest the radiance of the Dharma-gold.
This clarifies that the secret treasury is inconceivable. △ Second, responding to conditions so that it may be taught:

Although the principle of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is free from marks and quiescent, if one realizes it by transcending conceptual thought, then through the four *siddhāntas*, teaching without teaching causes sentient beings to obtain immeasurable benefit.
The text itself is divided into four parts; first, it clarifies that there must be a connection with conditions for it to be taught.
Regarding the statement, "Because there are causes and conditions, it can also be said":
after the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* mentions the four kinds of the ineffable (*anabhilāpya*), it immediately states that because there are causes and conditions, it can also be said.

Is this not to say that one may formulate four explanations in accordance with conditions? As for "because there are causes and conditions," these refer to the ten causes and conditions (*daśa-pratyaya*) among the twelve [links of dependent origination].
Within this, only the two links of future birth and old age and death are excluded, as these are the results produced by causes and conditions.
From past ignorance up to the present, these ten are all productive causes and conditions that bring about the fruits obtained through the four teachings. Why is this?
It is because the link of ignorance is precisely the mind of craving and grasping from the past, which exists due to [the presence of] existence (*bhava*).
Because of this mind, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas manifest the various names and meanings of the four teachings;
once one both loves and grasps them, one gives rise to the four types of karmic action based upon those four teachings—this is "ignorance conditions action.

This karma is able to sustain the consciousness of the person who has received the teachings as it comes to take rebirth in the mother’s womb—this is "action conditions consciousness. This consciousness then follows along with the karmic conditions of the four teachings to achieve its formation.
The fourfold fruits of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and so forth are precisely "consciousness conditions name-and-form" up to "contact conditions feeling.
Since the four teachings [of the *Abhidharmakośa*] explain that karma induces these five fruits, within the mind of feeling there arises craving for those four teachings;
this is "feeling conditions craving. Craving necessarily leads to grasping at the dharmas of the four teachings; this is "craving conditions grasping. If craving and grasping become deep, then...
Being able to diligently cultivate the four types of teaching and practice constitutes "existence" (*bhava*), which is precisely the condition for grasping (*upādāna*).

Since existence inevitably brings about its fruit, one will achieve the fruits of the noble ones (*ārya*) in the present or the future. This is because sentient beings possess ten causes and conditions;

therefore, the various noble ones preach the fourfold teaching: first, to cause those who have not yet planted [the seeds] to plant them; second, to cause those who have already planted them to ripen them through the four methods.

By means of the four dharmas, it is taught that those who have already reached maturity attain liberation; thus, there is this benefit, and for this reason, one must not fail to speak in accordance with conditions.
II. Clarifying that this teaching is worthy of veneration: Generally speaking, teachings are adapted to conditions throughout a single lifetime via the four teachings.
However, here, in response to specific capacities, the five meanings of this sutra are revealed. Each of these five meanings is individually most venerable. This is further divided into two parts.
The initial listing of the sutra contains five meanings:
first, its name is "Golden," which signifies that it surpasses all other jewels; second, its essence is the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature);

third, its principle is the profound and wondrous merit in which the Tathāgata dwells and which adorns Bodhisattvas; fourth, its central theme consists of these merits; and fifth, it illuminates the various heavens, causing their hearts to rejoice.
Because it is utilized for this purpose, its title is designated as the "King of Sūtras," which encompasses all other scriptures.

Regarding the phrase "named after gold" and so forth: the name consists of three characters; first, [the title] must necessarily be complete; second, because gold is supreme, its radiance is likewise so.
Taking the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) as its essence, although it is universally accessible to all Tathāgatas, it specifically refers to the realization of the fruit (*phala-sākṣātkriyā*).

The "pervasion" (*sāmānya*) is its height, and the "limitation" (*viśeṣa*) is its extreme. The three characters specifically cited as "meaning" (*artha*) are precisely what marks the ultimate primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Regarding "adorned Bodhisattvas" and so forth, the subsequent text establishes the thesis by exclusively taking the fruit;
here, "Bodhisattva" refers to one who has realized the fruit. Since they are able to adorn profound and wondrous merits, they are indeed the fruit.
The four virtues represent the ultimate pinnacle of profundity and subtlety. Although the words are associated with causes, the intent lies precisely in the fruits.

Regarding the phrase "illuminating all the heavens," it means that when the light of the *dharmatā* illuminates all the devas and spirits—none of whom are anything other than great Bodhisattvas—their progress on the Path will necessarily increase.

Therefore, the minds of those of great transformative power (*mahopāya*) give rise to Dharma-joy. This reveals the power and function of the Sūtra as both vast and profound; thus, the text is titled the "King of Sūtras."

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the many passages in this section that describe the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* as the king of all sutras. Because a king has the power to govern and command, this teaching subsumes all other scriptures.
However, the commentary explains that the "king of sutras" is the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), formed by the union of principle (*artha*) and text (*vyañjana*).

Furthermore, this sutra is a king among the nine types of sutras, attaining mastery over them; the text is the means of expression (*vyañjaka*), while the principle is that which is expressed (*vyaṅgya*).

Because the principles and the text are harmonized, the subject and object mutually merge; whether it be the teaching (*dharma*) or the principle (*artha*), both are termed the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). All are the Kings of Sutras (*sūtra-rāja*).

The commentary uses "King of Sutras" to describe the essence, which is precisely that which is expounded—the Middle Way. If it were not the Middle Way, the teaching could not expound the Middle Way principle.
Be careful not to provide a biased interpretation by using the name of the expounded [Middle Way] to designate the teaching that expounds it as the "Middle Way Teaching. △ Second.
To summarize and demonstrate what is worthy of veneration:
it is named "Noble" alone; its essence is "Supreme" alone; its tenet is "Profound" alone; its function is "Great" alone; and its teaching is "Kingly" alone.
Because it takes "Gold" as its name, it is noble; because it takes the principle of the fruit as its essence, it is the ultimate consummation of the three bodies (*trikāya*);
because its doctrine is profound, there is nothing it does not benefit; and because its function is great, the characters are identical with the Middle Way.
Therefore, each of the five chapters is lofty and vast. △ Third, the explanation of its venerability: how all sages protect and uphold it. Part one: protection by the ultimate fruit.
Therefore, the essence of non-duality is constantly sustained by the four World-Honored Buddhas; it is likewise so throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions.
That which is expressed as the "wondrous middle" wherein all phenomena converge is called the essence of non-duality, and all Tathāgatas have realized this essence.
Therefore, by relying upon this, it is maintained and constantly protected so that the eight inversions do not arise in sentient beings.

Because the sutra represents the four wisdoms, it mentions the four Buddhas; yet in reality, this essence has no Buddha who does not protect it, which is why it says that the same applies throughout the three periods of time and the ten directions.
Thus, the subsequent sutra states: "The Buddhas of the ten directions should keep this sutra in mind. △ Second.
The Great Powerful One reveres it;
all Bodhisattvas from throughout the other directions pay distant homage to the Tree Deity, the Good Woman, shedding tears as they offer praise.
The devas cover it with celestial majesty, the earth deities moisten it with terrestrial fertility, and Great Eloquence bestows upon it eloquence.
The merit of the Way is augmented by wealth and treasures.

Regarding the passage "All bodhisattvas, etc.," the Chapter Praising the Buddha states: "At that time, an immeasurable hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions of assemblies of bodhisattvas departed from this world and arrived at the land of the Tathāgata Golden Jewel Canopy Mountain King."
In that land, they have already prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground to pay homage to the Buddha; joining their palms toward the Buddha, they praise him with one voice.
The commentary states: "The assembly of those offering praise is set forth as being in that land; therefore, it says 'pervading the other directions.
As for 'paying remote homage to the tree deity and the virtuous daughter,' this is also from the text of this chapter, the verses of praise by the Bodhi-tree deity."
The middle section states: "I constantly practice the supreme great compassion, weeping and shedding tears as I desire to see the Buddha;

the devas cover me," and so forth. This is explained in detail in the *Caturmahārājakāyika-parivarta* and the *Samantabhadra-vidyādhara-parivarta*, which state that through their supernatural powers, they always protect those who preach and listen, as well as the kings and the territories of their lands, including the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā.
In the "Chapter on Mahāprajñāpāramitā-devī" and the "Chapter on Śrī-devī," the benefits for those who practice according to this sutra are extensively elucidated within each chapter.
These bodhisattvas and celestial deities are mostly former Buddhas who have returned, or perhaps partial manifestations sent down to respond;
they pay distant homage and extol the merits of the Tathāgata, protecting and benefiting both those who preach and those who listen.
All [these teachings] are for the purpose of revering the King of Sutras and circulating the Vaipulya; if the Dharma-gate were not supremely wondrous, how could it provide such assistance?
△ Fourth, it clarifies that because it is preached, its benefits are comprehensive and vast.

All realms of existence are completely parched, and the three miserable paths are cleared of their feverish afflictions; to state the essential point, all unprecedented events in the entire world have appeared.
Regarding "all realms of existence are completely parched," the Chapter on Repentance states: "Within the three realms of existence, the great ocean of birth and death is a turbulent flood."
The waves of water agitate and disturb my mind; its flavor is bitter and poisonous, most coarse and astringent.
The Tathāgata’s Net-Luminosity can cause it to dry up, for it prevents one from emerging within the three realms of existence—desire, form, and formlessness.

Regarding the removal of the heat and affliction of the three miserable paths, the Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings states: "This sutra can cause the various rivers of the hells, animals, and hungry ghosts [to dry up]."
Regarding the phrase "withered, parched, and exhausted; to summarize the essentials," the *Ayuṣpramāṇa-parivarta* states:
"At that time, all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, received celestial bliss; those with impaired faculties immediately attained their restoration.
To summarize the essentials: all beneficial and unprecedented matters throughout every world were likewise realized."

The *Jùchūxiànshuō jīng* (Sutra on the Manifestation of Appearances) not only explains the benefits of [this teaching] exhaustively and its ability to eliminate the retributive sufferings of the three miserable realms and all states of existence, but it should also clarify how one may depart from suffering and attain happiness through twenty-five cycles across the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).

Only when this can cause the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* to manifest ultimately is it considered a complete discourse on the signs of the manifestation of unprecedented events. △ Second, the narrative of the proclamation.

The general meaning elucidated above—how the Tathāgata established his teachings by responding to conditions from the principle of primordial quiescence—all describes the intent behind the Tathāgata’s preaching of the sūtra.
Now, this is the Master Chih-i’s own account of how he employs his intellectual power to grasp the meaning and explain the title, manifesting the significance according to the text;
this constitutes the general intent for interpreting the sūtra. This section is divided into four parts, the first of which is the Sage’s praise and protection.

For this reason, the World-Honored King Golden Dragon (Suvarṇaprabhāsa-rāja) has praised the Earth Deity throughout the three periods of time, and she has made a vow to protect those who preach [this sutra].
Having intended to begin the discourse, he first reflects upon the supreme sages who have praised it incessantly and protected the Dharma without weariness;
thus, the aspiration for the holy has a long-standing tradition. As for the "Praise by the Golden Dragon throughout the Three Periods," it refers to the Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa in a past life.
As a king named King Golden Dragon (Suvarṇanāga), he extensively expounded the chapters and verses and praised all Buddhas, vowing that in the future he would encounter Śākyamuni Buddha.

Now his vow has been fulfilled; thus, within this assembly, he praises the Buddha with verses. King Golden Dragon was one who praised the Bodhisattva Faith and Appearance (Śraddhālakṣaṇa) in the past, and he is one who praises him in the present; furthermore, he made a vow that there shall be no [future] [separation].
For incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, in every place of birth, he has seen golden drums in his dreams at night and recounted them as they truly were during the day;
this is precisely the praise of the future [Buddha]. This is the praise of that one person throughout the three periods of time. Question:

Since the Golden Dragon was praised throughout the three periods of time for the Buddha, how can it be compared to the proclamation of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, given that the persons and the Dharma are different? How can these two be reconciled? Answer: By grasping [the essence].
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* is the unsurpassed true Dharma as its fruit; the Buddha is the unsurpassed provisional person.
There is no person apart from the Dharma, and no Dharma apart from the person. These words in praise of the Buddha proclaim the subtle and wondrous mind-and-form;
this mind-and-form is precisely the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*. Just as the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa took refuge in the Triple Gem out of great compassion for the salvation of the world.
This refers to the Buddha taking that physical body as the Dharma; to praise the Buddha in this way is precisely to extol the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* in its essential nature.

Regarding the Earth Goddess and others: in that chapter, she addresses the Buddha with firm resolve, saying, "Wherever this sutra is circulated, you should prepare a lion throne and have the speaker of the Dharma sit upon it to widely proclaim this [teaching]."
I shall always serve as his attendant while remaining within the assembly, concealing my form beneath the Dharma seat, and supporting his feet upon my head;
this is because the Sage honors the Dharma and thereby respects persons. △ Second, the general rules for a teacher.
If even the supreme sages were thus, how much more so ordinary people?

If two such sages, having attained profound realization, still extolled [the teaching] throughout kalpas and humbled themselves to venerate and protect it, how much more so those of the lower rank among external ordinary beings who receive the Dharma and exert themselves in its practice—would they not propagate and proclaim it? △ Third, the arising of speech based on the meaning.
Daring to entrust myself to this principle, I wish to speak forthwith.
Entrusting myself to the meaning of the various sages who protect the Dharma, I shall set forth five chapters of discourse that accord with the sutras.
△ Fourth, invoking the Dharma to seek benefit.
A drop of dew entering the sea and birds heading toward a mountain truly rely upon a slight condition to share equally in the salty color [of the sea].

The drop of dew and the birds are metaphors for the goodness of one who penetrates the Sūtras; entering the sea and heading toward the mountain are metaphors for this goodness conforming to the nature [of reality].
"Truly relying upon a slight condition" refers to the aforementioned metaphorical goodness; "sharing equally in the salty color" refers to the benefit now hoped for.
This means that even a tiny drop of dew-like minor merit is wished to share the single salty flavor of the ocean of the same nature;
even a fragmentary condition involving birds is wished to share the wondrous color of a single Buddha-body. It is said that Mount Sumeru is composed of four treasures:

gold in the east, silver in the west, lapis lazuli in the south, and crystal in the north. Birds dwelling near these places all take on the same color as their surroundings. Yet, with a single thought—
To rejoice in [the merit of] those such as Shanggong who have circulated [this text] for five grades as vast as space is indeed a virtue comparable to a drop of dew;

it is specifically because the Great Master, looking from the mundane toward the sagely, humbled himself and revered the Sūtra, intending to admonish future generations not to boast of their own achievements.
△ Second, the Explanation of the Profound Meaning (Xuanyi) in two parts: first, listing the chapters and providing the structural outline.
In explaining this sutra, the main body is divided into two parts: first, the explanation of the title; second, the explanation of the text. The explanation of the title consists of five sections:

first, the explanation of the name; second, the discernment of the essence; third, the clarification of the primary tenet; fourth, the discussion of its function; and fifth, the analysis of its doctrinal characteristics. These five chapters are further divided into two parts:
first, a general explanation; second, a detailed explanation. The general explanation, in turn, has two sections: first, the sequential origination; second, the differentiation.
The initial explanation of the title constitutes the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), while the second explanation of the text constitutes the *Wenju* (Textual Commentary).

Since this fascicle is titled simply "Profound Meaning," its structural outline follows that convention; therefore, it does not list the two segments of "Explanation of the Title" and "Explanation of the Text.

Now, as for the listing of the chapter headings and the structural analysis (*kepan*), what prevents us from judging the subsequent *Wenju* as the "Explanation of the Text" and this current *Xuanyi* as the "Explanation of the Title"?

In the explanation of the title, five chapters are first listed as the subject matter to be explained; these five chapters are then treated through two types of exegesis, namely the "comprehensive" and the "detailed.

Since both of these exegeses explain all five chapters, [the text proceeds]. II. Exegesis according to the topical outline (kē) has two parts: A. The comprehensive exegesis. This has two sub-sections: 1.
The arising [of the teaching]; 2. The discernment [of its distinctions]. If one were to provide a comprehensive exegesis at length, it would be as follows: [as in the Dharma...]
Huai-xuan provides a general commentary on the five chapters through seven sections: first, he sets forth the headings to facilitate memorization and arouse the mind of mindfulness;
second, he cites evidence from the Buddha’s words to inspire the mind of faith; third, he establishes the sequence to prevent confusion and arouse the mind of concentration;
fourth, fifth, and sixth, he analyzes the combinations and distinctions, and reconciles differences, to arouse the mind of wisdom; seventh, he contemplates the mind.

Because one hears [the teaching] and immediately practices it by giving rise to a mind of diligence, the present text is abbreviated and provides only two cycles, merely generating two types of minds:
the generation of concentration and the differentiation of the generation of wisdom. Whether concentration or wisdom is established, all practices are thereby accomplished.
Of these two, the first is the generation [of concentration].

Regarding the "arising": in this Sahā world, vocal sound constitutes the Buddha-work. Sometimes one first hears the name from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), or sometimes one hears the name from within the scriptures;
therefore, "hearing the name" is placed first. Because of hearing the name, one next recognizes the essence of the Dharma;

once that essence is manifested, one next practices the practice, which is the "principle" (*zong*). When the principle is established, it possesses power, and power is precisely the "function" (*yòng*). This function is able to...

To benefit beings and, by benefiting beings, to teach others so they may hear [the Dharma]: this is the beginning of one’s own practice. To bestow the teaching is the commencement of transforming others.
Only the Sage possesses both the beginning and the end—such is the sequence of the arising of the five chapters.
That which is designated as "first" refers to the capacity for signification; therefore, names are conventional designations that must necessarily rely upon real dharmas, namely sound.

It is through the modulation of sound that names and phrases are formed. Since one infers the conventional by means of the real, this treatise maintains that in this land, the Buddha’s work is accomplished through vocal sound.
However, if the name is derived from the Buddha or a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), it is based on sound; if the name is derived from a scriptural volume, it is based on the written word.
Although it is based on form (*rūpa*), because that form is a collection of the sounds of the teachings, it is also called "hearing the name" (*nāmadheya-śravaṇa*) from the scriptural scrolls;
this refers to the initial reception of names and phrases during one's own practice (*svacaryā*). As for the body [of the teaching] being second:

the name is the signifier (*vācaka*), like a finger pointing at the moon; the body is the signified (*vācya*), like the moon pointed out by the finger. If one loses the intended meaning, one clings to the finger as being the moon.

If one is merely deluded about the moon, one will also lose sight of the finger; yet if one attains the meaning, one forgets the name. Having attained the essence, one does not remain ignorant of the name.

Since this treatise aims at attaining the meaning, it says: "Because of hearing the name, one next recognizes the essence of the Dharma. As for the third section, "The Thesis" (*zong*), the thesis is precisely practice (*xing*).
Practice is that which enables progress and advancement from cause to fruit; if one does not recognize the essence, then [practice] will not be accomplished.

Practicing this teaching still accords with the previous three teachings; even when one realizes the Middle Truth and cultivates contemplation by taking that principle as an object, it may be called the "practice of manifesting the essence" (*tixian cixing*).
Now, we clarify the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*), in which cultivation arises entirely from nature (*xing*). If one does not recognize nature, what could serve as cultivation?
Nature is original enlightenment (*benjue*), and cultivation is initial enlightenment (*shijue*). Original enlightenment is without thought and pervades all places.
Since this very awakening constitutes initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*), the inconceivable realm is itself the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) that contemplates it;

only then is it the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*). Thus, one knows that while the manifestation of the essence is brief in its phrasing, the subsequent section on function is expansive in its expression yet concise in its meaning; one must skillfully understand this.

Fourth, regarding "function," it is because the teaching is established that there is then powerful function. To say "the teaching is established" means that the manifestation of the essence has been completed.
The Essence gives rise to the Principle, and the Principle in turn reveals the Essence; the Perfect Mirror emits light, and the light in turn reveals the mirror.
Once the mirror has been revealed, the manifestation of images leaves nothing out. Therefore, when the Principle is established, it is able to universally benefit all things.

Since the Teaching follows, its function is to benefit all things. The method for benefiting all things lies in the imparting of instruction; thus, the Teaching consists of the five aspects: hearing the name and so forth.
However, both "Name" (míng) and "Teaching" (jiào) are capable of explicating principle; these are divided into two chapters based on the distinction between self and others.

The chapter on "Name" begins with the initial reception [of the teaching] for one's own practice, while the chapter on "Teaching" begins with the first bestowal for the transformation of others. Regarding the phrase "having a beginning and an end," this refers to the beginning and end of the two [processes]:

seeking the essence through the name and the establishment of the function through the completion of the school—this constitutes the beginning and end of one's own practice. As for "bestowal," it refers to the initial application.
Instructing and benefiting others, they in turn seek out names and even give rise to practice; thus, from beginning to end, the process is complete.
Therefore, one knows that within the five chapters there are two beginnings and two ends. The text mentions two beginnings to manifest the two ends. △ Second, the discrimination [of the two], first:
the preliminary analysis, third: the posing of the question.

Regarding the term "distinguishing" (*jianbie*): "distinguishing" here means to examine and analyze. Question: If it were abbreviated, there would be only one; if it were expanded, it would be immeasurable.
Now, these five chapters are neither expansive nor do they constitute a mere abbreviation. For what reason are there exactly five?
This establishes the opening question by means of the extreme brevity and the extreme extensiveness, thereby introducing the response situated between them.

△ Second, the general response: The answer is neither brief nor extensive. Because it is not brief, it is not a single [point]; because it is not extensive, it is not manifold. Extensiveness causes wisdom to regress;
brevity results in the meaning being incomplete. I shall now speak from the middle way so that the meaning is easy to understand and clarify.
If the number of titles and sections is too extensive, it will be difficult to memorize and maintain, causing those who practice contemplation to retreat when they see the limit;
if the chapters and segments are too brief, the revealed meanings will not be comprehensive, preventing those who study the teachings from generating understanding.

Therefore, five chapters are established so that the abundance and brevity are balanced, enabling the practitioner to achieve both the meaning and the contemplation, and making it easy to clarify the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
[The preceding section] is concluded. △ Third, the summary and indication.
Within the five chapters, the meaning is as follows.
△ Second, the detailed analysis. Part one: the formal analysis. Part one: [the analysis] based on the six types.

"Distinct" (*bie*) means differentiation. The preceding chapter [on the "Manifestation of the Essence"] takes the three characters as a whole to form a title, while the following three chapters take the three characters individually to establish distinctions;
the final chapter combines both the general and the specific to clarify the characteristics of the teaching.

Furthermore, the chapter on the Manifestation of the Essence clarifies principle (*li*), while the remaining four chapters clarify phenomena (*shi*). Moreover, the first three chapters concern the cause (*yin*), while the latter two chapters concern the fruit (*guo*). Furthermore, the preceding...

The first four chapters concern practice, while the final chapter concerns teaching; furthermore, the first four chapters concern practice for one's own benefit, while the final chapter concerns practice for the benefit of others;
moreover, the first four chapters concern noble silence, while the final chapter concerns the noble proclamation of the Dharma.

This refers to the five chapters consisting of six pairs of distinctions: general and specific, principle and phenomenon, cause and effect, teaching and practice, self and other, and speech and silence.

Regarding "general and specific": the preceding chapter is the explanation of the title; the three characters "Jin-guang-ming" (Golden Light) taken as a whole constitute the designating name (*nāman*).
These three characters represent the essence (*svabhāva*), the doctrine (*artha*), and the function (*karman*). Taking these three characters separately, "Jin" (Gold) is used because—

"Distinct" refers to the essence (*tattva*) by means of its radiance; "distinct" refers to the doctrine (*siddhānta*) by means of its illumination; and "distinct" refers to the function (*vṛtti*). Therefore, it is called "distinct.

The subsequent chapter is the "characteristics of the teachings" (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*). That which encompasses both the general and the distinct is the "characteristics of the flavor of the teachings" (*śāsana-rasa-lakṣaṇa*) within the four chapters that distinguish the general and the distinct.
Next, regarding "principle and phenomena": "essence" (*tattva*) is the principle revealed by these four chapters. Fourth...
The "Chapter" (*zhāng*) refers to the phenomena arising from the essence (*tǐ*). Regarding the three causes and two effects: the former three are causes and the latter two are effects;

this is based on the subsequent clarification that the thesis (*zōng*) definitely resides in the effect. It would be more appropriate to say that the former two are causes and the latter three are effects, for fear that the text may be erroneous.
However, the essence itself is neither cause nor effect, but rather the principle manifested by cause and effect; by seeking it through its name, one attains it.

The essence (*tǐ*) is still the principle revealed through faith and understanding within the causes; it is not yet the principle revealed as the fruit of the established thesis (*zōng*). Therefore, it is categorized under the "causes.
The four preceding aspects of the Four Teachings pertain to practice (*xíng*), because they are the practices applied by practitioners toward the subsequent teachings.

Why is this? First, the name refers to the dharma of practice; second, the essence is the root of practice; third, the thesis is the fruit of practice; fourth, the function is the virtue of practice. Fifth, [the essence].
Furthermore, he names all five chapters "Practice" (*caryā*) and divides them such that the first four belong to the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*).

Although those belonging to self-benefit involve the application of mastery (*vaśitā*), they are categorized as self-benefit because their causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*) are manifested [for that purpose].

Only the final chapter on teaching belongs to the benefit of others (*parārtha*). They are all called "practice" because both types of benefit are performed through them. Sixth, the explanation of silence.
Since the first four chapters concern one's own practice, which requires the complete forgetting of words, they all belong to silence;

the final chapter concerns transforming others by establishing teachings according to their capacities, and thus it belongs to speech. Both are called "sacred" because seeing beyond speech and silence is the dharma of the Sage.
△ Second, applying this principle to other meanings.

Through such various forms of analytical discernment, all other meanings—such as those concerning the six categories, understanding and practice (*adhimukti-pratipatti*), cultivation and realization (*bhāvanā-sākṣātkriyā*), bondage and liberation (*bandhana-mokṣa*), essence and function (*tattva-vṛtti*), and response and resonance (*yinggan*)—may likewise be analyzed according to the characteristics of the five chapters;
however, to avoid prolixity, they are here abbreviated. △ Second, manifesting [the meaning] by means of analogies, part one.
Establishing the analogy:

Now, within this illustration, it is clearly shown that [the treasury] contains great wealth, like jewels within a bag; yet if one does not reach in and show them to others, no one will know of their existence.
All of these serve as analogies for the purpose of analytical discrimination.

"Manifesting" (*xian*) means "to reveal" (*shi*). "The middle" (*zhongdang*) refers to the five chapters. "Clearly encompassing the richness" (*fenming baofu*) refers to the virtues of both the Dharma and its metaphors.
"Encompassing the richness" is like having jewels within a bag; "clearly manifesting" is like reaching in to show them to others. Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Explaining the Buddha’s sutras is like having jewels in a bag—if the mouth is tied shut, people will not know [what is inside]; one should therefore explain the Buddha’s teachings."

The *Sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* explains its underlying principles; here, too, this same analogy is employed to illustrate six pairs, which is why it is said that "all are provided as analogies for analysis. △ Second, the synthesis of the six types.
The "jewel within the bag" serves as a metaphor for the general three characters; "probing it to show others" serves as a metaphor for the specific three characters.
"The jewel within the bag" serves as a metaphor for the principle (*li*) in one chapter; "probing it to show others" serves as a metaphor for the clarification of affairs (*shi*) in another chapter.
The remaining examples may be understood by analogy in this manner.

The general within the particular, the particular within the general, their mutual correspondence, and the analogy of what can be seen—these four chapters fully establish the principle, like a bag containing jewels.

To establish the principle in its entirety is like showing the jewels to a person by reaching into the bag; to possess the fruit-virtue based on the cause is like the jewels being revealed from the bag due to the cause;

to manifest the fruit through the cause is like reaching into the bag to show the jewels; and to apply the aggregates of practice to the teaching is like the teaching explaining the practice, as if the jewels were within the bag.
To discover and show the method for benefiting others, one must necessarily practice it oneself; it is like discovering a treasure in one's own bag and then using that treasure to benefit others.
To discover and show it while remaining silent and attaining perfect realization is like having a treasure in one's bag but not speaking of it after realizing it.

To discover and show it through teaching is like discovering a treasure and then speaking of it. These analogies apply not only to these six pairs, but to all [the stages] alike. △ Second, the detailed explanation of the above.
Since all [five] chapters are comprehensively explained [in this section], it is called the "General Explanation" (*sōshaku*). Now, however, the five chapters are explained one by one.

When explaining the "Explanation of Names" (*shimei*), the other four types of explanation are not mentioned; since this is the case for all four, they shall be explained separately. The main body is divided into five parts. First is the "Explanation of Names.
"Name" (*myō*) refers to the terminology listed throughout the entire work; here, we present it collectively by taking the title as the name.
This itself constitutes two parts: namely, the general and the specific. The single character "sūtra" (經) is the general name, as it applies universally to all sections [of the canon].
The three characters "Jin" (金), etc., are the specific name, as they specifically title this particular sūtra.

When our school explains the titles of various sūtras, we simply divide them into these two categories—the general and the specific—and do not claim that the word "sūtra" is the expressive designation (*vācaka*) for the meaning.
Regarding this subject matter, those who receive the teachings of the Mountain School must first understand the initial explanation of the specific names.

Second, as for the detailed explanation, there are five chapters; now, we shall first explain the chapter on "Names. If one follows the title of the four-fascicle version: [The text proceeds with the structural outline. *Note: This passage serves as a structural introduction to a commentary on a Buddhist treatise, likely concerning the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* or a related work associated with the Tiantai (Mount Tiantai) tradition.*
It simply uses the three characters [Jin-guang-ming] and lacks the two characters "Emperor" (Dì-wáng). If one follows the meaning of the sūtra text, there is the sense of being the "King of Sūtras";
whether these words are spoken or not, neither is problematic.
Since the current four-fascicle version is a translation by Dharmakṣema, it is distinguished solely by the title of the three characters "Jin-guang-ming."

Regarding the two characters "Emperor-King" (帝王) in the title: if one refers to the seven-fascicle version translated by Paramārtha, the title includes the characters "Emperor-King" following the words "Suvarṇaprabhāsa.
Although these words "Emperor-King" do not appear in the title of this present edition, they are nonetheless implied within the meaning of the scripture as the "King of Sutras" (*sūtrarāja*).
Therefore, as for whether or not to include these two characters in the explanation of the title, it depends on the context.

There is no contradiction in explaining these two approaches; furthermore, it should be understood that when the Great Master frequently proclaimed this scripture, the inclusion or omission of the monarch’s name during the interpretation of the title was adjusted according to the occasion, which is why the profound text inherently exists in both expanded and abbreviated forms. II.

Interpretation based on the sequence of the text’s meaning, divided into two parts: A. First, interpreting the first two characters based on the text. 1. Interpreting them according to the doctrinal meaning, namely:

Regarding the two aspects of teaching and the elucidation of meaning and principle, the second is explained in terms of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*): that is, the accomplishment of practice through the cultivation of contemplation.

This is because this school clarifies both doctrine and practice, and presents both meaning and contemplation together, desiring that those who receive the teachings achieve success in both understanding and practice. The first two [sections] initially set forth and enumerate [the categories].

Now, the explanation of the name consists of five parts: (1) the general and specific [categories], (2) the translation, (3) the analogy, (4) the exegesis according to the text, and (5) the exegesis of the essential nature.

Among these five, the first two include both general and specific titles, while the latter three are exclusively specific names. Of these three, the first two are established in accordance with ancient tradition.

Regarding the latter two [sections], which concern only the present meaning, within these two, the section on "Text and Principle" (*li-shi*) has the principle (*li*) existing independently of the text.

**2. The Main Explanation of the Five [Categories]** **A. General and Specific** **1. Distinguishing and Indicating the General and Specific** **a. A General Clarification of the Threefold General and Specific**

Regarding the terms "universal" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*): teachings possess both universal and particular aspects; based on these teachings, practice is clarified, and practice likewise possesses universal and particular aspects. From practice, principle is revealed, and principle also possesses universal and particular aspects.

This is because the Great Master’s profound understanding of these two names did not merely refer to the universal and particular teachings, but indeed referred to [the universal and particular aspects of practice and principle as well].
Because there are both general and specific aspects regarding both practice and principle, it is said that one clarifies practice based on the teachings;

since practice has general and specific aspects, and principle is manifested through practice, principle likewise has general and specific aspects. Thus, each of these three—practice, principle, and their combination—is twofold, and these names are invoked accordingly.

Therefore, among the various sections [of the canon], those that establish these two names solely from the perspective of principle are the *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* and others, which constitute the "Treasury" (garbha) section.

Regarding those scriptures that are common to both the wondrous conventional and the ultimate truth, yet establish two names based specifically on their practice—such as the *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* and others:
since the *Śūraṅgama* differs from the partial [Hīnayāna] samādhis, it is established as a sūtra of specific practice;

whereas those that are common to both, yet establish two names based solely on their teaching—such as the *Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching* and others: since the *Bequeathed Teaching* differs [from other teachings], [it is established as a sūtra of general practice].
The various teachings refer to the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra*), while the scriptures refer to the Shared Teaching (*sāmānyavyavahāra*).

Alternatively, "teaching" may be designated as the distinct name and "practice and principle" as the shared name, as in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* and other such texts; since these are teachings, the scriptures they expound constitute practice and principle.
Alternatively, "principle" may be designated as the distinct name and "teaching" as the shared name, as in the *Ratnakaraṇḍa-sūtra* and others, where it refers to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

This sutra is like a treasure chest containing both teaching and principle; how much more so for those other sections where principle itself constitutes the sutra, of which there are not a few examples.
This particular section states that the Buddhas of the ten directions constantly keep this sutra in mind;

the *Avataṃsaka* says that from within a single atom one brings forth a great scroll of scripture; and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says that this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* Dharma-treasury is profound, firm, and far-reaching.

"No one can reach it," and it is further said that by being protected and remembered by all Buddhas, planting the roots of myriad virtues, entering the stage of right determination (*samyaktva-niyāma*), and giving rise to the mind that seeks to save all sentient beings—one who accomplishes these four dharmas may obtain this sutra. The Commentary states:

"The four phrases are precisely the opening, showing, awakening, and entry into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). Is it not a sublime principle that one obtains the sutra through this knowledge and vision? Thus it is said.
Regarding the practice, the *Shorter Amitābha Sūtra* states: "The Buddhas extend their broad and long tongues and speak words of truth:
'You sentient beings, you should believe this discourse on the inconceivable merit that is protected and remembered by all Buddhas.
Since the sūtra points to merit as that which is protected and remembered, and since a sūtra is not itself a practice, [how can it be so? The Buddha himself...
Question: What is the meaning of the title *The Sūtra on Being Protected and Mindfully Kept by All Buddhas*? The Buddha himself explains:

"If good men or women hear this sūtra and receive and uphold it, and hear the names of the Buddhas, these people shall be protected and mindfully kept by all Buddhas and shall attain non-retrogression from unexcelled bodhi.
Thus, taking the *Sūtra on Being Protected and Mindfully Kept* as the subject of the question, one is able to practice.
If one asks whether it is not the case that practice constitutes the sūtra, the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states that when that Buddha speaks of practice, he always says he is "expounding the sūtra.
Thus, we know that the principle of practice is frequently designated as "sūtra" in various sources; it cannot be maintained that only the teaching (doctrine) is called a sūtra.
Since the sūtra fully possesses these three—teaching, practice, and principle—the distinct names for each possessing these three are clearly evident.
△ Second, the selection of two and the application of the teachings.
Setting aside for now the practice and principle, we shall clarify only the general and specific aspects of the teachings.

Regarding the three general and three specific [teachings], since our school’s commentaries on the titles of the various sections have already been exhaustive, we shall set those two aside and proceed with this.

The explanation clarifying the general and specific characteristics of the teaching is already sufficient to distinguish it from the interpretations of other schools regarding the title of the scripture. Why is this so?

It is because various masters take only the character *jīng* (sūtra) to be the "teaching as the expressive means" (*neng-quán jiào*), while regarding the remaining characters as the "principle as the expressed content" (*suǒ-quán lǐ*).
How could they know that both names reside within the teaching itself? △ Third, clarifying the functional efficacy of the teaching.
Now, principle has no names or words, yet names and words name the principle; it is like empty space, which has no measurements, yet measurements are applied to empty space.
As the *Tianwang Prajñā* Sūtra says: "Dhāraṇī has no characters, yet characters reveal dhāraṇī."

The two teachings—the general and the specific—are established in mutual dependence because they are able to express the principle (*tattva*). Question: Here it is said that "the principle has no names, while names name the principle.

This seems immediately contradictory to the *Dangti Zhang* (Chapter on the Essential Nature), which states that the True Truth (*satyā*) has names while the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti*) has no names.

How are these two views to be reconciled? Answer: That [text] distinguishes between the True and the Conventional; this [text] concerns names and principles. That [text] refers to the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya*), whereas this refers to the teaching as a means of expression. Thus, there is no contradiction.

The ultimate truth is explained as "named" because it is that which ordinary people perceive as conventional reality; since this ultimate truth is inherently endowed with its definitive names and meanings, it is said to be "named.

Because conventional reality lacks substantial meaning, it is said to be "nameless. Now, when both principle and teaching are discussed according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*), the statement that "principle has no names" serves to manifest its original quiescence, which is free from the marks of names and words. Conversely, when names and words are used to designate the principle, [it is understood as such].
It is not meant that the names attached by ordinary people to appearances are the true names of the Perfect Teaching;
rather, because the inherent qualities of the principle can respond to all names, every single name does not fail to name the principle. To take a metaphor from space:
though space has neither length nor shortness, it can respond to the measurements of length and shortness; thus, for every *zhang* and every *chi*, there is none that is not [space].

The "Chapter on the Non-substantiality of Space" states: "Since the existence of names in the ultimate truth is discussed from the perspective of perfect [teaching], it is not an existence that is definitively existent;
rather, it is a name for that which is nameless. Therefore, the 'existence of names' therein and the 'namelessness' here are identical in meaning.

The *Awakening of Faith* likewise clarifies the meaning of True Suchness (*tathatā*) by first explaining its transcendence of language and subsequently explaining its reliance upon language, thus distinguishing these two aspects.
Because there is only one True Suchness (*tathatā*), Jingxi said: "The nature is fundamentally nameless, yet it is fully endowed with all names.
Thus, we know that the present text is not at all inconsistent with the "Chapter on the Essential Substance" (*dangti zhang*). Furthermore, it cites the meaning of the *prajñā-pāramitā* dhāraṇī:
although there are no words, it is called a "dhāraṇī. If it did not fully possess the true meaning of names, how could it be called a profound dhāraṇī?
Seeing that existence and non-existence do not contradict each other in meaning. △ Fourth, the correct elucidation of the commonality and particularity of the teaching:
If one follows the words that manifest [the meaning], these names are common; if one follows the reasons by which they are manifested, these names are particular.
Although the function of the teaching was explained above, its general and specific natures have not yet been explicitly clarified.

Now, we take the written word (*vyañjana*) as the general nature of the teaching, while taking that which constitutes the teaching as its specific nature. Why is this? Whether it elucidates good or evil, or reveals the partial or the perfect, all employ the written word;
thus, the teaching is general. That which constitutes it is the capacity to express the intended meaning (*abhiprāya*); thus, it is specific.
Furthermore, words follow the shifts of the underlying intent (*abhiprāya*); because the intents differ, the teachings become distinct.

One should know that the universal (*sāmānya*) constitutes the particular (*viśeṣa*), for it employs words to express its meaning; yet the particular does not depart from the universal, as it uses words to convey that intent.
Since both the universal and the particular now reside within the teaching, both are capable of manifesting [the truth]. △

Second, the general and specific titles of the two sutras. First, a comprehensive presentation of all sections. Second, the actual application of the general and specific titles to explain the headings. First, the general. What is meant by "general"?
As the Sage has taught: a single sutra, a single time, a single location, a single section, a single verse, or a single phrase.
Every single word is composed of characters; from these characters, they are collectively designated as "sūtra.
The sacred teachings encompassing the entire era of oral instruction are none other than characters.

From "sūtra" down to a single "word," the term "one" (*eka*) is used to signify selecting one from among many—that is, selecting one sūtra from within the multitude of sūtras, or even selecting one from among a host of utterances.

To cite a single phrase and list them is to broaden the scope; to count them numerically, there are fewer at the beginning and more at the end—meaning the sūtras are few while the time [of their teaching] is many, even down to fewer phrases and more words. All such instances are the teachings of the Sage;

since his teaching necessarily consists of written characters, one knows that written characters constitute the universal essence of the teaching. Because these characters are universal, they are collectively termed "sūtra. △ Second, the specific classification (divided into two parts). First:
Clarifying the distinct characteristics.
What are these distinct [characteristics]? There are four: first, to prevent confusion regarding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and to bring joy and delight to the ears;

second, to adapt to what is appropriate for conversion and to develop past roots of goodness; third, to confront karmic obstructions so that evil is extinguished and transgressions removed; fourth, to provide clear instruction.
The principle suddenly dawned upon him as a wondrous realization;

he was thus able to manifest the underlying reason for this. Although the words and phrases spoken by the Sage are manifold, their intended meanings are fully encompassed within the four *siddhāntas*, leaving no meaning unexhausted.
The *loka-siddhānta* ensures that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) remains undisturbed, just as the *Avataṃsaka* differs from the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā*.

The *Vaipulya* (fangdeng) differs from the *Prajñāpāramitā* because it causes one to rejoice; the *Puruṣasamvṛti-siddhānta* (human standpoint) differs in its expediency because it causes the arousal of wholesome roots;
the *Pratipakṣa-siddhānta* (remedial standpoint) is distinct because it destroys evil conditions and causes the extinction of transgressions;

and the *Paramārtha-siddhānta* (ultimate standpoint) is distinguished because it leads to wondrous awakening through the specific capacities for entering the principle. Therefore, it is said that the names and characteristics of the various sūtras differ. △

The two [categories of] "binding" (*bandhana*) and "harmonizing" (*siddhi*) correspond to the four *siddhāntas*. Because the reasons for delighting, harmonizing, confronting, and awakening differ respectively, they are termed "distinct.

It can be understood that delighting, harmonizing, confronting, and awakening are assigned to the four *siddhāntas*. If one explains a single sutra, it proceeds entirely from these four; thus, these four [apply to] that [sutra].

Since these four intentions are not the same, various sutras are designated as distinct based upon them. Second, using metaphors to clarify the universal and the particular, thereby establishing the teaching:
It is like salt and plum combined to produce various flavors, or the interlacing of warp and woof to form various patterns and embroideries.
The salt and the plum—saltiness and acidity—are used as metaphors for the commonality and distinctions among the warp and woof of the sutras;
the flavors and the embroidery are used as metaphors for the differences between the names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) of the various sutras. △ Second, the twofold judgment of this sutra:
first, the explanation.
Because it distinguishes itself from others, there are the three characters "Jin-guang-ming" (Golden Light) to mark how this teaching differs from all other teachings;
because it follows the common terminology of the language, there is the single character "jing" (sūtra), which is the general designation for all scriptures.
