Regarding the phrase "from the distinct reasons," etc., this separately clarifies the fourfold *siddhi* (purposes) of the present sutra:

there are those with the capacity of the *loka* (worldly) type who, upon hearing [of the Buddha], rejoice in and praise the permanence of the three bodies; there are those with the capacity of the *puruṣakāra* (human effort) type who, being suited to hearing the praise of the three bodies, give rise to wholesome roots;

there are those with the capacity for *pratipakṣa* (remedy) who are capable of practicing repentance to destroy the evils of the three obstructions; and there are those with the capacity for *paramārtha* (ultimate truth) who are fit for awakening.
Because the principle of the sphere of action of all Buddhas is distinguished from this specific intention, this sutra is taught;
although there are four *siddhāntas*, all derive benefit from the Dharma-gate of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, and thus three characters are cited to manifest the distinctiveness of its teaching.
Regarding the phrase "from the common verbal expressions," although the four *siddhāntas* differ from those of other sutras, each and every one of them necessarily requires written words.
The essence of the title-text permeates all sections; therefore, the character for "Sūtra" (經) is employed to indicate that the teaching is universal. △ Second, the conclusion:
Because this present sūtra combines both the universal and the specific, it is titled the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (金光明經).
△ Second, the translation.

Regarding the two translations, the Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated that if the foreign sounds were preserved in full, it should be called *Suvabhanapavapoyudatamaindracaryanasūtra*. Here, *suvabhan* means "gold."
*Bappa* means "light"; *udaya* means "shining"; *indra* means "emperor" (*di*); *rājan* means "king" (*wang*);
and *sūtra* means "scripture" (*jing*). Foreigners also refer to [the Buddha] as *buddha*, which does not exist here [in China].

Furthermore, when the two characters for "emperor-king" (*dì-wáng*) are abbreviated and only three characters remain, it is because the Han people prefer brevity, and the translators have thus economized on them.
It was simply translated as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*. The translations by other masters do not reach the level of detail found here.
Although the current title follows the version by Paramārtha, the title of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-rāja-sūtra* translated by Paramārtha is the most detailed;
therefore, the Great Master (Xuanzang) adopted it to establish the correspondence between the Chinese and Sanskrit titles, as discussed in the preceding text.
Regarding the title "Detailed and Concise Account of Emperors and Kings," it makes no difference whether one explains it or not. △ Third, the explanation by way of analogy:

If one follows the fourth section, the "Explanation Attached to the Text," which clarifies that the meaning of refuting analogies is remote and not the Buddha’s word, then one can verify that the "Explanation Attached to the Text" and the "Explanation of the Essential Nature" constitute the primary intent here; whereas the "Explanation by Way of Analogy" [is secondary].
Although the textual expressions are extensive, it appears that the ancient masters, despite employing analogies for their explanations, did not fully encompass the meaning expounded by this sutra;
consequently, the Great Master (Zhiyi) followed their use of analogies while ensuring they universally illustrated all the perfectly interfused dharma-gates.
Although these dharma-gates are revealed through analogy, they serve as a preliminary indication of the actual substance of the dharmas within the formal exegesis.
The various alternative names for the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* arise simply because the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*) possesses immeasurable virtues and thus has immeasurable names.
It is called the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*; it is also called the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Vimukti; it is also called the Dharma-, Sambhoga-, and Nirmāṇa-kāyas;

it is also called the Perfect, the Conditioned, and the Developing [Truths]; and even down to being called Suffering, Delusion, and Karma. This is because one encompasses all and all enters into one, as they are integrated within this single principle.
Having already explained this meaning through analogies, we now arrive at its actual substance. There are only three fixed characters; these are not mere metaphors but the Dharma itself.
Since the Dharma is necessarily all-pervasive and harmonious, it is non-dual and without distinction throughout all things.

However, if one can understand that "Golden Light" (*Suvarṇaprabhāsa*) is the name of one among these three dharmas, then one will comprehend the intent behind the title established for this sutra. This...

Regarding my own [explanation], there are two parts: first, the ancient masters’ interpretation; second, the enumeration school’s interpretation. Regarding the first, there are three sections: first, the narrative;

second, the Sautrāntikas (the "Old Scripturalists") use three characters as metaphors for the three virtues: gold represents the *dharmakāya*, light represents *prajñā*, and brilliance represents liberation (*vimukti*).

The "former masters of the sutras" refers to those who have long been lecturers on this sutra; they originally propagated the Sāṃkhya and Nyāya systems while concurrently lecturing on this sutra, using analogies to explain the title in relation to the Three Virtues (triguṇa). △ Second, the refutation.

If the Master says that the Sāṃkhya system only clarifies the two bodies—the true and the responsive—and that interpreting it as three bodies through these two explanations is inconvenient for the treatise;
yet if one were to adopt the scriptural text [of the *Mahāyāna-saṃparigraha-śāstra*], there is not a single passage therein that clarifies the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

If one were to provide a separate interpretation of its meaning, what meaning would remain uncomprehended such that one should specifically use it as a metaphor for the three virtues? Since this both contradicts your own treatise and fails to accord with the sūtras, it is not what we employ here.

Zhang’an recorded the meanings of Zhizhe, hence he says: "If the Great Master says [it], sometimes it is also called 'the Tiantai Master says,' or 'the present Master says. First, one refutes those who violate the fundamental tenets.

Since the original treatise establishes only two bodies, for what reason does the commentary on the sutra employ the three virtues? If one opens up the two bodies to explain the three virtues, then one's own school..."
Because it is undermined, it is said to be "inconvenient for the treatise. Next, [the author] refutes the claim that it contradicts the sūtras:

if one says that although the root treatise mentions only two bodies, three virtues must be employed in order to conform to the sūtra text, then where does the sūtra text explicitly state these three virtues?
If one says that although there is no explicit text in the sūtra, they must exist by inferring the meaning, then what would be impossible? They should possess all three.
How could the Dharma consist of only three virtues? Since this would contradict our fundamental treatise and fail to accord with the present sutra, it is not accepted.
△ Second, the followers of the *Dichilun* (Treatise on the Stages);

first, their exposition: The followers of the *Dichilun* say that upon the substance of gold there is an inherent capacity for luminosity, which serves as an analogy for how the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) arises from its essence.
Relying on the power of one's own prajñā and liberation, one should simply establish the two meanings of essence and function; there is no need to differentiate them from the perspective of light.

As for the "Dì rén" (Earth-person), he originally propagated the *Huáyán Shìdì lùn* (Treatise on the Ten Stages of the Avataṃsaka) and concurrently lectured on this sutra. This master’s interpretation of the title is as follows.
Condensing the three into two, although there is radiance and luminosity upon the golden substance, if one regards them in relation to the golden essence itself, they are both termed "function.
Furthermore, since it is determined that this function does not come from without, it is said to be "inherent.

By analogy, although *prajñā* (wisdom) and liberation are two distinct virtues, if one regards them in relation to the *dharmakāya*, they are both termed "function. These two virtues do not arise from cultivation.

Because it is established, it is said that [the title] exists inherently; this master explains the three characters of the current title solely through the two meanings of essence (*tǐ*) and function (*yòng*).
△ Second, the refutation:

If the Great Master says, "The *Dilun* fortunately clarifies the three Buddhas, and explaining the title through these three Buddhas is naturally convenient in meaning," yet he nonetheless discards them...

If the three bodies were derived from essence and function (*tǐyòng*), that would not accord with the intent of this treatise. Furthermore, both the new and old versions of the sutra texts equally speak of the three bodies and do not mention essence and function;
thus, it would also contradict our own treatise and fail to harmonize with the sutras. Whether one advances or retreats [in argument], there is no way out; therefore, this position is not accepted.
The treatise clarifies the three Buddhas because it explains the ancient sutra; thus, there are three Buddhas: first, Vairocana, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*);
second, Rocana, the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); and third, Śākyamuni, the Response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

This precisely accords with the meaning of the Dharma-body, Response-body, and Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) found in this sutra. If one were to use these three Buddhas as the title for this sutra, there would be three [versions].

Since the analogies employed in the text do not contradict the meaning of the sūtras and śāstras, it is said that [the author] has established the three bodies (*trikāya*) as the very nature of his own system.
If one were to claim that although the fundamental treatise speaks of the three buddhas, it must discuss their essence and function (*tattva-vṛtti*) in order to conform to this sūtra,
then in this new version of the sūtra, the chapter titles are explicitly established on the basis of the three bodies.

The three internal bodies are brilliantly manifest and can be enumerated. Although this chapter is omitted in the current and older editions, the names and meanings of the three bodies appear extensively throughout the sutra.
For instance, the "Chapter on the Four Heavenly Kings" states: "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space;

responding to things by manifesting forms is like the moon in water. Since the moon in the water is the *nirmāṇakāya* (the response body), how could there be no moon in the sky? [The moon in] the sky is the *dharmakāya*.
This is precisely the retribution-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), for it manifests the three bodies by means of two, due to the skillful discernment of the heavens.

Furthermore, as in the separate introduction, "The Tathāgata roams within the immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*": the Tathāgata Śākyamuni is the response-body (*saṃbhogakāya*); "roaming" necessarily refers to the wondrous wisdom of the reward-body;
and the profound and vast *dharmatā* is the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Moreover, in the Chapter on Repentance, it is said that "by striking a drum with a mallet, a great sound issues forth."

The sounding of the drum is the Dharmakāya; the striking of the mallet is the Saṃbhogakāya; and the emergence of sound is the Nirmāṇakāya. Thus, one knows that the names and meanings of the three bodies are not few.

How could there be any place where only the essence and function are mentioned? To do so would mean failing to accord with the sūtras when advancing and contradicting one’s own treatise when retreating;
therefore, this [interpretation] is also rejected.
*The Collected Edition of the Record of the Supplementary Exegesis on the Profound Meaning of the Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra*, Fascicle Upper-Upper and Fascicle Upper-Middle. △ Third:
Paramārtha personally translated this sūtra under the title *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-rāja-sūtra*, and he himself provided an analogy for it.
The explanation of this title is divided into two parts; the first part, consisting of three sections, provides an introduction. First is the enumeration.

The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha states that the three characters symbolize three sets of three dharmas: the first character symbolizes the three bodies (trikāya), the second symbolizes the three virtues (triguṇa), and the third symbolizes the three stages (trāvasthā).
Among the various masters, Paramārtha is somewhat superior, for he is able to use a single analogy to illustrate three dharma-gates, wherein each of these three dharmas is itself threefold.
Part Two: Explanation of the Three [Bodies]. First, the explanation of the three bodies (trikāya).
To use the three bodies as an analogy: the true reality of the golden substance represents the *dharmakāya*; the luminous function capable of illuminating represents the *saṃbhogakāya*;
and the clarity capable of universally benefiting represents the *nirmāṇakāya*.
In that sutra, although the names of the three bodies—*dharma*, *saṃbhoga*, and *nirmāṇa*—differ, their meaning is identical; this is the second [point regarding] the *saṃbhogakāya*.

(First tone) This body is the wondrous wisdom that accords with the Dharma; its meaning is the same as "retribution. Third, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) transforms according to the capacities of beings;
its meaning is the same as "response" (*yìng*). △ Second, the explanation of the three virtues.
Next, the analogy for the three virtues: gold has four meanings. First, its color does not change; second, its substance is unstained; third, it can be transformed without obstruction;
and fourth, it makes people wealthy. Gold is used as an analogy for the Dharma-body, which possesses the four virtues of permanence, purity, self, and bliss.

Light has one meaning: first, it can illuminate and discern; second, it can dispel darkness. This is used as an analogy for Prajñā, which illuminates objects and removes delusions. Clarity has two [meanings].

The meaning [of gold] has four aspects: first, being free from darkness; second, being vast and far-reaching; third, [acting as] a metaphor for liberation, wherein all burdens are forever exhausted and all有缘 (those with whom one has a karmic connection) are extensively benefited;

and fourth, [acting as] a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*, which is fully endowed with the four virtues. Each individual quality of the dharma is illustrated by these metaphors, their characteristics being clearly evident.
Furthermore, "light" possesses two meanings each, serving as metaphors for both *prajñā* and liberation, each possessing two virtues. "Light" refers to the removal of darkness.
The text states: "What is the distinction between 'clarity' (*prakāśa*) and 'the absence of darkness' (*tama-abhāva*)? Because light can destroy darkness, it is called 'dispelling darkness';

because it does not arise [again], it is called 'absence. Thus, dispelling darkness is used as a metaphor for Prajñā dispelling delusions; the absence of darkness is a metaphor for liberation (*vimukti*), where all burdens are forever exhausted.
Although this master was dim regarding the mutual inclusion of the three virtues (*triguṇa-sampad*), his application of these metaphors to the Dharma is not without merit.
Thus. △ Third, the explanation of the three stages.

Regarding the subsequent three stages: the stage of the primary cause (正因位) prior to the Way of Suchness is when the nature of gold already exists; the stage of the internal cause (了因位) within the Way of Suchness is when the essence is revealed through radiant fusion;
and the stage of the external cause (緣因位) subsequent to the Way of Suchness is when it is clearly free from blemish and impurity.

Furthermore, using three characters as metaphors for the correct [nature], the conditions, and the completion, the meaning of the text becomes clear when the three natures are correlated with these three positions.
△ Third, the selection and discrimination (*liao-jian*).
That school’s selection and discrimination states: "The Dharma-body is real, while the two bodies are not real; the Dharma-body possesses the four virtues, and the Prajñā..."

Liberation each possesses two qualities: the primary cause is that which is inherently possessed; the causal condition for its arising is that which is presently existing; and the causal condition for its manifestation is that which is yet to come.

To distinguish the three bodies: the *dharmakāya* is real because it is the fundamental nature (*prakṛti*); the other two bodies are not real because they are accomplished through cultivation. This is the distinction.

Regarding the three virtues: because the *dharmakāya* is the universal essence (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), it possesses four virtues; because the other two are specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), each possesses two virtues. To distinguish the three positions:

the direct cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) exists in the nature (*prakṛti*), and thus its original presence is realized; the causal condition (*upādāna-hetu*) is cultivated through realization, and thus its present existence is realized;

the conditional cause (*ālambana-hetu*) exists in the fruit (*phala*), and thus its future existence is realized. △ Second, refuting [other views] by explaining the meaning through the "True Truth" (*satyārtha*), citing the words of various masters.

Now, fearing that later students will fail to see their errors and instead cling to what is wrong as being right, I wish to clarify the present perfect and subtle discourse against those unreconciled meanings; therefore, the refutation in this text is somewhat extensive.
The text has two parts: first, the general refutation.
The Great Master [Zhiyi] stated that the threefold interpretation of the "three threes" (the ninefold classification) failed to clarify the meaning.
This is because that [interpretation] explains the current title by means of three sets of three dharmas; thus, the Great Master critiqued these three meanings as being uncomprehending:
first, the meaning of one cause and one fruit; second, the distinct and the perfect; and third, the meaning of the dharma-nature. Since these do not accord with the text, they are rejected.

Because there is discordance and lack of correspondence, it is said that they are "not fully understood" (avyakta). △ Second, the specific refutation has three parts: first, the presentation of the three errors:
(1) the failure of cause and effect to interpenetrate; (2) the discordance with the perfect and distinct; and (3) the lack of correspondence with the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*).

△ Second, the explanation of the three faults. First, the failure of cause and effect to correspond. Why do cause and effect fail to correspond? The three bodies and three virtues are originally names for perfection within the state of fruition; yet now they are divided and assigned such that the three virtues appear incomplete and deficient. Why is this? If the Dharma-body were prior to the Path, it would have to be a cause. If it were already the fruit, how could it be incomplete? If it were already complete, why would it require the subsequent cultivation of the Path? Furthermore, if the Dharma-body were originally the fruit, then the other two bodies would likewise be fruits, and there would be no distinction between cause and effect. This would mean that the Buddha-fruit is not attained through the practice of the Path, which contradicts the principle that the Path is cultivated to attain the fruit. Therefore, the Dharma-body cannot be established as the cause. If one insists that the Dharma-body is the cause, then the other two bodies must also be causes, and the three virtues must all be causes. If they are all causes, then the three bodies and three virtues are not the fruit, and the name "Buddha-fruit" would be meaningless. Thus, the Dharma-body cannot be established as the cause. If one insists that the Dharma-body is the fruit, then the other two bodies must also be fruits, and the three virtues must all be fruits. If they are all fruits, then the three bodies and three virtues are not the cause, and the name "Dharma-body" would be meaningless. Thus, the Dharma-body cannot be established as the fruit. Consequently, the Dharma-body cannot be established as either cause or fruit. If one insists that the Dharma-body is neither cause nor fruit, then the other two bodies must also be neither cause nor fruit, and the three virtues must also be neither cause nor fruit. If the aforementioned Dharma-body is the Dharma-body of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*), then it should not be the Dharma-body of fruition;
if it is the Dharma-body of inherent virtue, why would inherent virtue consist solely of the Dharma-body?

There should likewise be the wisdom (*prajñā*) of inherent virtue and the liberation (*vimukti*) of inherent virtue (and so forth). If one were to say that wisdom is that which exists within the path, [then it cannot be the Dharma-body of inherent virtue].
What kind of *prajñā* is this? If it is the *prajñā* that exists on the level of the fruit (*phala*), it should not be present within the path (*mārga*).

If it is the *prajñā* obtained by partial realization (*vibhāga-prāpti*), for what reason is there no "dharma-body obtained by partial realization" or "liberation obtained by partial realization"? (And so forth.

If liberation were to exist only after the path, then since all manner of virtues would be gathered after the path, why would there be liberation alone? Viewed from this perspective, cause and effect do not correspond.

Question: Regarding the True Dharma, why do you refute the position that it is divided into three causes corresponding to three stages, claiming that such a division leaves the Three Virtues incomplete and deficient?
Answer: All three dharmas are in fact a single triad of dharmas. Because they possess manifold virtues, they have manifold names.

Because they are eternal, blissful, self, and pure, they are called the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*). Because they are worthy of honor and respect, they are called the Three Jewels (*triratna*). It is not so.
Because they are unborn and unceasing, they are called the three nirvāṇas; because they are the gathering of all dharmas, they are called the three bodies (trikāya);
because they are the lineage of the Tathāgata, they are called the three causes; and because phenomena penetrate into principle, they are called the three paths.

Since the essence of these dharma-gates is fundamentally not distinct, the establishment of the three causes is itself the establishment of the three bodies and the three virtues. (The two preceding sections contain the commentary.)
The phrase "it is said" means that one should follow the Great Sūtra’s exposition on the mutual possession of the three perfect virtues (*triguṇa*).

Regarding the *dharmakāya*, it is stated directly as *dharmakāya* and not merely as *kāya*; the *dharmakāya* necessarily possesses *prajñā* and *vimukti*. Regarding *prajñā*, it is stated directly as *prajñā* and not merely as *jñāna*;
*prajñā* necessarily possesses *vimukti*. When the *dharmakāya* is scrutinized, it yields *vimukti*, which should be combined with the commentary (and so forth).

For the reasons stated above, this is briefly explained through direct interpretation: liberation is not liberation apart from the liberation that is necessarily endowed with the *dharmakāya* and *prajñā*.

Since these have been separately established, it would follow that each of the three positions possesses only a single virtue; thus, the cause would not encompass the fruit, and the fruit would not encompass the cause.
Therefore, it is said that they do not interpenetrate. △ Second, the discrepancy regarding the perfect and the partial.

Regarding those who deviate from the Perfect [Teaching], if one were to explain the Perfect Teaching, it is self-evident that the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) possesses permanence, bliss, self, and purity (nitya-sukha-ātman-śubha).
(And so forth. Since Prajñā and the Dharma-body are in mutual resonance, and the Dharma-body already possesses these four virtues, how could Prajñā not likewise possess them?

Liberation is so called because it is free from the bonds of the fruit; bliss is so called because it is free from the bonds of the cause; purity is so called because it is free from the bonds of both cause and fruit; and self is so called because it is neither cause nor fruit.

Because it is the fruit, it is eternally perfect; it is taught as being perfectly complete and without deficiency. Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), if one were to explain it separately according to this sutra:
the Sutra states that the *dharmakāya* is eternal and real; "real" refers to the quality of self (*ātman*). The purity of wisdom in the *saṃbhogakāya* is the quality of purity (*śubha*).
The purity of samādhi in the *nirmāṇakāya* is the quality of bliss (*sukha*). The Tripiṭaka masters teach that the *dharmakāya* alone [possesses these qualities].
Because each of the two bodies possesses the four virtues, and each virtue is itself composed of three qualities, both are inconsistent with the Perfect [Teaching] and distinct from it.
First, the characteristics of the four virtues of the Perfect and the Distinct are set forth, and only then are their inconsistencies and defects refuted. Regarding the four virtues of the Perfect:
the Dharma-body is the three virtues within the nature; because the Dharma-body is eternal and self, it is *prajñā* (wisdom), and thus it is pure liberation.

Therefore, these four are delighted in as being within the nature; they are designated as the Dharmakāya. When the nature fully gives rise to cultivation, the three wisdoms are necessarily accomplished.
Because wisdom is in profound accord with the qualities of the nature, it is designated as Prajñā-jñāna.

Because it accords with the nature, liberation responds to conditions; since it necessarily accomplishes the three liberations by arising from the fullness of the nature, the nature thus possesses all four.

The meaning of virtue arising from its function is designated simply as "liberation. Because the *prajñā* that accords with and is identical to the nature possesses the four [virtues] and its characteristics are easy to understand, they are not shown separately.

Liberation arises in response to capacities and accomplishes external functions; because its characteristics—possessing virtues identical to the nature—are difficult to understand, they are now shown separately.
Since the fruit is liberation from the two types of death and from this suffering, it is called the virtue of bliss.
Because one is liberated from these defilements by means of the five abodes, it is called the quality of purity (*śuddha-guṇa*).

Because its nature is eternally free from the two bonds and is thus sovereign, it is called the quality of self (*ātma-guṇa*). Delusion is the cause and death is the fruit; these are phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.

Since it is primordially liberated and not subject to such causes and fruits, it is called the quality of permanence (*nitya-guṇa*). Although these four qualities are explained in terms of being free from bondage, that bondage is fundamentally empty.

Therefore, while the four virtues are entirely identical [to those of the Buddha], the differentiation of the four virtues is established according to the three bodies (*trikāya*). The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) possesses two types of permanence, which is the virtue of permanence (*nityatā-guṇa*);
its reality is the virtue of self (*ātman-guṇa*), for it is only because the Dharma-body is firm and substantial that it possesses the meanings of sovereignty and mastery;

this is the true virtue of self. The Enjoyment-body (*saṃbhogakāya*) uses wisdom to illuminate and shatter the defilements of delusion, corresponding specifically to the virtue of purity (*śubhatā-guṇa*). The Transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*)... [is the virtue of bliss].
The *samādhi* of Śūraṅgama—the universal manifestation of the form-body (*rūpakāya*)—is called the "virtue of bliss" because it extracts suffering where there is no [conventional] pleasure;

this specifically pertains to the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*). Thus, the three bodies (*trikāya*) are now correlated with the four virtues (*catvāri guṇāni*). Herein, we clarify the four virtues of both the Perfect (*pūrṇa*) and the Distinct (*viśeṣa*) teachings.
This is because these two teachings generally do not differ in their sections. When people hear it said that the three bodies possess the four virtues, they lose the intended meaning.

To explain by means of separation and distinction is precisely the Separate Teaching (*pr̥thag-vinaya*). To explain by means of mutual inclusion and fulfillment for those who have attained the essential meaning is called the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-vinaya*).
One should know that each and every body is itself the Three Bodies; therefore, each and every body possesses the Four Virtues (*catvāro guṇāḥ*).
If the Three Bodies were not fused, the Four Virtues would be separate. Thus, one who skillfully expounds the Separate Teaching [must acknowledge] that it inherently possesses the Four Virtues.
Discussing the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), each [of the three teachings] possesses the four virtues; when the distinct is fused, it is the Perfect; when the Perfect is divided, it is the Distinct.

Having clarified these two teachings, one then refutes their contradictions: they contradict the Distinct because the four virtues common to them are not established; they contradict the Perfect because the individual four virtues of each are not established.
△ Third, they do not accord with the Dharma-nature (Faxing). The fact that the three dharmas do not change is what is called "nature" (xing). First.
All three dharmas each possess two aspects: cultivation and nature; one resides in nature, while the two modes of cultivation—contrary and compliant—both reside in nature.

One aspect of nature is fully present in both delusion and enlightenment, whereas the two aspects of cultivation pertain to them. Consequently, these three dharmas horizontally encompass the ten realms, including both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as form and mind, and vertically penetrate the three stages, the causes and effects of delusion and enlightenment. Therefore, the Sūtra calls them "immeasurable and profoundly deep dharmas."
Regarding its nature: if one speaks of this *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena), then within each of the three stages, all three are fully present, each one penetrating through to the others.

To speak of them as being "fully present" here is precisely to refute other [positions]. This itself constitutes four parts; first, citing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* to refute the [notion of] the Path.
Regarding that which does not accord with the *dharmatā*, let us cite one sutra: as stated in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, "The sentient beings are like Maitreya;
they are one and not two. Such is the *dharmakāya* of the nature-merit (*prakṛti-guṇa*). All sentient beings are the very mark of *bodhi*;
it cannot be further attained—this is the *prajñā* of the nature-merit. All sentient beings are the very mark of *nirvāṇa*; it cannot be further extinguished. This...
The nature-virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and liberation (*vimukti*) are likewise; how could these three meanings not constitute the stage prior to the path (*mārga-pūrva-avasthā*)?
How could there be only the gold without its radiance?
Based on these three passages, one may verify that the stage prior to the path does not consist of a single dharma alone; rather, one must understand that *bodhi* is [the fundamental reality].

The wisdom-virtue (*jñāna-guṇa*) reaches its fruition and only then realizes *nirvāṇa*; this is the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), which reaches its fruition through the total extinction of delusions.
Since the Sūtra clearly states that these cannot be obtained again nor extinguished again, they must be the fruition-virtues already inherent within the nature.
Is this not the "Golden Light" possessed prior to the Path? Others ask: how can a single gold be called the "Dharmatā"? △ Second, citing the *Avataṃsaka*.

In the *Yanjing poyi* (Commentary on the Subduing of Demons), it is further stated that the *Avataṃsaka* says: "At the very moment of first generating the mind [of enlightenment], one immediately attains perfect awakening. All bodies of wisdom are not realized through another;
the pure and wondrous Dharma-body is serene and responds to all things. This wondrous Dharma-body is the virtue of the Dharma-body, and the body of wisdom is..."
The Prajñā-quality corresponds to all things, which is precisely the Saṃbhogakāya; this is the quality of liberation.

These three bodies increase progressively at each stage (*bhūmi*), like the gradual waxing of the moon. How could it be that the beginning of the Path is merely the position of the causal state? Why, then, would there be only Prajñā within the causal state?

"One who first resolves their mind" refers to the stage of the Initial Resolve (*prathamacittotpāda-vihāra*). "Attaining perfect enlightenment immediately" means being able to manifest the eight phases of a Buddha.

This is the first position within the ten stages (*daśavihāra*) of the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*). Prior to entering these stages, one practices the Perfect Path in a comprehensive manner; upon ascending to the stages, the Perfect Path is fully manifested. This manifestation arises from the three aspects of the nature (*prakṛti*):
namely, the three bodies such as the Wisdom Body (*jñānakāya*), the three virtues, and all three dharmas. For now, let us consider them by way of the "one-three."

By refuting the True Truth (satyadharma), the middle stage of the Path is established; from the first dwelling (prathama-bhūmi) onwards until Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), all are termed the middle stage of the Path.
In this stage, the three dharmas gradually increase like the moon. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of it as perfect and round, calling it the immeasurable and profound Dharma-nature;
thus, both are realized simultaneously. To verify this by dividing it [into separate stages] is truly inappropriate. △
The meaning of the "three fingers" refutes [the view] after the Path;
that which follows the Path possesses the three virtues as explained above—this matter may be understood.
Regarding "possessing the three as explained above," the preceding text refuting the non-communication of cause and effect states: "The three bodies and the three virtues are the root."
This is the name for perfection regarding the fruit, yet here it is distributed among the three virtues [of liberation, wisdom, and power], which are incomplete and deficient.

Furthermore, since it is said that after the Path all manner of virtues converge extensively, how could there be only liberation? Because that interpretation contradicts itself, I shall not separately cite further scriptures.
△ Fourth, a general refutation based on the Perfect [Teaching].

If one knows that [the qualities] prior to the stage of perfect nature, the qualities of the path of perfection, and the ultimate qualities of the final perfection are all suddenly partitioned into separate locations as being merely singular, how can this be so?
According to the previously cited sūtras, since each stage is perfectly complete, how could they each be a single entity? △ Third, refutation by means of analogy.

Is this not to confine the numinous phoenix within a dove’s nest and turn the divine dragon back into a rabbit’s burrow? To humiliate the majestic power of its scales and feathers is surely not the perfect discourse on the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).

When the sutras speak of the nature of reality as immeasurable and profoundly deep—like the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra* (Golden Light)—it pervades horizontally and extends vertically; it is beyond all measure.
Lacking the requisite qualities, one occupies no station; lacking penetration, one does not attain mastery. This is like the majestic spirit of the phoenix or the divine wonders of the dragon.
As for what is explained by the True Dharma, if one’s virtue is incomplete and one’s position is obstructed, it is as if being cramped within a dove’s nest or circling within a rabbit’s burrow.
How could this not be a disgrace to the scales and fins of the Dragon Gate, or to the plumage and regalia of the Vermilion Cave? In both cases, there is no display of noble power.

The first three phrases of the preceding section are all metaphors, while the final phrase is the application to the Dharma; therefore, it is said that this is not a complete exposition of the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
△ Second, the Master’s present interpretation has six parts, the first of which is to contrast the present with the past.
The Master of Tiantai, when examining the meaning of this sutra, maintains that it is not so.
He distinguishes himself from all other masters; therefore, he states categorically, "the meaning is not so. △ Second, refuting narrow interpretations based on the sutra.
What scripture says is that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is immeasurable and its profound principle encompasses everything;
it is called the "King of Sutras" because there is nothing it does not include—how could it concern itself with merely the three groups of nine dharmas?

If the wheel is immeasurable, it is not less than the phenomena, for it accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); thus, it is said to be preeminent in its principle, encompassing all without exception.
How could this King of Sutras of the Middle Way differ from that principle? Now, following the perspective of phenomena, what is there that it does not include?
This is like the horizontal expanse of the Dharma-realm and the verticality of the Three Truths: they are undivided yet divided. How could it be merely...?
The "Three Times Nine Dharmas" specifically excludes the True Truth (satyadharma). Third, the explanation of the title by way of its correspondence to the Dharma:
one should know that the three characters [of the title] universally illustrate all horizontal dharma-gates, which corresponds to the teaching of the immeasurability of the Dharma-nature;
they universally illustrate all vertical dharma-gates, which corresponds to the profound purport of the Dharma-nature—only thus does it accord with this King of Sutras.
The Sūtra states that "immeasurable intent" (wúliàngyì) reveals its horizontal pervasiveness, while "profound intent" (shēnshēnyì) manifests its vertical penetration.

Now, by using these three characters as universal metaphors for all horizontal and vertical Dharma-gates, one accords with the intent of the Sūtra and does not violate the meaning of the King [of Sutras].
△ Fourth, abandoning the extensive for the essential.

Comprehensively encompassing all that is long and broad, there is no teaching not subsumed within it; this meaning is profound and vast, beyond the reach of words or conceptual thought, and thus we provisionally rely upon ten sets of three dharmas as an introductory gateway.
According to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*, the dharma-gates it illustrates are long and vast, without limit; what teachings or names and characteristics would not be subsumed therein?

Yet, as these are both profound and extensive, fearing that the initial mind’s thoughts and speech might fail to reach them, I have selected the essentials from all of them and discussed ten [points] as the primary gateway for practitioners to enter and awaken. If one enters this gate, what dharma will there be that is not seen? △
Section Five: The Chapter on Enumeration.
This further consists of three points: first, the indication of the number ten; second, the explanation of the ten characteristics; third, the discernment of the ten dharmas.
△ Sixth: The Main Explanation. This has three parts: first, the indication of the number ten; second, the formal indication of the names and numbers.

Regarding the statement that ten categories are indicated, these refer to: the three virtues, the three jewels, the three nirvanas, the three bodies, the three Great Vehicles, the three enlightenments, the three prajñas, the three Buddha-natures, the three consciousnesses, and the three paths.

△ Second, a brief demonstration of the functional capacity [of these ten dharmas], in two parts: First, showing that the ten dharmas encompass the beginning and the end by way of their arising in both reverse and direct order. Part one: The inquiry.
Why is it that, although the three categories of dharmas are immeasurable, only these ten dharmas are selected? What is the underlying intention?
△ Second, the explanation [of the ten stages] has three parts; first, a brief demonstration.
These ten dharmas encompass the beginning and the end; now they are presented in two sequences: reverse and direct.
That one abandons the immeasurable and adopts these ten is because these ten encompass both the reverse and direct orders and include both the beginning and the end.

In the end, both sections are established in sequence. △ Second, the actual generation [of the teaching] has two parts: first, inferring the cause by reasoning from the effect through the perspective of the bestowal of the teaching;
second, returning to the True through the perspective of establishing practice and following the cultivation, which is the arising of these two from the beginning:
first, establishing all teachings from the non-abiding source of *dharmatā*; second, [establishing them] from the non-abiding of ignorance.
Question: Regarding the statement that "all dharmas are established based on the fundamental non-abiding nature," upon what textual authority is this said?
Answer: This is clarified in the section on the Essential Substance (*tattva-vastu*). It explains that the various sages establish names based on the Truth (*tathatā*).

As it cites the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*: "From the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. Since this passage is cited as proof that names are established based on the Truth, is this not indeed the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)?

Is it because they are non-abiding that all teachings are established? However, if one discusses this fully, the establishment of all phenomena from the root of non-abiding does not go beyond four layers.
As the *Myōryaku* (Wondrous Joy) states: "In principle, there are the nature-virtues and the conditions; in phenomena, there are the cultivated virtues and the three causes.
When deluded, these flow as the three paths; when awakened, they become the supreme functions within the fruit. Thus, these four layers are all...

[The preceding text] was established based on delusion regarding the true reality (*tattva*). Now, the first section [of this passage] corresponds to the "superior function" within the fourth fruit [of that text], while the subsequent section corresponds to the three causes of the second [category], the "cultivated virtues. Question:

Since the first section begins from the secret treasury (*guhyakośa*) and ends with the three paths, it should collectively correspond to delusion; yet, why does the flow of the three paths [in this text] proceed in reverse?

Question: Is the teaching established based on the preeminent function within the fruit? Answer: It is now stated that the "Secret Treasury" (Guhyagarbha) is revealed by means of the Three Jewels and so forth;
how could one be deluded regarding the principle such that it would depend upon the Three Jewels and the various triads of phenomena?

Therefore, one should know that it is only appropriate to explain this as a teaching arising in reliance upon the principle. Moreover, the two modes of arising—contrary and conformable—here correspond to the text of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
The explanation of the phrases regarding seeing, hearing, awakening, entering, and penetrating concerns the gates of wisdom according to the stages.
Since the intention regarding the arising of the four meanings—whether in direct or reverse order—is the same, that text states: "Seeing arises from the stages; the stages are established by wisdom;

wisdom is generated by the gates; and the gates are penetrated by contemplation. Thus, because the gates are penetrated, wisdom is perfected; because wisdom is perfected, the stages are established; and because the stages are established, [the goal is attained].

Therefore, the *Jilishi* (Record of Explanations) states: "Regarding this sequential and reverse arising, the first [section] clarifies the 'basis' (*suo-you*) by means of the 'capable' (*neng*), and the second clarifies the 'capable' by means of the 'basis.

Is it not the case that in the first instance of the present text, the basis is clarified by means of the capable? And is it not the case that in the second instance, the capable is clarified by means of the basis?
Only after grasping this meaning can one properly interpret the text. As for the initial passage: [The text continues with the specific analysis of the first and second instances.]
Initially, from the root of non-abiding, all dharmas are established. Now, as for the three virtues, they are called the Secret Treasury (*guhyagarbha*);

the manifestation of the Secret Treasury depends upon the Three Jewels; the Three Jewels depend upon the three types of *nirvāṇa*; the three types of *nirvāṇa* depend upon the three bodies (*trikāya*);

the three bodies depend upon the three Great Vehicles (*mahāyāna*); the three Great Vehicles depend upon the three types of enlightenment (*bodhi*); the three types of enlightenment depend upon the three types of *prajñā*.
The three Buddha-natures arise from the three consciousnesses, and the three consciousnesses arise from the three paths; thus, all phenomena are established based on the *dharmatā*.

The principle of the Three Virtues (*triguṇa*) is the ultimate realization of the Buddha, transcending names and characteristics, and is called the "Secret Treasury" (*guhyagarbha*); this treasury is attained.

It is revealed that the accomplishment of merit arises from the union of awakened wisdom (*bodhi-jñāna*) and the principle of non-awakening; therefore, the Tathāgata manifests the Three Jewels (*triratna*).

These Three Jewels are established by virtue of the quality of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), and thus the three types of nirvāṇa are taught. The attainment of nirvāṇa further depends upon the quality of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*), and thus the three bodies (*trikāya*) are taught.
Because the bodies are reached by means of vehicles, the three Great Vehicles (*mahāyāna*) are taught. Because the vehicles are traversed through practice, [the stages of the path are taught].
The three types of awakening (*bodhi*) are taught because awakening is illuminated by wisdom; the three types of *prajñā* are taught because *prajñā* arises from its essential nature;

the three Buddha-natures (*buddhadhātu*) are taught because the seed-nature fundamentally consists of the understanding of names and meanings; the three consciousnesses are taught because the basis of understanding is the principle that consists of the three obstructions;
and the three paths are taught because they all depend on the three virtues. The secret nature of reality (*dharmatā*) is without solidity.
Because the nature of abiding is such, the Great Sage takes this dharma-nature—non-abiding—as the foundation to establish nine names and characteristics, as well as all the teachings;
these arise successively, and subsequently, ten dharmas are established for explanation. △ Second, regarding the establishment of practice and its progressive cultivation:
that is, returning to the True from the delusory.
If all dharmas are established with ignorance as their root, then all sentient beings are without exception endowed with the twelve links of dependent origination.
When they overturn the delusions of the three paths and give rise to understanding, this constitutes the three consciousnesses.

From consciousness, causes are established, which constitute the three Buddha-natures. From these causes, wisdom arises, which constitutes the three *prajñās*. From wisdom, practice arises, which constitutes the three [Buddhas].

Awakening proceeds from practice and advancement, whereby the three vehicles of the Mahāyāna are accomplished; through the accomplishment of wisdom and virtue, the three bodies (trikāya) are accomplished;

through the accomplishment of the virtue of cessation, the three nirvāṇas are accomplished; through the accomplishment of the virtue of grace that benefits sentient beings, the Three Jewels (triratna) are accomplished;
and by entering ultimate quiescence into these three virtues, the Secret Treasury (guhyagarbha) is accomplished.

Above, it was explained that the Great Awakened One realizes the treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-garbha*) because of non-abiding (*apratiṣṭhāna*); thus, the establishment of all teachings culminates in the three paths.

Now, it is explained that sentient beings dwell within the three paths; because of non-abiding, they accomplish the various active dharmas (*saṃskāra-dharma*), which ultimately lead to the three virtues.
Furthermore, these three paths take ignorance (*avidyā*) as their beginning; because ignorance is itself luminous (*vidyā*), karma and suffering both revolve and transform.
Delusion becomes understanding through the discernment of sacred teachings; thus, the three types of consciousness become the seeds of the vehicle, which are called the causes of Buddhahood.
Consequently, they constitute the three Buddha-natures. By perfuming the original enlightenment (*ālaya-vijñāna*), wisdom is awakened, termed the three types of *prajñā*.

Through the practice of the path of wisdom, one traverses the great direct path to accomplish the three types of *bodhi*-wisdom. Through the practice of wisdom, one accords with the nature; there is nothing that is not carried and sustained. Thus, it is accomplished.
Distinguishing the three vehicles of the Mahāyāna, the superior wisdom of retribution is darkly harmonized above and responds below, thereby accomplishing the three bodies (*trikāya*).

These bodies are eternally free from delusion, neither arising nor ceasing, and are termed the "three nirvāṇas" (*trividha-nirvāṇa*). Because they possess the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), exercise mastery, bestow grace, and benefit all things, they manifest as the Three Jewels (*triratna*).
Having perfected the merit of benefiting others, self and other find rest together, returning to the three virtues (*triguṇa*). This sequence of arising serves as the basis for what follows.
The ten layers are established through the contemplation of the mind. △ Third, the summary and demonstration:
This constitutes the sequence of the inverse and the direct.

By investigating the origins of the teachings in the inverse order and practicing the contemplative exercises in the direct order, all are brought into systematic arrangement. △ Second, regarding the immeasurable and profound...
A profound understanding that all ten dharmas are entirely lofty and vast. Part Three: The Inquiry.
How, furthermore, is the meaning of "profound and immeasurable"?
△ Part Two: The Explanation. Section One: Clarifying Immeasurability by Way of Universal Inclusion. Subsection One: Clarifying that Each Possesses the Ten Dharmas.
The "Infinite Meanings" refers to a single Dharma-gate that encompasses nine Dharma-gates. The three virtues (triguṇa) worthy of reverence are the Three Jewels (Triratna).

The non-arising and non-ceasing of these three virtues are the three types of Nirvāṇa. The complete possession of these three virtues and the gathering of all dharmas is called the Three Bodies (Trikāya).
Their capacity for transport and support is the Three Great Vehicles (Mahāyāna). That which cannot be categorized as anything else is called the Threefold Bodhi (Tri-bodhi).

Awakened clarity and purity are called the three kinds of *prajñā*, which are the seeds of the Tathāgata; they are called the three Buddha-natures (*buddhatva*), and when distinguished without error, they are called the three consciousnesses.
Because phenomena penetrate principle through these very events, they are called the three paths. This constitutes the "one-three" Dharma-gate, which encompasses nine "three" Dharma-gates;
all other "three" Dharma-gates may be understood by analogy with this.
Since the Dharma-realm of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) is boundless, what dharma-gate is there that it does not encompass?
Moreover, following its essentials, it possesses nine kinds [of aspects]. Because its self-substance is fundamentally eternal, blissful, self, and pure, it is called the "three virtues.

That which possesses these virtues and that which is possessed by them correspond to the ten dharmas. Since this is so for the three virtues, the mutual possession of the remaining nine can be understood through reflection. Therefore—
Not fully set forth. △ Second, explaining that each possesses all:

furthermore, each possesses all one-dharma gates, all two-dharma gates, all three-dharma gates, four-dharma gates, five-dharma gates, six-dharma gates, seven-dharma gates, eight-dharma gates, nine-dharma gates, ten-dharma gates, and hundred-dharma gates.
One may likewise know that there are a thousand dharma-gates, ten thousand dharma-gates, a hundred million dharma-gates, and dharma-gates as numerous as one *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*,
two *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka*, or even a hundred thousand million billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* sands.
Since the "one" and the "nine-threes" are explained according to their essential meaning, one should know that each individual [element] possesses all three dharma-gates.
Because the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*) is unimpeded and can correspond to all numerical categories, a single dharma-gate can encompass all "one-number" dharma-gates;
furthermore, it encompasses all "two-number" dharma-gates, and so on, up to dharma-gates with names as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. There is no end to them.
Because one cannot fully explain the immeasurable meaning of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), yet is not obscured regarding it here, it is said that "it can be known.
△ Third, citing the sutra to provide proof and conclusion.
The sutra says: "One dharma-gate has immeasurable dharma-gates as its retinue; to understand the immeasurable within the one is [the true understanding]."
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) signifies the sense of being immeasurably vast and expansive.
In this scripture, the *Avataṃsaka*, a single dharma is taken as the sovereign of a dharma-gate (*dharmamukha*), while all others serve as its retinue.

Just as it is with this one dharma, so it is with each and every one; thus, within a single phenomenon, one is able to comprehend the immeasurable. It is in this way that [the teaching is established].
The explanation thus accords with the immeasurable meanings of the *dharmatā*. △ Second, clarifying the profound depth by means of the vertical dimension:
previously, regarding the immeasurable, we began from a single dharma and extended to dharmas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; was this not vertically high?

However, that did not yet rely on the meaning of stages (*bhūmi*), so it belonged entirely to the horizontal; this is the horizontal within the vertical. Now, in clarifying the profound depth, every single dharma-gate is examined in terms of...
The three stages and the six identities each manifest the horizontal dharmas to reveal their respective vertical depths; the text has three parts.

First, a collective discussion based on ten dharmas: as for the profound meaning, it is manifested by relying on the three stages, just as when ten dharma-gates are discussed collectively—namely, the three paths and the three consciousnesses.
The Three Virtues and Three Jewels in their state as the fundamental basis (mūla-avasthā) are the "when-to-be" state; the remainder are the "presently existing" state.
Thus, the meaning of the profound and vertically lofty nature of the Dharma-nature (dharmatā) is also established.

The three paths and the three consciousnesses are phenomena of delusion and thus belong to the "inherently existing" (benyou). The three virtues and the Three Jewels are phenomena subsequent to fruition and thus belong to the "to-be-existing" (dangyou).

When the three Buddha-dharmas reach the three nirvāṇas—beginning from the subtle cause and culminating in the attainment of the great fruit—all are within the path and thus belong to the "presently existing" (xiangyou). If one is muddled regarding the profound and vast meaning of these three dharmas...
Regarding the current pairing and what is called "division," one must understand that the thirteen are merely a single three.

This is because the single *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is immeasurable and profound, possessing ten kinds of virtues and established with ten names. The single three is not separate from the thirteen, nor are the thirteen divided [from it].

If those three paths are already contained within their state of being fundamental, they have already subsumed the nine threes; if one speaks of the three virtues as being in their future state, [they likewise encompass them].
Regarding the "position" (*bhūmi*), it also subsumes nine; among these, eight are all like this. △ Second, regarding one dharma possessing nine:
furthermore, a single dharma-gate possesses nine dharma-gates. Taking its three paths and three consciousnesses constitutes the "original position";
taking its three virtues and three jewels constitutes the "corresponding position"; and taking the remainder constitutes the "manifest position. Thus, the profound meaning is also established.
Furthermore, regarding "one category": one dharma possesses nine capacities, and all ten [capacities] are likewise matched to the three positions by these ten divisions.
Since these ten are complete within a single dharma, it should be understood that a single dharma pervades all three positions.
This demonstrates that the preceding divisions correspond [to the positions], and thus they are not mutually exclusive. △ Third, the section on each possessing six aspects.

Furthermore, each and every dharma-gate possesses the principle of six stages of position: the stage of the original existence (*mūla-avasthā*), the stage of ultimate consummation (*niṣṭhā-avasthā*), and the remaining [four] stages which constitute the stage of present existence (*vartamāna-avasthā*). This profound meaning is also established;
this is what is meant by the profound sense of the vertical height of the *dharmatā*.
To demonstrate each individual dharma-gate: within each of the ten, and within each of those ten, there are nine;

within each of these nine, there is one dharma, continuing even unto immeasurable river-sands of individual dharma-gates, none of which fail to vertically penetrate the stages of the six identities (*ṣaḍ-yoga*). Why is this?
It is because the essence of each and every dharma is the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature), which is immeasurably profound. While the vast ground of sentient beings is entirely deluded, [only]...
If one is fortunate enough to receive instruction on this principle, knowing the names of each and every dharma as the profound and vast *dharmatā* constitutes the stage of the five ranks;
observing and practicing this knowledge constitutes the stage of the purification of the six sense faculties; a semblance knowledge constitutes the forty-one stages of partial realization;
and ultimate knowledge regarding each and every dharma constitutes the stage of wondrous enlightenment, which is profoundly and vastly deep.

Because it is the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), it establishes the meaning of verticality. Furthermore, by correlating the six stages of realization (liu ji) with the three positions, all are discussed in terms of horizontal breadth rather than vertical depth;
therefore, they are simply concluded as the meaning of "profound depth. △ Third, the conclusion and return [to the source].
One should know that the three characters "Jin-guang-ming" (Golden Light) are universally illustrative of all horizontal dharma-gates; thus they are called "immeasurable.

They are universally illustrative of all vertical dharma-gates; thus they are called "profound. Only a text that accords with the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) truly conforms to the intent of this King of Sutras.

By using these three characters as universal metaphors for both the horizontal and vertical dimensions, reaching the furthest limits and the ultimate depths, the meaning of the Dharma-nature Sūtra and its literary intent are both fully realized.
△ Second, the explanation of the ten characteristics, part four: first, the heading.
Next, regarding the explanation of the characteristics of the ten kinds of triple dharmas:
△ Second, connecting the preceding with what follows.
The ten names have already been listed as before; the ten characteristics shall now be analyzed.
△ Third, the exhortation to have faith and understanding:
If one were to differentiate the characteristics of form—such as blue, yellow, sameness, or difference—one should employ the fleshly eye;

if one were to differentiate the characteristics of phenomena—such as depth, shallowness, sameness, or difference—one should employ the wisdom-eye. Since practitioners of the present age lack the wisdom-eye, they should employ faith and understanding.
Distinguishing the characteristics of similarity and difference,
one takes the purport of the Great Sūtra to discern the superiority and inferiority of the human flesh-eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) in comparison to the Buddha’s wisdom-eye (*jñāna-cakṣus*).

While the ordinary person’s flesh-eye can only distinguish the similarities and differences of physical forms, the five grades of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-bhāvanā*), though still consisting of the flesh-eye, are designated as [the "wisdom-eye"].
The Buddha-eye can perceive the secret treasury of the Buddha-nature. My present explanation of the ten kinds of threefold dharmas reveals that each is a secret;
were it not for the Buddha-eye, how could the Three Wisdoms distinguish their depth or shallowness, or their similarities and differences?

Regarding depth and shallowness, in contrast to the three teachings, all are shallow except for the Perfect [Teaching], which alone is deep. Regarding similarities and differences, the fact that the ten are identical to the one within the Perfect Teaching constitutes their similarity.
One is precisely ten; thus, difference and identity, sameness and distinctness, shallowness and depth are all manifest simultaneously.
The Great Master has already attained this eye of wisdom, and now, out of compassion for practitioners who have not yet opened this eye, he proclaims the ten dharmas of the partial and the perfect.
Therefore, he exhorts [them] to have deep faith and give rise to the perfect understanding, relying upon the names and designations to distinguish the ten gates. △ Four: The Correct [Exposition].
The Explanation of the Ten Characteristics, Part Two: First, the Correct Explanation of the Ten; Third, the Three Virtues, Part Four: First, the Brief Indication by Stating the Names.
Regarding the first point, explaining the characteristics of the three virtues: what are the three? What are the virtues? The Dharma-body, Prajñā, and Liberation constitute the three.
Eternity, Bliss, Self, and Purity constitute the virtues.

The third is the essence of the Dharma (*dharmatā*), and the fourth is its virtuous characteristics (*guṇa-lakṣaṇa*). △ Second, the detailed explanation according to the Perfect and Vast [Teaching], in two parts.

First, the explanation of the three [aspects]. Regarding "Dharma" (*dharma*): it is called "Dharma" because it is that which may be taken as a standard; all Buddhas take it as their standard and thereby attain Buddhahood. Thus, a sutra says:
"That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is precisely the Dharma. Regarding "Body" (*kāya*): it means an accumulation. A single dharma encompasses all dharmas without any deficiency or omission.
It is called the *Śarīra-sūtra*. It says: "My body is the true and virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) of all sentient beings. You should know that 'body' (*śarīra*) means an accumulation.
Prajñā is the awakening to the gathering and dispersing of all phenomena; it is neither gathering nor dispersing, which is precisely the awakening to the dharmas of the three truths.
Liberation (*vimukti*) is being unstained by and non-abiding in all phenomena; this is called liberation. This is what is meant.
It is threefold.
Regarding "following the track" (*anugati*) to explain "Dharma": who would not follow the profound and vast *dharmatā*?

However, because the nine realms, though they follow it, act in opposition to it, they form a path of suffering within the *dharmakāya*. The Buddhas, by following the track, are able to bring about [liberation] even within this path of suffering.
Regarding the explanation of the *dharmakāya* as a "collection" (*cita*): a single color and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way;
all realms are one, and all are thus—this is called a "collection. That all sentient beings are equal [to the Buddha] is because the Buddha-body possesses all dharmas;
if each sentient being truly knows and realizes even a single dharma, they truly know the Buddha.
This is because one truly recognizes the Buddha; thus, the Buddha is the true and virtuous spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) for all.
The *Avataṃsaka* also states: "All phenomena are neither born nor extinguished. If one can understand in this way, one shall behold Vairocana.

Regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*, when [phenomena] are assembled, it is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), illuminated by provisional wisdom (*prajñā*); when they are dispersed, it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Because the wisdom of emptiness illuminates them, all phenomena are dispersed and destroyed; because the wisdom of the Middle illuminates the Middle Truth—which is neither of the two extremes—all phenomena transcend all dependencies.
These three wisdoms within a single mind are called Prajñā. Within the liberation of this [Prajñā], no phenomenon transcends the Three Truths of the Real, the Conventional, and the Middle.
Since one is neither stained by nor dwells in these three, they are called the Three Liberations, which are precisely the three delusions and afflictions.
They are forever non-corresponding. △ Second, the explanation of the virtues (guṇa) has three parts. First, clarifying the four virtues of the Dharma-body. What constitutes these virtues?
Each and every dharma is endowed with the names of permanence, bliss, self, and purity; this is termed "virtue. The Dharma-body is free from the two types of death and is thus permanent;
it does not undergo the two extremes and is thus blissful; it possesses the eight masteries and is thus the self; its bodily karma is pure, as is its verbal [karma].
When karma is pure and mental karma is pure, it is pure because there is nothing with which to compare it; yet, for the sake of instruction, one may provisionally employ worldly gold as a metaphor.
Just as worldly gold does not change or become defiled even when transformed into wealth and status, so too is the fourfold virtue of the Dharma-body.

Each and every dharma—from the birth of a Buddha, the reliance on the Dharma-body and its environment, down to a single particle of space and a single moment of thought—is perfectly complete with the four subtle virtues (*catur-guṇa*).
Regarding the virtue of purity as clarified through the three karmas: the three karmas of the ten realms are fundamentally and primordially free from the six defilements;

this is called the purity of the *dharmakāya*. These four virtues of the *dharmakāya* are subtle and beyond comparison, yet they are provisionally designated as follows: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
The four meanings of "World-Gold" (*jagat-svarṇa*) serve as metaphors. △ Second, clarifying the four virtues of *prajñā*.
Because *prajñā* spontaneously possesses these four virtues—just as wisdom is in accord with the suchness of the object—the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"Because form (*rūpa*) is pure, *prajñā* is pure. By extension, this establishes all such meanings as the permanence of form, the bliss of form, and the self of form. Furthermore, it says: "Form is great..."
Therefore, because the great form of *prajñā* is boundless, *prajñā* is boundless; this is because the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is vast, and thus *prajñā* is also vast.
By analogy, one should say: because form is profound, *prajñā* is also profound;
this is because the nature of phenomena is vertically lofty, and thus *prajñā* is also vertically lofty. One should know that it is clear that *prajñā* likewise possesses these four virtues.
The wisdom that is the very essence returns to merge with that essence; since they are non-dual, how could the merit of this wisdom be less than that of the Dharmakāya?
Therefore, Prajñāpāramitā also possesses the four virtues. In the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, there is this principle regarding the statement "form is pure":

because the form of the aggregates (*skandha*) is itself the nature [of reality], it is the Dharmakāya. Thus, while the Dharmakāya should inherently possess the four virtues, this [text] speaks of them as being "swept away" merely to eliminate conceptual characteristics.

To cite one instance, a pure quality does not exist in isolation; it must necessarily possess the other three. Thus, it is said that because form (*rūpa*) is eternal, so too are wisdom (*prajñā*), bliss (*sukha*), and self (*ātman*).

When it is said that "all meanings are established," this refers to the fact that the essence itself possesses the meaning of being cool and unchanging, the meaning of true cognition, the meaning of pervasive illumination, and even the meaning of all merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Since wisdom is already in profound union with the essence, Prajñā fulfills all these meanings. For this reason, the scripture further cites that "form is great" and "form is boundless" to establish the meaning of vastness;
by analogy, it clarifies the meaning of vertical height through profundity, for Prajñā possesses both.

As for the object being merely form: form occupies the beginning of the aggregates and is the foremost of the Dharma-realm; therefore, the scripture first mentions it, as form already encompasses [all].

The four virtues—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—pervade the aggregates of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; the elements, sense bases, truths, conditions, the six perfections, the factors of enlightenment, and up to the knowledge of all modes, all are permanent, blissful, self, and pure. Therefore, Prajñā is permanent, blissful, self, and pure;
this is how Prajñā possesses the four virtues. △ Third, the four virtues of liberation.
Liberation likewise possesses four virtues. As for liberation, it is the eternal exhaustion of all evils; thus, impermanence, suffering, non-self, and impurity are all exhausted.
It is also the universal convergence of all virtues; thus, permanence, bliss, self, and purity are universally converged.
Since the previous refutation of the "ancient texts" already separately enumerated four [points], the present section clarifies them collectively according to their meaning. There are two points:

first, regarding the eternal exhaustion of all evils. Since all evils do not exceed the four [faults] such as impermanence (*anitya*) and so forth, once these four faults are abandoned, one necessarily possesses the four virtues (*guṇa*).
If discussed specifically, attachments such as impermanence pertain only to the Two Vehicles; however, if discussed generally...
Being free from obstacles such as impermanence, only a Buddha can exhaustively realize this; now, speaking in general terms, we turn next to the various wholesome qualities.
Although these wholesome dharmas are numerous, how could they exceed the four virtues? Since their gathering is comprehensive, these virtues must be without deficiency.
Therefore, liberation is fully endowed with the four virtues. △ Third, citing evidence for the perfection of its essence.

The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states: "True liberation is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Dharmakāya. One should know that liberation is identical to the Tathāgata’s permanence, bliss, self, and purity.
Furthermore, the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states: "The perfection of the three dots is called Mahāparinirvāṇa. These dots are characters.
One should know that the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Liberation are all characters. Thus, one knows the three [dots].
Since each point is fully equipped with the four virtues, it is said that being "endowed with the three causes" refers to the three wisdoms. Each of these three wisdoms possesses the four virtues;
the complete possession of these three virtues is called the "Secret Treasury. Thus, the term "complete possession" necessarily implies the presence of the four virtues.
Regarding the citation of the three passages: the meaning of the first passage clarifies that liberation is identical to the Dharmakāya and is fully endowed with the four virtues.
The second passage discusses the three virtues in general, intending to show that they reside within the Dharmakāya;

since the Dharmakāya which is illuminated must possess the three virtues, although the sūtra lacks a specific mention of *prajñā*, it extensively explains the three causes, for these causes are the nature of wisdom. Thus, there are three causes.
Because it is perfect, each of the three wisdoms possesses four virtues. Regarding the statement that "the three points are complete," the *Sukhāvatīvyūha* (Chapter on Lamentation) says:
"What is called the secret treasury? It is like the three dots of the letter *i*. If they are aligned horizontally, they do not form an *i*;
if they are vertical, they also do not form one. Only when they are like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara do they constitute [the letter]."
In this way, I also understand that the Dharma of liberation is not *nirvāṇa*, the body of the Tathāgata is not *nirvāṇa*, and the Mahāprajñā is also not *nirvāṇa*.
That these three dharmas are distinct from one another is likewise not *nirvāṇa*.
Only when these three dharmas are free from the characteristics of being either vertical or horizontal, or identical or different, can they be named Great *Nirvāṇa*.
As for the three dots that constitute the character [for "three"], they are like the three dots of the Indian letter *i*;
furthermore, in the cursive script of this land, the lower part of certain characters also has fine lines connecting three dots. Thus we know that every dot is a written character.
By this analogy, each of the three dharmas is mutually complete within the Great Nirvana; the three dots fully possess the four virtues. If one is deluded regarding these three...
Each dot is a textual convention established so that all three dots are fully endowed with the four virtues. The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is permanence, and Prajñā is purity;
liberation (*vimukti*) is bliss. Since each dot subsumes two [virtues], the three dots together constitute the four virtues.
Thus, one knows that the Dharma-body of the three dots is precisely what possesses the four virtues; likewise for the Prajñā of the three dots and the liberation of the three dots.
Because they are currently endowed with the four virtues, it is said that they are "completely prepared" (*sibei*) and "fully possessed" (*juzu*).
Regarding the statement that each of the three wisdoms possesses the four virtues: wisdom is *prajñā*, which subsumes the other two; since both are termed "wisdom," they constitute the three wisdoms.
Because the three virtues are taken as the three wisdoms, each of the three wisdoms is made to possess the four virtues. If the three virtues are thus, [so too are the three wisdoms].
Because it is peaceful and inconceivable, it is named the "Secret Treasury. △ Fourth, concluding the preceding and introducing what follows:
One should know that the perfection of the four virtues is its characteristic. If one grasps the meaning of this single chapter, the remaining nine can be understood;
yet, unable to illuminate them fully, I shall speak of them briefly once more.
This is because the Three Virtues and the Nine Dharma Gates are non-dual and without distinction; when one chapter is understood, the remaining nine should likewise be known.
Yet, fearing that the listeners have not yet exhausted the profound meaning, I cannot remain silent but must further proclaim and clarify it.
△ Second, the Two Treasures: first, the explanation of the meaning according to the Perfect [Teaching].
What are the three? The Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha—these three are worthy of honor and respect, and are thus called "Treasures.
The ultimate principle worthy of honor is called the Dharma Jewel; the wisdom that awakens to this principle worthy of honor is called the Buddha Jewel;
and the harmony in which Vairocana pervades all places, such that phenomena are themselves the principle, is worthy of honor and is called the Sangha Jewel. These Three Jewels are all...
Because it is eternal, blissful, self, and pure—being eternal, blissful, self, and pure—it is worthy of honor and respect.
Since the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha all possess these four virtues, they are worthy of respect; thus, these three are called "Treasures.
Their essence is not distinct from the three virtues, for they consist of the union of awakening and non-awakening, as well as the sense of being worthy of respect.

Therefore, based on their meanings, the names of the Three Jewels are established. Now, it is clarified that the Three Jewels are of one essence; however, because the text is concise, this is difficult to perceive.
In the *Mysterious Meaning of Avalokiteśvara*, the characteristics are somewhat more detailed; I shall now transcribe it in full to manifest this meaning. That text states:

"By means of the wisdom of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), one awakens to and realizes that all phenomena are neither empty nor existent; therefore, they are called the Buddha Jewel. That which is awakened to..."
The principle of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) being fully endowed with the three truths is the Dharma Jewel.

When such awakened wisdom is in harmony with both principle and phenomena, it is called the Sangha Jewel. Being in harmony with phenomena refers to the sages and saints of the three previous teachings;
