First, regarding the passage from the *Śūnyatā-saṃkṣobha-sūtra* that says "emptiness disturbs the mind" and so forth: this refers to the text in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* that critiques the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna).

In the Lesser Vehicle, emptiness is explained as the principle of quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirodha*), whereas conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are regarded as delusive disturbances. In the Mahāyāna, the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) is explained as the nature of quiescent extinction;
thus, both emptiness and existence are considered disturbances to the mind. Although one may be free from the disturbance of existence, one still remains disturbed by emptiness.
Now, when practicing contemplation, if the mind becomes attached to emptiness, this mental factor of the mind is designated as "the deluded mind of sentient beings regarding emptiness.

This mental factor of emptiness is called "wisdom" only in contrast to the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). However, in the present discussion of the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti-vipaśyanā*), this wisdom is itself a delusion;

therefore, it is said that such "wisdom-delusion" is profoundly blind and dark. When those of the Lesser Vehicle realize emptiness, they attain the three unconditioned states (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), namely, cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).

The unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) includes non-analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) and space (ākāśa). Because the bodhicitta and roots of goodness cannot grow in these places, they are disparaged as "pits.
Regarding the phrase "birds that are enemies of the Mahāyāna," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom), fascicle 30, states:
"For example, in a desolate marsh there is a tree named śamālī; its branches and twigs are broad and vast, and many large birds gather there to roost at night."
The pigeon arrived last and perched upon a branch; the branch immediately broke under its weight.
The *śarabha* spirit asked, "The vultures were both able to support themselves, so why is it that you cannot sustain even this small bird?
The tree spirit replied, "This bird has come from the tree of my enemy, having eaten its fruit and now perching upon me; it might well defecate here."

If the seedling falls to the ground, an evil tree will grow again and its harm will surely be great; for this reason, harboring such anxiety, one would rather abandon a single branch so that what is preserved is greater.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he has no such fear toward the various non-Buddhists, celestial Māras, and the like, yet he fears the two vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas); the two vehicles, in turn, regard the Bodhisattva in the same manner as those [non-Buddhists and Māras].

The bird destroys that Mahāyāna mind and forever extinguishes the mind of the Buddha-vehicle; now, taking this meaning, I clarify the contemplation of breaking through emptiness to emerge into the provisional and achieve Bodhi.
Next, "If true... and below, it correctly clarifies the characteristics of the Bodhi-mind of the provisional contemplation.

Because the true is itself the provisional, it is established based upon emptiness. This Bodhi-mind—its meaning of "delivering" (*tù*) and its meaning of "pervading" (*tōng*)—both pertain to the sensory objects (*viṣaya*).

That which is provisionally taught is all discourse on provisional contemplation; it does not exceed three meanings: knowing the illness, knowing the medicine, and administering the medicine according to the illness so that it may be taken and practiced.
From the section "Distinguishing" (*vibhaṅga*) below, by means of "Distinguishing," the four *siddhāntas* are clarified.

By relying on these four *siddhāntas*, the three meanings are collectively elucidated. They may differ slightly, such as the *loka-siddhānta*, which concerns worldly appropriateness and the generation of wholesome roots.
This is the person using medicine to treat consciousness; it is the application of antidotes to meet the occasion and accord with principle—this is the primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
These four clear understandings constitute the completion of the contemplation of the four provisional designations (*catuḥ-prajñapti*). △ Third, breaking through extremes to enter the Middle Way.

Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the remedy for a floating mind, and the provisional (*prajñapti*) is the remedy for a sunken mind. Because there is illness, there is medicine; once the medicine remains, it becomes an illness in itself.

When the illness departs, the medicine ceases; thus, both should be relinquished. By transcending both emptiness and the provisional, and by the simultaneous disappearance of the two extremes, one awakens to the *bodhicitta* of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of the Middle Way.
This enables one to deliver sentient beings—those whose mental factors are caught between the two extremes—and to penetrate through ignorance.
Because one abides in the Middle Way by means of the non-abiding Dharma, it is said that "abiding in the Middle gives rise to the Bodhicitta.
Previously, when the two contemplations were raised, they were not yet free from the arising of faults; now, these are to be abandoned.

Taking the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) as well as the *pāramitā*-obscuring delusions (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*) as the diseases of floating and sinking, emptiness and the provisional are the medicines for these two diseases. Because the disease increases in a biased manner, the medicine [is applied accordingly].
If one relies exclusively on medicine, it becomes a cause for illness; because falling into either of the two extremes increases the disease of ignorance, both must be abandoned.

Next, regarding "neither empty nor non-empty," this correctly clarifies the contemplation of the Middle Way Bodhicitta. Herein, the meanings of "moderation" (*du*) and "pervasion" (*tong*) are both explained in terms of ignorance being itself the Middle.
When the mind is devoid of subject and object, it is called the "non-abiding dharma"; only through this dharma can [the Middle Way] be realized.
Abiding in the Middle Way. △ Third, the correspondence between the Perfect [Teaching] and the Dharma. Part one: Clarifying the Perfect.
It is not the case that the sequence of contemplation at the time of teaching is the same as the sequence of practice.

To make the characteristics of the desire-realm manifest, one must rely on sequential contemplation; yet when integrated according to principle, there is no before or after—these three aspects are identical.
If one has already clarified its meaning. △ Second, the correspondence with the Dharma:
within the single mind, the three types of bodhicitta are as follows: if one contemplates it as the center, this is the condition for generating the unsurpassed bodhicitta;

if one contemplates it as emptiness, this is the condition for generating the pure bodhicitta; if one contemplates it as the provisional, this is the condition for generating the luminous [bodhicitta].
One gives rise to the ultimate bodhicitta.
Now, regarding the three types of *sambodhi*, they are called "True Nature Bodhi" (*tathatā-bodhi*) because all three are wondrously transcendent;

they are also called "Unsurpassed Real Wisdom Bodhi" (*anuttara-tattvajñāna-bodhi*) because all three sweep away all signs; and they are also called "Pure Expedient Means Bodhi" (*viśuddha-upāya-bodhi*).

Because all three are sovereign and encompass everything without omission, they are also called "ultimate. Because the three reside within a single mind, each of the three contains the other three, for their essence is fused.
Thus, their manifestation is simultaneous; therefore, the essence itself is named *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* (Golden Light).
△ Third, the conclusion.

This is the contemplation of the mind regarding the three aspects of *sambodhi* in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, with the six stages of realization (*liù jí*) as previously described, and again as previously described.
△ Sixth, the contemplation of the three aspects of the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*). Part one: the heading.
Next, the contemplation of the mind regarding the three aspects of the Great Vehicle in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*.
△ Second, the explanation of the three [sections]: First, the general establishment of the method of contemplation.
Contemplating a single moment of mind as being simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle is the Three Great Vehicles.

△ Second, clarifying contemplation in relation to objects; for practicing the Perfect Threefold Contemplation in accordance with the Three Great Vehicles, one must necessarily understand the principle of object and contemplation.
This accords with the "vehicle" (*yāna*), for the meaning of "vehicle" is that of "transporting. There are three kinds of Mahāyāna, and there is no dharma that it does not transport.

Since its nature inherently possesses this capacity for transport, whether one practices in opposition to or in accordance with reality, transport occurs as a matter of course. Now, in essence, even when practicing in opposition, every thought-moment involves the four modes of transport;

each transport is itself the nature, and this nature is the Three Truths, which thus constitute the Three Contemplations. In the practice of accord, this wondrous transport is divided into three parts, the first of which is as follows: [The text continues: "First..."
Clarifying the four phases as the object of observation:
Although one contemplates a single moment of mind, in reality there are four phases. This mind revolves without ceasing;

that is to say, from the phase of "not yet intending" it moves to the phase of "intending," and from the phase of "intending" it moves to the phase of "having already intended. From the phase of not yet intending, it proceeds to the phase of intending; from the phase of intending, it proceeds to the phase of having already intended.

From one thought-moment it is carried to the next, and having done so, it arises again; thus, moment after moment, its movement is inexhaustible and knows no rest, like one with eyes closed on a boat who does not perceive its speed.

To "observe a single thought-moment" means to take up a single thought-moment as it arises; because the mind shifts according to objects, arising and ceasing are continuously transported, and thus it is called "one."
In a single thought-moment, there are no instances where the four phases do not occur; from the moment they have not yet arrived until they have already ended, they begin again.

Because ordinary fools are unaware that they are being shifted by these phases, closing one's eyes is used as a metaphor for their lack of awareness, while the movement of a boat serves as a metaphor for the four phases of the mind’s rapid transition.
△ Second, explaining the three movements as contemplation:
Contemplating that a single movement of mind is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle; each and every movement of mind is likewise so.
From mind to mind, there is nothing that is not simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle. This is to move from the Three Truths to the Three Truths. No...
When one does not [perceive] the three truths at the time of the four movements, this is called "movement by movement.
A practitioner of the Perfect Teaching knows that the nature of the mind in each moment is the secret treasury;

because this secret treasury is all-pervasive and has never for a moment been lacking, there is not a single movement that is not empty, provisional, and middle. One who grasps this meaning finds that as the four movements progress, the three contemplations increasingly advance.

Because one progresses further, it is said that when the firewood is abundant, the fire blazes; when the wind increases, the bellows are sought. For this reason, the Great Master often instructed the assembly:
"With a real mind, bind to a real object; with real conditions, they arise in succession; as reality and reality mutually infuse one another, one naturally enters the principle of reality.
Regarding "with a real mind, binding to a real object," this means the three contemplations (sanguan) bind to the three truths (sandì). Regarding "real conditions in succession"—

First, regarding "arising," this refers to the successive transition of the four phases (*catur-yoga*). These four phases are the objects; as objects, they serve as the conditions for contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), just as fuel assists fire.
As for "the realities mutually infuse one another": the reality of the three contemplations infuses the reality of the three truths, and these real objects, in turn, infuse the real mind.
Through this continuous mutual infusion, one naturally accords with the contemplative practice and attains entry into the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*).
Abiding initially within the reality of principle, this involves employing the three contemplations to drive the four movements;

it is also the movement of the four movements that drives the movement of the three contemplations. All of these may be termed "using movement to drive movement. △ Third, clarifying what is attained by confronting what is lost.
If one follows the four movements, one enters birth and death; if one follows the three movements, one enters nirvana.
If one is deluded regarding the Three Truths and merely follows the four movements, then birth and death will be endless;

if one contemplates the four movements as being identical to the Three Truths, then nirvana is present right now. △ Third, the contemplation contrasted with the vehicles (two parts): first, the contrast according to the Dharma.

The contemplation of emptiness rides upon the vehicle of following to transport one to the ultimate truth; the contemplation of the provisional rides upon the vehicle of attainment to transport one to the conventional truth;
and the contemplation of the middle rides upon the vehicle of principle to transport one to the middle truth.
The Three Vehicles constitute the Great Vehicle; the Three Truths are the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). It moves without moving, and arrives without arriving.

△ Second, praising by way of persons: The Three Vehicles are themselves the One Vehicle. This vehicle is subtle, wondrous, pure, and supreme; it is that which Avalokiteśvara, Samantabhadra, and other great beings [ride].
Because it is mounted upon, it is called the Mahāyāna (Great Vehicle).

Regarding the statement that the three vehicles are identical to the one vehicle: the vehicle of principle (*li-cheng*) serves as the body of the chariot; thus, in its height and breadth, nothing surpasses it.

The vehicle of practice (*sui-cheng*) serves as the white ox; thus, its speed is like the wind. The attainment of the vehicle consists in being endowed with the means of deliverance (*pāramitā*); thus, its adornments are beyond compare. Although... [the text continues].

Though three, they are one; though one, they are three. This subtle and wondrous vehicle is that which the Great Beings—Avalokiteśvara and Samantabhadra—ride upon through their contemplative practice;
therefore, it is called "Great. △ Third, the conclusion.
This is the contemplation of the mind through the three [aspects] of the Mahāyāna *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, consisting of the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-yoga*) as previously described above.
△ Seventh, the contemplation of the three bodies (*trikāya*): first, the heading;
second, the contemplation of the three bodies of the mind according to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*.
△ Second, the explanation of the three [sections]: First, establishing contemplation to manifest the Dharma; second, clarifying contemplation in relation to the mind.

Regarding the cultivation of the contemplation of the Three Bodies within a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa-citta*), it is essential that both the object and the contemplation possess the meaning of "body.

Therefore, first it is clarified that a single mind can give rise to the ten realms, thereby manifesting that a single thought-moment is endowed with the bodies of the ten realms; subsequently, by giving rise to the three contemplations within those ten realms, [the principle] is revealed.
The ten realms are none other than the three bodies. The first section is divided into three parts; the first clarifies the ten aspects.
If one contemplates a single thought-moment as being simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle, this is precisely the three bodies. Why is this? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"The mind is like a skilled painter, creating all manner of five aggregates. If the mind conditions matters of breaking the precepts, it is the body of hell.

Conditioned by shamelessness, lack of remorse, arrogance, and anger, one receives the body of an animal; conditioned by flattery and the pursuit of fame, one receives the body of a hungry ghost (*preta*); conditioned by jealousy and contention, one receives the body of an asura;
conditioned by observing the five precepts to prevent the five evils, one receives the body of a human;

conditioned by practicing the ten wholesome deeds to prevent the ten evils, one receives the body of a deva; and conditioned by meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) to prevent distraction, one receives the body of a deva. [These are further rooted in] contemplating impermanence, suffering, and emptiness.

Emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are the conditions for the bodies of the Two Vehicles; compassion and the six perfections are the conditions for the body of a Bodhisattva; and true suchness and the real mark are the conditions for the body of a Buddha.

Now, regarding the wonderful interpretation of our school concerning the *Avataṃsaka* teaching that "the mind creates," there are two meanings. First is creation by principle (*li-zao*), where "creation" refers to...
The two aspects being complete means that phenomenal creation (*sāṃvṛtikarman*) spans the three periods of time and creates the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). That is to say, the past creates the present;
the past and present create the future; and the present creates the present. All these phenomenal creations exist only because they are grounded in the completeness of the principle (*li*).

Therefore, every single body within the ten realms is entirely the cultivation (*bhāvanā*) arising from the nature (*dharmatā*). Although it is entirely the nature, through the formation of causes, it evokes results without the slightest deficiency.
If there is even a slight lapse, such as a mind that violates the precepts, it can create the various instruments of suffering in hell, which are prepared and awaited in advance;
therefore, within the bodies of the ten realms, all things—whether provisional or real, as well as the primary and secondary environments—arise from nothing external.
△ Second, distinguishing between the difficult and the easy.
It is difficult to ascend and easy to fall because the mind frequently dwells upon unwholesome bodies.
This is truly because sentient beings, through beginningless conditioning, have accumulated more evil than good; thus, their mental states mostly dwell upon unwholesome bodies.

Before they can harness the Five Vehicles, they wander among the Four Evil Destinies. Who would say that ascending is difficult and falling is easy? This is surely so when one cultivates contemplation.
The practitioner should constantly examine the mind within the ten realms. △ Third, the conclusion on Mind-Only:
Thus one knows that all bodies are created by the mind, just as the single great earth can produce various kinds of sprouts.
The analogy for the Dharma can be seen [in the following]. △ Next, regarding the passage on cultivating the three contemplations within this mind-object to manifest the three bodies:
first is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
If one contemplates the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*) and penetrates their emptiness and non-existence, then all bodies produced from the mind are likewise [empty].
"Emptiness and non-existence" refers to the overturning of the great earth such that all grasses and trees are utterly destroyed; therefore, it is said to be "immediately empty.
"Thoroughly penetrating the five aggregates of clinging as being empty and non-existent" is a statement from the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* concerning the mind of the aggregates of clinging.

"Five" refers to the five ways in which clinging arises: namely, clinging to existence, clinging to non-existence, clinging to both existence and non-existence, and clinging to neither existence nor non-existence.

That which is neither attained nor un-attained is also called the contemplation of the five aggregates of grasping (*pañcopādānaskandha*). When one contemplates that this single aggregate is empty and non-existent, then the ten realms all become unobtainable.
This is like the analogy of the earth: when the mind is empty, the grasses and trees are utterly destroyed, and the entire body becomes empty.
△ Second, the provisional (*prajñapti*).
If one were identical to emptiness, one would sink forever into the silence of extinction;
being unable even to produce a single body from a single empty mind, how could one manifest bodies by sporting through the five realms of existence?

One would be unable to manifest a Buddha-body for those who are to be saved by a Buddha-body, nor manifest the various bodies of the three vehicles, the fourfold assembly, or the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others for those who are to be saved thereby.
Because they manifest themselves in all ways to participate in the activities of others, it is said that they "provisionally assume bodies identical to those of the six realms.

If one contemplates the emptiness of the ten realms within a single thought-moment, one already possesses the three truths; yet, here the emptiness is specifically refuted in order to reveal the merit of establishing dharmas through the contemplation of the provisional.
Furthermore, fearing that practitioners of the Perfect Teaching might regress from the Great Vehicle to grasp at the Small, the text employs the perspective of the Two Vehicles to refute emptiness.
The mind of ash-like quiescence and emptiness cannot give rise to the ten realms; only when the response [of the Buddha] manifests can the provisional observation (*jia-guan*) be revealed.

To say that "the formless does not appear" and that it is "identical to the six paths" must be a textual error, for this very text states that it is for the purpose of manifesting the Buddha-body and the three vehicles.
Within the third section, there are two parts: first, the attachment [to the provisional], and second, the refutation of partiality.
To contemplate the body in such a manner, falling into these two extremes, is not a skillful contemplation of the body.
The same applies to the refutation of the mind; it is like using provisional contemplation to refute emptiness. II. Abandoning the Three to Reveal the Middle.
Regarding "skillfully contemplating the body," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "One does not obtain the eight-foot form of the body; one does not obtain the characteristics of the body. Five...
The embryo is not the body; it is not the cause of the body through the nourishment of food and drink; it is not the fruit of the body as a recompense for the five precepts;
it is not the body as an aggregation of the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus); it is not the body as a single entity formed by the conventional and the real;
it is not the body as two things formed by the four great elements; this already is not the one body, nor is it the various individual bodies.
One cannot grasp that body-consciousness is moment-to-moment impermanent; one cannot grasp that the body and so forth are empty within the body; all six realms equally possess a body.
One cannot grasp that the body is the basis for cultivation, nor that the dharma can be cultivated by relying on the body.

One cannot grasp the "cultivator"—that is, the practitioner—nor the body itself, nor the characteristics of the body, nor even the cultivation of the body, nor the cultivator. All these are likewise [ungraspable].

Because the nature of the body, the characteristics of the body, and even the nature of the cultivation of the body and the nature of the cultivator are ultimately pure—this being the intended meaning—it is said that they are "identical with the Middle. Question:
Since the primary purpose is to clarify the Middle, why is it necessary to negate [the extremes]? Answer: The *Madhyamāgama* itself provides a commentary, stating: "Ma" refers to...
"Non-attachment to the meaning of *māyā-dharma* (illusory phenomena)" refers to non-attachment to the Middle Way.

Since the *Shiqian* (Sub-commentary on the *Zhiguan*) establishes the doctrine of the Middle Way based on this, we know that the "forgetting of the self" is precisely the Middle Observation (*zhongguan*). In the text, first thirteen points are listed regarding the inability to forget the body;
even in the provisional (*jia*), one cannot forget the body. This is like forgetting the body in emptiness; such is the meaning of emptiness. It is also...
Not attaining the nature of the body and losing it within the nature of the body—this is the meaning of "the middle. Within emptiness, each is combined and fully forgotten;

these thirteen points are briefly cited by taking the beginning and the end, hence the phrase "up to and including" (*zhì yú*). If one speaks of dispelling delusive attachments, then the three truths are all lost;
if one discusses the manifestation of principle, then the three truths are all illumined. From the nature of the eight-foot body to the nature of the five viscera, and so forth...

Since it has been established that both the nature of cultivation and the nature of the cultivator consist of the thirteen dharmas as being inherently complete (*xingju*), let us take the human body as a starting point for our discourse.
It is logically consistent that each of the ten bodies possesses these thirteen [dharmas], and that each and every one of them is the very nature itself;
thus, the ten realms each possess the ten dharmas, and each is identical to the nature. Because this treatise focuses on the forgetting [of duality] in this context, the ultimate truth is revealed.
Through purity, it is revealed that the ten bodies are all identical to the Middle Way. △ Third, correlating the contemplation with the bodies:
"identical to the Middle" refers to the Dharma-body; "identical to emptiness" refers to the Reward-body; and "identical to the provisional" refers to the Response-body.

△ Three Bonds. This is called the Contemplation of the Mind; the three bodies, the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*, and the six stages of "as-it-is" (*yathābhūta*) are as explained previously and may be understood accordingly.
△ Eighth: Contemplating the Three Nirvāṇas. Part One: The Title.
Next is the contemplation of the three nirvāṇas of the mind as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
△ Second, the explanation that all three types of nirvāṇa must possess the four virtues (*caturguṇa*) to be designated as "perfectly ultimate" (*pariniṣṭhita*).

Therefore, in contemplating these three, each and every one is realized as permanent, blissful, self, and pure. Since the method of contemplation is identical, the three are now distinguished according to their three respective objects.
Although the characteristics manifest as a single nirvāṇa within a single object, one must know that each and every one is complete with all three;
if this were not so, how could they cause all three to possess the four virtues? This meaning has already been explained in detail in the preceding text, which is divided into three parts:
first, observing the nature-purity by means of the retributive mind.

Contemplate with clarity that the nature of the mind is fundamentally quiescent, neither defiled nor pure: because it is not defiled, it is called "arising"; because it is not pure, it is called "ceasing.

Since arising and ceasing cannot destroy it, it is eternal; since they cannot defile it, it is pure; since they cannot obstruct it, it is self; since it cannot be experienced [as an object], it is bliss.
This is the nirvana of the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi-nirvāṇa*).

The retributive mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and fundamentally pure, making its nature easy to manifest. Since the nature of the mind is already quiescent, how could it merely be quiescent regarding defilement?

It is also fundamentally quiescent regarding purity. Therefore, the original nature is neither defiled nor pure. If it were subject to defilement or purification, its nature would be subject to arising and ceasing.

Thus, it is said that being defiled is called "arising," and being purified is called "ceasing. Since the meaning of the four virtues of non-arising and non-ceasing is established, and since it has been stated that there is "arising":
Because cessation cannot destroy it, its permanence is verified by the three phrases of non-defilement, non-obstruction, and non-reception;

all must be said to involve arising and ceasing, though they are abbreviated here to avoid prolixity. Because it possesses these four virtues, it is called "nature-detached"; because it is free from arising and ceasing, it is called "pure";
thus it is named "Nirvana of Nature-Purity. △ Second, observing perfect purity through the arousal of the mind.
If delusive thoughts arise, one should observe them all with right contemplation, causing this right contemplation to accord with the dharma-nature (dharmatā).
Such that delusive thoughts cannot defile it, cannot destroy it, cannot obstruct it, and cannot be received by it— this state of eternal bliss, selfhood, purity,
and permanence is precisely the perfectly pure nirvana.

Regarding delusive thoughts and afflictions, one should contemplate perfect purity (*pariśuddhi*). This perfect purity is wisdom; it must be discussed in terms of its function of destroying delusions.
One employs the three correct contemplations (*samyag-darśana*) to destroy the three delusive thoughts, causing them to be untainted by the nature of the Three Truths (*trīṇi satyāni*):

because they are pure, they are not destroyed; because they are eternal, they are unobstructed; because there is no self, they are not received. Thus, the four virtues are manifested and the three delusions are subsumed within the Perfect [Truth].
Because it is utterly pure, it does not arise; because it is perfect, it does not cease; therefore, it is called "Perfectly Pure Nirvana.

△ Third, regarding the purity of skillful means through the contemplation of the various mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*): furthermore, by observing all mental factors with right contemplation, the mental factors do not function, and the mental factors cannot cause destruction.
That which can be defiled but cannot be obstructed and cannot be received is called the "expediently pure nirvana.
Because all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are created through mental construction, one relies upon them to contemplate expedient purity.

For those in whom conditioned phenomena no longer function, they do not follow deluded thoughts to create the karma of birth and death; rather, by following correct contemplation, they perform inconceivable karma. This is the transformation.
The eighty thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) are transformed into eighty thousand *samādhis*, *dhāraṇīs*, and so forth;

because these numbers have thus been transmuted, one does not destroy skillful means (*upāya*), is not defiled by skillful means, is not obstructed by skillful means, and does not grasp at skillful means, thereby purifying skillful means and accomplishing the four virtues.
Because these four virtues benefit others, they are called "skillful means. Because the various numerical categories no longer function, it is called [the unconditioned].

Because it is utterly pure, it does not arise; because it is a skillful means (*upāya*), it does not cease. This is how all numerical categories, in their very essence, constitute the skillful means of *nirvāṇa*.
△ Third, the conclusion: This is called the contemplation of the mind as the three *nirvāṇas*. The six stages of identity (*liù jí*) in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* are as previously explained.
This may be understood. △ Ninth, the contemplation of the Three Jewels: first, the heading;
next, the contemplation of the mind as the Three Jewels of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
△ Second, the explanation: first, establishing the contemplation to manifest the Dharma.
Contemplate closely that the single thought-moment is simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle; this is itself the Three Jewels.
△ Second, clarifying the contemplation by means of the dharmas: First, discussing the Three Jewels collectively by means of the truths, wisdom, and their union.
Second, establishing the Three Jewels individually by means of the nature of cultivation and their union. The intent of this explanation is, in brief, because the three...

Regarding the mutual relationship between the nature and the manifestations of the Jewels, there is both opening and closing. First, by discussing the closing based on the opening, one Threefold Jewel is established through nine meanings.
Next, by discussing the opening based on the closing, three Threefold Jewels are established within the three names. The first section has three parts;
the first relies on the sūtra to establish the names.
What is it that non-awakening is called the Jewel of Dharma, awakening is called the Jewel of Buddha, and harmony is called the Jewel of Sangha?
They are a single essence; the Buddha is termed awakening, the Dharma is termed non-awakening, and the Sangha is termed harmony. △ Second, explaining the characteristics by way of their meaning.
Because the principle of the three truths is not awakened to, it is the Dharma Jewel; because the wisdom of the three truths is able to awaken, it is the Buddha Jewel;

and because the three truths and the three wisdoms are in mutual correspondence and harmony, they constitute the Sangha Jewel. Without the truth, wisdom does not arise; without wisdom, the truth is not revealed.
If the truth and wisdom are not in harmony, they cannot manifest the great function to benefit sentient beings.

Since these Three Jewels emerge as different names for the same Three Virtues (*triguṇa*), and each of the Three Virtues mutually contains the other, it is discussed that each of the Three Jewels possesses all three.
Therefore, the Three Jewels do not exist in isolation. Of these, one is the unawakened nature (*prakṛti*), while the other two are cultivated (*bhāvanā*).

Each of the two cultivated aspects also has its own three, and the nature itself likewise has its three. Since the three within this nature have not yet been awakened to, they are collectively termed "unawakened" (*abodha*), even though...
Because one has not yet awakened to the principle that the fundamental truths are inherently correct, they are called the Three Truths; this constitutes the Jewel of the Dharma.
When the practice arises from the complete nature and the wisdom of the Three Truths is perfected, one is able to awaken—this is therefore called the Jewel of the Buddha.

Because these three types of awakening-wisdom correspond to and harmonize with the three truths of the nature, they are called the Jewel of the Sangha. Without the dharmas of the Three Truths, there would be no Three Wisdoms, and without the Truths, there would be no Buddha.
The wisdom-harmonious Sangha of the three liberations. △ Third, the meaning of the summary dedication to the Treasures:
These three types are all worthy of honor and respect; therefore, they are all called "Treasures. The six [aspects] are as previously described.

This Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha—the wisdom of the truths, the perfection of the ultimate, the wondrous function, the vastness, the reality, the worthy respect, and the accomplishment of the meaning of treasure—are all thus, not merely the ultimate fruit.
△ Next, the text is divided into three parts; first, regarding the nature-endowment (*prakṛti-guṇa*), the three are equally unawakened.

Furthermore, the failure to awaken to the middle truth is called the Jewel of the Dharma; the failure to awaken to the ultimate truth is called the Jewel of the Buddha; and the failure to awaken to the conventional truth is called the Jewel of the Sangha.
Because these three truths abide in their original nature and have not yet given rise to the wisdom that realizes them through cultivated virtue, all three truths are termed "unawakened."
When awakened, these three truths are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) within the Three Virtues; as such, they correspond to the Dharma Jewel.
Because they are true wisdom (*prajñā*), they correspond to the Buddha Jewel; because they are conventional liberation, they correspond to the Sangha Jewel.

If one did not point to the three truths within delusion as the Three Jewels, how could it be manifested that the two types of cultivation are subsumed within the nature? This would not be possible without awakening.
Then there would be no Buddha or Sangha. △ Second, regarding the cultivation of virtue: all three are awakening.

Knowing that which is the Middle Way and detached from the two extremes is called the Dharma Jewel; knowing that which is emptiness is called the Buddha Jewel; knowing that which is the provisional is called the Sangha Jewel.
The three types of knowledge exist within cultivation and are all capable of awakening and comprehension; therefore, the Three Jewels are all established based on the name "knowledge.
These three knowledges are also the three virtues: the essence of the knowledge of the ultimate is the Dharma-body, and thus it corresponds to the Jewel of the Dharma;

the essence of the knowledge of emptiness is Prajñā, and thus it corresponds to the Jewel of the Buddha; the essence of the knowledge of the conventional is liberation, and thus it corresponds to the Jewel of the Sangha.
If the Sangha Jewel did not take the three wisdoms as the Three Jewels, how could one know that enlightened wisdom is able to encompass both the rational essence and its transformative function?
△ Third, regarding the correspondence of the three being in harmonious union.

The harmony between the provisional (事) and the principle (理) is called the Dharma Jewel; the harmony between emptiness (空) and the provisional and principle is called the Buddha Jewel; and the harmony between the provisional and the principle and the conventional (假) is called the Sangha Jewel.

Because the three types of wisdom (三智) pertain to cultivation (修), they all belong to the provisional; because the three truths (三諦) pertain to nature (性), they all belong to the principle. Thus, the three truths and the three [wisdoms]...
Since wisdom is in all cases associated [with these three], it is therefore explained through their harmony in relation to the Three Jewels; for these three are also the three virtues (*guṇa*).
Among the Three Jewels, the essence of the harmony between phenomenon and principle is the *dharmakāya*, and thus corresponds to the Jewel of Dharma.

The essence of the harmony between phenomenon and principle is *prajñā*, and thus corresponds to the Jewel of the Buddha. The essence of the harmony between phenomenon and principle is liberation (*vimukti*), and thus corresponds to the Jewel of the Saṃgha.

Therefore, although the Jewel of the Sangha consists of these three virtues, because they accord with the meaning of the correspondence between the Truths and Wisdom, there is liberation through all three together.
If these three meanings were not the Three Jewels, why would the three liberations be presented in conjunction with the three Truths and Wisdom?
Furthermore, according to our own school, why must there be three for each—regarding the Truths, regarding Wisdom, and regarding Liberation? What is the underlying intention here?

Those who read the two commentaries on the opening and closing of the Three Treasures of the Contemplation of the Mind in the *Jinwen* (Modern Script) edition and become startled or doubtful should know that they have not yet understood the intent behind the "three threes" of this school’s teachings and contemplations;
their mere talk and mere practice will yield no share in realization. Furthermore, regarding the harmony of phenomena and principle:

within a single thought-moment, the ten realms can be distinguished as phenomena and principle; if these three wisdoms accord with the three truths of the nine realms, [the ultimate unity is realized].
When names and phenomena are in harmony, if the three types of wisdom accord with the Buddha-realm and the three truths, this is the harmony of name and principle;
the harmony of phenomena refers to the Three Teachings and Three Treasures, while the harmony of principle refers to the Perfect Teaching and the Three Treasures.

In a single thought-moment, phenomenon and principle are not divided, yet their meanings are distinct. Regarding this, the third point of Master Gushan’s *Threefold Refutation* states: [The text continues with the refutation.]

Furthermore, it is said: "Non-awakening to the ultimate truth is called the Dharma; non-awakening to the true reality is called the Buddha; and non-awakening to the conventional truth is called the Sangha.
Now, "Buddha" is a Sanskrit term meaning "the Awakened One. Since this term is established based on the accomplishment of contemplation, how could it possibly contradict its own meaning?

Could it be that "Buddha" translates as "non-awakening"? Such talk is merely the ravings of one who is intoxicated by delusion; what benefit does it provide for the principles of the Dharma? The commentary states:

The Buddha is translated as "the Awakened One" (*buddha*). Who does not know that the previous classification established the name "Dharma Jewel" for those who are unawakened and the name "Buddha Jewel" for those who are awakened?

The combination [of these] is the "Sangha Jewel. These names and meanings are as clear as the sun. Now, in the subsequent explanation, the text states three times regarding the Buddha Jewel that he "knows.
Is this not the meaning of "Awakening"? Since "Buddha" was translated based on this sense of awakening, it is now said here to be "Ultimate Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*).

"Non-awakening is called the Buddha Jewel; non-awakening is called the Sangha Jewel. This is intended to lead people to understand that within the Dharma Jewel itself, the Buddha and Sangha are fully present.
Since these Three Jewels take the Dharma as their primary essence, all three are said to be "non-awakening.

Because this corresponds to the meaning of the *prajñā* of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*) according to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it is the Buddha in the conventional sense who possesses this awakening.

Because they have attained liberation, they are called the Sangha; yet none of them possess the wisdom of awakening or non-awakening. Therefore, the Three Jewels are collectively termed "non-awakening.
Those people do not understand that the True Dharma of the Dharma Jewel is the nature of *prajñā*; thus, they falsely refute it by claiming that "non-awakening" is the opposite of the Buddha.
Furthermore, the three aspects of the Buddha Jewel are all established from "knowing," while the three aspects of the Sangha Jewel are all established from "harmony."
The *Sūtra of the Increase of Intention* (*Saṃcayagāthā*) states: "To know is called the Buddha; to be free from [conceptualization] is the Dharma; to be non-existent is the Saṅgha.

Since all three are described as "knowing," this is an opening of the Three Jewels based on the meaning of "awakening" (*bodhi*). Since the meaning of awakening is thus established, it is logically consistent that the meanings of "non-awakening" (*abodhi*) and "harmony" (*saṃgha*) should each also be opened into three.
Because the faculties of sentient beings were sharp during the Buddha's lifetime, there was no need to explain them exhaustively; only in such a manner can they be so named.
The Three Jewels as a single essence are non-dual and indistinguishable from the three virtues; were it otherwise, how could one contemplate them as fused and wondrous in a single thought-moment?
If such meanings were not personally proclaimed by the four types of eloquence, how could one reach the ultimate pinnacle of the Three Jewels?
Thus we know that correct speech may seem contrary to expectation, yet others cannot believe it; this is indeed a delusive deception born of spiritual intoxication.
This will lead to total ruin. △ Third, concluding the teaching and returning to the title:
that which is "Middle" is named Gold; that which is "Emptiness" is named Light; that which is "Provisional" is named Brightness.
△ Third, the conclusion.
This constitutes the contemplation of the Three Jewels within the mind; the six stages of realization (*ṣaḍ-yoga*) are as previously described.
△ Tenth: Contemplating the Three Virtues. First, the heading.
Next, regarding the contemplation of the Three Virtues within the mind in the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa*:
△ Second, the explanation of the three [aspects], which has three parts: first, the direct listing of the three contemplations.
One contemplates the single thought-moment as being simultaneously empty, provisionally existent, and the Middle Way.

△ Second, clarifying the virtues through contemplation, which has two parts: first, the primary virtue of correct contemplation; within this, first, clarifying the contemplation by way of the Perfect [Teaching]. First...
To demonstrate contemplation: because it is empty, when one is empty, all are empty; there is neither the provisional nor the middle, yet it is not an emptiness that is void.

It has no accumulation, yet it is called a "treasury" (*kośa*); because this treasury is fully complete, it is termed "virtue. Because it is provisional, when one is provisional, all are provisional. There is no [middle].
Within emptiness and the absence of self-nature, there is no reliance on the provisional; yet, because it encompasses all phenomena, it is also called a "treasury" (*garbha*).

Because this treasury is fully endowed, it is termed a "virtue. Since it is precisely the Middle Way, within this one, all things are the Middle. There is nothing empty and nothing provisional that is not the Middle.
Because the Middle encompasses all phenomena, it is also called a "treasury. Because this treasury is fully endowed, it is designated as a "virtue."

The essence of the three perfect virtues (triguṇa) necessarily possesses one another; each one is itself the three. Neither vertical nor horizontal, this alone is called the Secret Treasury (*guhyakośa*).
Although the Great Master’s stage was that of the fifth grade, he was able to know the Tathāgata’s profound secret treasury.
Taking this secret treasury as both truth and contemplation, he integrated all objects within it. Now, realizing that the nature of a single thought-moment is these three virtues...
Because the three virtues constitute the three contemplations, it is clarified that each of the three contemplations mutually encompasses the others.

At the beginning of each, the word "immediately" (*ji*) is used to indicate that the single thought-moment is itself the three truths. Thus, when it first says "immediately empty," it does not mean immediately the partial emptiness;
rather, it means contemplating the single thought-moment as the perfect emptiness. This emptiness is able to shatter the mutual attachments among the three truths; therefore, it is said:

"One emptiness is all emptiness" means that there is nothing—neither the provisional nor the middle—that is not empty. This does not mean that the contemplation of emptiness alone destroys the marks of phenomena;
the provisional and the middle can likewise destroy the marks of phenomena. Why is this? Because destroying marks through emptiness is to destroy the conventional by means of the real;
destroying marks through the provisional is to destroy the real by means of the conventional; and destroying marks through the middle is to simultaneously negate both extremes.
These three [emptinesses] suddenly shatter [the notion of] names; when they are ultimately empty, once the marks have been shattered, what accumulation could there be?

Nevertheless, they fully possess the Three Truths—neither vertical nor horizontal—which is the Secret Treasury. Because it can store and is fully endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity, it is called the virtue of *prajñā*.
Next, it says: "It is precisely the provisional, yet not identical to the partial provisional; this is the contemplation of a single thought-moment as the wondrous provisional. This...
Because it is able to provisionally establish the dharmas of the three truths, it is said that "the one is provisional, and all are provisional.

When it is said that there is nothing empty or middle that is not provisional, this does not mean that only the contemplation of the provisional can establish dharmas within emptiness and the middle; the other two contemplations can also establish dharmas.

Why? Because establishing dharmas through emptiness means establishing the conventional within the ultimate, and establishing dharmas through the provisional means establishing the ultimate within the conventional.
The conventional view establishes the Middle Way to simultaneously illumine the two truths; these three established together are termed "wondrous conventionality" (*miaojia*).

Since they encompass the three truths without being either vertical or horizontal, they are called the "Secret Treasury" (*mimizang*). This treasury is fully endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which are termed the "virtue of liberation.
Next, it is said that "the Middle is not identical [to the conventional]," yet this refers to the Middle that possesses all virtues within a single thought-moment (*ekacitta*).
Because this [Middle Way] contains the wondrous Dharma of the three truths within itself, it is said that "within one, all are included.

To say there is nothing that is not empty, not provisional, and not the Middle means that it is not only the Middle that contemplates phenomena as being beyond dependence; emptiness and the provisional are likewise able to be beyond dependence in their respective places.

Why is this? Because emptiness is the Middle, the Truth of Ultimate Reality (paramārtha-satya) is beyond dependence; because the provisional is the Middle, the Truth of Conventional Reality (saṃvṛti-satya) [is beyond dependence].

Because the Middle is the Middle that transcends all dependence, it simultaneously negates and simultaneously illuminates, severing all forms of relative dependence. These three aspects being suddenly severed is called "Perfect Middle" (*yuanzhong*).

Since it encompasses the Three Truths without being either vertical or horizontal, it is named the "Secret Treasury. This Treasury is fully endowed with permanence, bliss, self, and purity, which are termed the virtues of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya-guṇa*).
Regarding the various phrases listed in the contemplation of these three virtues, they exist solely in their state of detachment.

Within the partial refutations, the partial establishments, and the distinct contemplations, one who grasps this meaning finds both subject and object stilled, such that speech and thought are entirely forgotten;
thus it is called "inconceivable contemplation. Only in this way is the secret treasury of the three virtues revealed.
△ Second, the explanation of the Perfect [Teaching].

Although it is said that the one contains the immeasurable and the immeasurable contains the one, and that they arise from one another in a reciprocal succession, the wise who understand that these arisings are not real have nothing to fear.
One should know that the one is neither few nor many; it is neither one nor many, yet it does not lose its nature as one or many.
It is inconceivable; it is neither vertical nor horizontal, neither unified nor distinct.
From "one" up to "fearlessness," all are words from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. "One" refers to taking up a single dharma;
"immeasurable" refers to all dharmas. If one subsumes all dharmas within the three truths (*trisatya*), there is nothing left out.
Furthermore, among these three truths, each truth may be designated as "one. Thus, this "one" and "three" revolve and interpenetrate one another.

The arising [of this contemplation] is as explained in the text of the "Contemplation on Manifesting": there is this contemplative understanding that hearing of one does not diminish the three virtues, and hearing of the three does not increase the one;

one should know that below, it further uses the one and the many to form four propositions, manifesting the inconceivable, transcending the vertical and horizontal, and accomplishing the Contemplation of the Secret Treasury. △ Second, entrusting the Buddha’s meritorious virtues, part two.
Initially, the manifestation of virtue is established through contemplation.
Because all Buddhas take the Middle Way as their essence, they are called the Dharma-body; because they take Emptiness as their life-force, they are called Prajñā;
because they take the Provisional as their power, they are called Liberation. Each of these is eternally blissful, self, and pure, without any deficiency or diminution.
Therefore, it is called the "Three Virtues.

The Buddha-body, life-force, and power are accomplished through the three contemplations; how much more so since the essence and the others are empty, provisional, and the middle, which cannot be divided into the means of accomplishment and that which is accomplished.
△ Second, explaining why the Buddha’s body receives the name of "Treasury" (Garbha).
Each and every one is called the "Secret Treasury" because the Dharma-realm contains and stores within it a great abundance.
△ Second, praising the mind and its objects has two parts; first, praising the essentials based on the sutras.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The liberation of all Buddhas should be sought within the mental activities of all sentient beings."
All Buddhas possess the three kinds of liberation: true nature (*dharmatā*), real wisdom (*prajñā*), and skillful means (*upāya*).
Although it is here said simply "liberation," this is intended to convey that within one there are many. These three liberations are non-dual and indistinguishable from the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

However, because the Buddha-dharma is so sublime, it is difficult for those at the initial stage; since the mind and the Buddha are without difference, contemplating the mind makes it easy. Thus it is.

Therefore, one is instructed to seek [the truth] within the activities of the mind; the mind of sentient beings is itself emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. The middle is the true nature; emptiness is real wisdom;
the provisional is skillful means. Although their levels differ, their nature is non-dual.

Thus, by contemplating the mind, one attains the liberation of Buddhahood. Now, when contemplating these ten dharmas, the principle is the same for all. △ Second, the analogy of the three being without difference.
"You should know that my mind is thus, and sentient beings are also thus; since it is so for them and for me, it is likewise for all Buddhas.
Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction.

Since the three virtues and three liberations of other beings and other Buddhas are identical to the three virtues of one's own mind, how could they differ from what is contemplated? △ Third, the conclusion.
Regarding the title of the *Dharmapada*:
one who grasps this meaning realizes that the "Middle" (zhong) is gold, the "Empty" (kong) is light, and the "Provisional" (jia) is clarity.
Since the three characters of the title are the names for the Three Virtues (triguṇa) in their essential nature, the three contemplations (sanzuan) are applied here in correspondence with gold.
The meaning of "equality" (等) shall manifest the three virtues (三德) through the three contemplations (三觀). △ Third, the conclusion:
This constitutes the three virtues of contemplating the mind (觀心三德) within the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* according to the six stages of identity (六即), as previously exemplified.
△ Third, refuting false emptiness (邪空) to reveal the merit of contemplating the mind, in three parts: first, describing that false emptiness.
In this world, there are practitioners of emptiness who cling to a deluded emptiness that does not accord with the Buddha’s sūtras.
Upon hearing this teaching on the contemplation of the mind, they raise an objection, saying: "If the contemplation of the mind is the Dharma-body, it should be equal in all places.

Why, then, do you give rise to reverence for scriptures and images while giving rise to contempt for paper and wood? Since reverence and contempt are distinct, there is no equality. Because there is no equality, [it is not] the Dharma."
Since the meaning of the body is not established, and because there is no equality, the wisdom of equality is not established; if that wisdom is absent, the reward-body (saṃbhogakāya) does not exist.
Furthermore, the meaning of the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) that brings others to maturity cannot be established. It is not as I [teach]:

regarding scriptures, images, paper, and wood with equal and impartial equanimity—this is called the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Possessing this wisdom of equality is the reward-body; employing this wisdom to transform others is the transformation-body.
The meaning of my three bodies as the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) is fully established; consider for yourself, what is the purpose of your contemplation?

All methods of contemplation now established rely upon the Buddha’s words. The Buddha commanded that one cultivate contemplation based on the sūtras so as to accord with the principle, and further taught that one should establish images to rely upon the semblance in order to contemplate the reality.
The sūtras expound the Buddha’s mind, and the images depict the Buddha’s physical form. If these two are not revered, what is there to contemplate?

By establishing the principle of "present action" as the primary cultivation and employing respectful ritual procedures as an auxiliary to the Path, worldly fools—unaware of this intent—erroneously cling to the view of a deluded emptiness.

They now claim that contemplating the mind and again showing reverence to scriptures and images contradicts equality, asserting that the cultivation of contemplation is thus difficult and that the Three Bodies cannot be realized; they then cling instead to the Buddha’s scriptures and the Buddha himself.
Regarding images and other paper or wood [objects], I do not give rise to a mind of reverence toward the scriptures and images, nor do I give rise to a mind of arrogance toward other paper and wood.

In practicing for myself and transforming others, the meaning of the three bodies is fulfilled; yet by means of this "emptiness of ignorance," I destroy the current practice that unites the primary and auxiliary [teachings]. △ Second, refutation by means of facts.

If one encounters such an objection, one should respond with three counter-arguments: First, you claim that scriptures and images made of paper or wood are equal [to those made of precious materials].

By what reasoning, then, do you show reverence to wooden images in the seven ancestral temples while showing fear and respect toward the Emperor’s edicts, yet give rise to contempt for Buddhist scriptures and images?
Once such fear and contempt arise, they cause all things to boil over into chaos. Why is this so?
First, do you possess the meaning of the equal Dharma-body? Second, toward those who study under the same teacher as yourself, you give rise to affection and protection;

yet toward those who study under a different teacher, you give rise to pride and resentment. Since love, pride, and resentment arise from delusion, the three poisons burn fiercely and all evils become even more severe—how could you possibly possess the wisdom of the Reward-body?
Third, you are addicted to the emptiness of delusion and lack the skillful means of wisdom.
Since you still do not delight in the situation of others, yet harbor pride and self-importance, you are a person of overweening conceit (*adhimāna*).

Your teacher has fallen into this error, and you have followed him in his fall. The poisonous influence has penetrated deeply; if you intend to transform others with such deviant energy while harmonizing your light, where then would your manifested body (*nirmāṇakāya*) be?

Since his attachment to the empty words of ignorance is both hollow and extravagant, we shall examine his anger and pride through three points; thus, the three bodies [of the Buddha] are not established.

First, the doctrine of equality is refuted as being unestablished: since you must revere and fear the imperial decrees of the temple, why do you treat the scriptures and images of the Buddha with such contempt?
Once fear and pride arise, the various afflictions (*kleśa*) blaze forth, and the Dharma of equality is not established.

1. First, regarding the body: when one is at ease, the two [extremes] are destroyed, yet wisdom is not perfected; as teacher and student are divided into two parts, both hatred and attachment are established.

Once hatred and attachment have arisen, this is verified as folly. Folly is not wisdom; thus the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) is lost. 2. Second, regarding transforming others: it is not accomplished because of delusion and emptiness.
Without the wisdom of skillful means, one is bound by attachment; one gives rise to the view of ordinary fools, and the mind of pride arises toward those who are superior.

It is traditionally said that such a master and disciple will inevitably fall into the perverse influences of the three poisons; as these enter the minds of others, there is no benefit whatsoever, and where, then, is their response-body?
△ Third, the observation of present virtues.
While I was at the stage of an ordinary person, I contemplated the true nature of reality as it is;

furthermore, desiring to reveal this true nature, I venerated scriptures and images so that wisdom would not be bound, and I led immeasurable people to honor what is good and abandon what is evil so that skillful means would not be bound.
How could my conduct possibly be the same as yours?
Those who falsely denigrate the contemplation of the mind based on superficial evidence have committed a grave error. To briefly establish the practice of contemplating the mind:

if one again reveres the scriptures and images, what merit does this entail? A brief discussion reveals two aspects: namely, skillful means accompanied by wisdom, and wisdom accompanied by skillful means.
When these two are both understood, they serve as the cause for the three bodies (*trikāya*); that is to say, it clarifies that both delusion and emptiness are [ultimately] identical.
Regarding the statement that "the bonds are not the root of the three bodies, yet they are the basis for the two merits": at the stage of an ordinary person, one cultivates perfect, true wisdom;
because this wisdom is supported by the skillful means of revering scriptures and images, it is not bound. Guided by this unbound wisdom, one respectfully admonishes and encourages sentient beings;

thus, one is further able to ensure that these skillful means are not bound. As for the cause of the three bodies being "wisdom with skillful means," it is because there is both wisdom and skillful means.

The ability to manifest the *saṃbhogakāya* through skillful means and wisdom, and the fact that the true reality revealed by the *saṃbhogakāya* is itself the *dharmakāya*—how could this be the same as establishing the three bodies based on a deluded emptiness? △ Second, re-explaining the two characters according to their meaning, part one:
the heading.
Regarding the current further explanation of the term "Emperor" (Dìwáng):
in the seven-fascicle version translated by Paramārtha, the title of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa* was additionally provided with the characters "Emperor" (Dìwáng).

As for the present *Chàn jīng* (Prophecy Scripture), it only indicates these three characters; therefore, the preceding text states that if one follows the four-fascicle title, one should simply use these three characters.
Regarding the two characters "Emperor" (Dìwáng), according to the scriptural text, they carry the meaning of "King of Sutras. Whether one explains them or not, there is no contradiction.
Although the Great Master’s commentary on the title previously relied on the literal text to discuss only these three characters, he now again clarifies "Emperor" based on its doctrinal significance.
Thus, in the "Chapter on Translation," this master fully cites both the Indic and Chinese terms from Paramārtha’s version.

The title of this translation is most detailed, serving as the foundation for the present re-explanation. △ Second, regarding the explanation, first it is interpreted according to the True Dharma (Paramārtha) school.
The Tripitaka Master Paramārtha stated:
"The Dharmakāya subsumes the Avataṃsaka, because the Avataṃsaka takes the Dharmakāya as its essence; [the Sambhogakāya...]"
Because Prajñāpāramitā subsumes wisdom, the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) subsumes nirvāṇa;
because nirvāṇa elucidates the hundredfold liberation, the four virtues, and so forth, this is the meaning of that Master’s elucidation of the sovereign governance of the Emperor.
After translating this sutra, Paramārtha explained the term "emperor" (*cakravartin*) through the sense of comprehensive integration.

He correlated the three bodies (*trikāya*) with the meanings of the three sutras, stating: "While other sutras each speak of only one body, this sutra possesses the names and meanings of all three bodies;
therefore, it is able to integrate sutras such as the *Avataṃsaka*. For this reason, it receives the title of 'Emperor,' which distinguishes and encompasses the three bodies."

The distinctions between superior and inferior [interpretations] are fully detailed as refuted in the commentary; this present explanation was surely made merely to suit the capacities of the audience.

△ Second, explaining the interpretation of the present master, in two parts: first, explaining that it must possess three meanings, in three sections: first, stating the names and providing a brief indication.
Now it is clarified that an Emperor-King (*dìwáng*) should possess three meanings: namely, Emperor (*dì*), Wisdom (*huì*), and King (*wáng*).
Because one wishes to correlate the teaching, contemplation, and the perfect [teaching] with the three dharmas, it is shown that an Emperor-King must necessarily possess the meaning of wisdom;

thus, divine planning and sagely strategy constitute "Emperor," while being the ultimate nobility constitutes "King" and the assembly of the court constitutes "Wisdom. These three meanings together are called "Emperor-Wisdom."
"King. △ Second, the explanation of the three meanings:

"Emperor" (Di) signifies the ultimate nobility, being most supreme and most venerable; "Wisdom" (Hui) signifies divine planning and sagely strategy; "King" (Wang) signifies that the myriad nations assemble in court.
Possessing these three meanings, he is called the Emperor-Wisdom-King (Dihuiwang).
This meaning remains merely an analogy for others, whereas according to our own Master, it refers to the actual substance itself. △ Third, citation of scripture to establish the proof:
This sutra is also thus;
the Tathāgata dwells within immeasurable and profoundly deep *dharmatā*, transcending all that is practiced by Bodhisattvas.

Regarding the exclusion of the śāstras: while the aforementioned sūtras and śāstras are all included, there are certain śāstras that must be excluded. These are the śāstras that do not accord with the principles of the Mahāyāna. Specifically, this refers to the śāstras of the Hīnayāna schools, such as the Sarvāstivāda and the Sautrāntika. For example, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and the *Nyāyānusāra-śāstra* are śāstras of the Sarvāstivāda school; although they occasionally cite Mahāyāna doctrines, their fundamental intent lies in the Small Vehicle. Similarly, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and the *Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra* are also śāstras of the Sarvāstivāda school and must likewise be excluded.
