Wisdom and abandonment are also general terms for the three bodies (*trikāya*) upon the fruit.
The lifespan is obtained through the cultivation of the path; therefore, it is called "fruition" (*vipāka*).

Since the attainment of fruition and the realization of retribution necessarily involve both wisdom and abandonment (*jñāna-prahāṇa*) in their entirety, and since these combined aspects of wisdom and abandonment collectively possess the three bodies (*trikāya*), one must understand them as follows: wisdom is the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*), and abandonment is the response body (*nirmāṇakāya*).

Because these two are entirely identical in essence to the dharma body (*dharmakāya*), it should be known that the present sutra clarifies the lifespan as the fruition which is capable of subsuming both.

Virtue and the three bodies. △ Second, clarifying the fusion and subtlety of the essence and substance. Part one: Regarding the mutual inclusion based on the three bodies being in accordance with their nature.

Since the three bodies at the level of fruition are in profound accord with the *dharmatā*, and since the *dharmatā* is neither permanent nor impermanent, the three bodies are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent.
Since the dharma-nature (dharmatā) can be both eternal and non-eternal, the three bodies (trikāya) can likewise be both eternal and non-eternal.
Question: How does the dharma-body (dharmakāya) further merge with the dharma-nature? Answer:

Since this text states that the three bodies on the level of fruition merge with the dharma-nature, it is because one cultivates the three [bodies] so as to merge them into the nature. Therefore, it is said that the dharma-nature is neither eternal nor non-eternal.
The eternal is able to be the eternal and the non-eternal; is this not the three natures?

Because the three bodies of the ultimate cultivation are in profound accord with the nature, each of the three bodies possesses three meanings. This arises because the three natures mutually contain one another to form nine, thereby causing the three bodies of cultivation to likewise form nine meanings, manifesting that there is no separate cultivation. Thus, the two [sets of] nine have no dual substance; they are simply one.
Nine times nine is merely three times three; it is not fixed as three times three, for it is merely one instance. To speak of "nine" is neither to diminish nor to increase;
the cultivation of nature is perfectly complete and wondrous—such is its meaning. △ Second, regarding the two bodies, because they are identical with the Dharma, they are inconceivable.
If one can realize impermanence, this is the lifespan of the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) as it is discussed in contrast to impermanence.

If one can realize permanence, this is the lifespan of the *saṃbhogakāya* (reward body). Since the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) is neither permanent nor impermanent and cannot be calculated, the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya* are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent and cannot be calculated. How then can one see their traces as short?
It is said that the Buddha’s lifespan is definitely short.

Previously, this was discussed in terms of the principle of separation, where both the cultivated and the innate natures each have three aspects; now, however, we proceed from the perspective of integration.

Thus, the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) are darkly merged with the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature). Since these two are identical to that nature, how could they be known by calculation? Therefore, the lifespan of the eighty *nirmāṇakāya*s is not [limited].

One may calculate that for this reason, all four verses state that the World-Honored One’s meaning here is that because the nature (*dharmatā*) is revealed through the vehicle of fruition (*phala-yāna*), the two bodies share the same lifespan as the *dharmatā*. △ Third, revealing the loss by addressing doubts.
This illustrates the meaning that the fruit can manifest the essence through non-recognition.

If one with the mark of faith (*śraddhā-lakṣaṇa*) knew that the fruit can manifest the essence as being neither permanent nor impermanent, yet capable of being both permanent and impermanent, they would never perceive its deficiency and would certainly not call it deficient.
△ Second, the explanation by way of analogy regarding transformative deeds has two parts: first, establishing the analogy.
Furthermore, just as the Buddha cannot be manifested as a deer or a horse by means of a deer or a horse— though the deer or horse is certainly the Buddha—
is it not the case that the deer or horse is produced by the Buddha’s transformation (nirmāṇa) and is not his actual body?
△ Second, the summary and explanation.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) can manifest as long or short, yet long and short are not the nature of phenomena itself.
What is called "long and short" is not the nature of phenomena; in reality, long and short are entirely the nature of phenomena.

It is simply because those who are deluded fixate rigidly on long and short and fail to recognize the nature of phenomena that they point to long and short and designate them as "not the nature of phenomena."
If one perceives the dharma-nature, one will certainly be able to discern length and shortness within it.
△ Second, the manifestation of attainment: If one perceives this meaning, one will indeed be able to manifest the essence;

the meaning of permanence is established, the meaning of being neither permanent nor impermanent is established, the meaning of impermanence is established, and the meaning of the ultimate thesis is established. If it were not so, none of these meanings would be established.
This is established.
If one perceives this meaning, it refers to the intent of establishing the present fruition as the thesis (*siddhānta*). If this intent is established, all other meanings are likewise established.
Why? Because the fruition that manifests the essence by unifying the two natures and discussing the three bodies is precisely the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (enjoyment body).

The meaning of the "body" (kāya) is established as being eternal; how could the essence manifested [by it] not be the Dharma-body? The meaning of being neither eternal nor non-eternal is thus established.

Since the Dharma-body and Reward-body are unified, the Response-body accords with the capacities of sentient beings—this is the meaning of non-eternality. These meanings are established through practice, based on the realization of the fruit.
Taking the realization of the fruit as the essential tenet, its meaning is well-established. The fruit is the pivotal point for manifesting the essence, just like [the example of] *tī* (a key).

The *Jiangmu* (Outline) establishes that [the text] is trustworthy and not deceptive. Regarding the question of the phrasing: "If it is said that the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) can be both permanent and impermanent, then being permanent would also mean it is the *nirmāṇakāya*.
Why, then, in the current text, is permanence attributed solely to the *vipākakāya* (retribution body), while the *nirmāṇakāya* is said to be only impermanent?

Answer: The *vipākakāya* is indeed the *dharmakāya*. It is the *dharmakāya* that employs these two modes—permanence and impermanence. It is the *dharmakāya* which [manifests as] the *vipākakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*. Therefore, permanence belongs to the *dharmakāya*, and the *nirmāṇakāya* is characterized by impermanence. Thus, there is no contradiction.
Because its essential nature does not belong exclusively to one side, the Dharma-body is said to be neither permanent nor impermanent.
While the Reward-body belongs to permanence and the Response-body should belong to impermanence, the text states that the Response-body can be permanent;

this is because it can manifest for humans and devas in countless ways, thereby revealing the function of the eternally abiding Dharma-nature, and is thus called "permanent. If compared to the Reward-body, however, the Response-body is short-lived.

Since both [positions] should be termed "impermanent," this does not contradict the explanation provided below. △ Second, distinguishing the incorrect interpretations of ancient masters, in two parts: first, the narrative.

Formerly, the text regarding "mountain-weights and ocean-drops" was used to claim that what is impermanent refers to the spatial boundaries of empty space (*ākāśa*), while [the essence of] empty space itself is not.

Furthermore, regarding the passage in the "Chapter on Sacrificing the Body" that seeks a permanent and blissful dwelling, these three unconditioned states are considered "permanent" because they are devoid of birth and death,
and "blissful" for that same reason.
△ Second, the refutation.
All such interpretations that attempt to explain the Mahāyāna through narrow-minded or convoluted reasoning fail entirely; they do not capture the essential tenets of the school.
Regarding this interpretation by the ancient masters, there are briefly two faults: first, they are unable to distinguish between the essential natures of the Great and Small Vehicles. Therefore...
The threefold interpretation of the three kinds of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [dharmas] in the Tripiṭaka and the four virtues of the fruit in the Vaipulya [sūtras] are both misunderstood.
Here, one does not realize that the fruit-principle of this sūtra reveals the essence; thus, the fruit-person, the fruit-dharma, and the fruit-lifespan are in harmony with the *dharmatā*.

Since the *dharmatā* is neither permanent nor impermanent, the fruit-person, the fruit-dharma, and the fruit[-lifespan] are likewise neither permanent nor impermanent. Yet, the *dharmatā* is capable of being both permanent and impermanent.
The fruits of Buddhahood and the dharmas of the fruits can be both eternal and impermanent, because the three bodies of the fruit are all identical with the nature (dharmatā).

For this reason, each of the three bodies mutually contains the others. Because ancient [masters] were deluded regarding this, they judged them to be impermanent based on the analogy of a drop in the ocean;
having thus lost the principle that cultivation and nature are mutually fused, although they established the core tenets of their scriptures, they were entirely devoid of essential meaning. △ Four.
Regarding the function of the treatise: because it accords with the fruit and the hidden essence of the school, it possesses a great utility. It is like a mirror or a drum;

by being polished or struck, it manifests images or emits sound. This general explanation of the name covers all three [aspects], but now we shall specifically demonstrate one. This is divided into three parts: first, indicating the general name.
The fourth [section] clarifies "function" (*yong*), which refers to "efficacy" (*li-yong*).

By explaining "function" through "efficacy," the meaning of the term is established. It is not merely the capacity for endurance; rather, the two meanings—efficacy and the absence of non-action—are mutually illuminating to demonstrate the universal name.
△ Second, the formal explanation of this scripture has two parts: first, indicating the four names.
The eradication of evil and the generation of good constitute the power and function of the Sūtra. It is called "power" because it eradicates evil, and "function" because it generates good;
it is called "merit" because it eradicates evil, and "virtue" because it generates good. These are partial designations; when discussed in their entirety, they are all fully present.
First, let us summarize the thesis that the cessation of evil and the production of good arise from the profound essence.
This is called "powerful function" (*li-yòng*), which spontaneously manifests as the capacity to extinguish evil and produce good for all sentient beings. If we distinguish them specifically:

"power" (*lì*) is able to extinguish evil, while "function" (*yòng*) is able to produce good. Because it extinguishes evil, power achieves its fulfillment; because it produces good, function achieves its virtue. Therefore...
To make it easy to understand, the text specifically mentions [the power] by citing its merits;
however, if one were to follow the principle exhaustively, each and every merit is capable of extinguishing evil and generating goodness. △ Second, clarifying the intent of the sutra, in two parts:
first, clarifying that the accomplishment of the fruit-wisdom is due to merits.
Now, the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) is a virtue belonging to the state of fruition;
this fruitional wisdom is adorned by immeasurable merits and eliminates all suffering while bestowing immeasurable bliss.
The "Introductory Chapter" states: "All-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*) serves as the root, adorned by immeasurable merits;
it eliminates all suffering and bestows immeasurable bliss. By means of this passage, the power of the sutra is clarified:

that which takes the wisdom of the fruition as the foundation for all practices reveals that those with the initial resolve realize their own fundamental nature is inherently endowed with these merits. Although...
Because the cultivation of adornment through immeasurable virtues is itself the nature of cultivation, there is nothing to be adorned;
because suffering is understood as being the nature itself, there is no suffering to be extinguished, and thus one is able to eliminate all suffering.

Because pleasure is known to be the nature itself, there is no pleasure to be bestowed, and thus one is able to universally bestow ultimate bliss. Question: As for what is now called the "wisdom of the fruit adorned with merit," this—

Question: When a practitioner cultivates repentance, praise, and so forth to eliminate evil and give rise to goodness while heading toward Bodhi, how can this be considered the power and function of the Sūtra?

Answer: The Buddha attained the essence of the Sūtra, and from that essence, power and function are manifested. What is meant by this? It refers to the teaching of repentance, praise, and the wisdom of emptiness;
when a practitioner cultivates these, they accomplish the power to eliminate evil and the skillful application to give rise to goodness. Thus it is adorned.

If one perfects fundamental wisdom to achieve Buddha-wisdom, how could it be accomplished through the power of the scriptures alone without cultivation? It is like a wonderful medicine of this world: if not taken, it has no efficacy.
△ Second, showing the power and function of the text’s intent and its sequential arrangement, in three parts: first, clarifying the two chapters of Repentance and Praise;
second, clarifying how the two practices result in fruition; third, clarifying the sequence of the two chapters. First, clarifying the sequence of the two chapters.
Suffering is the fruit of unwholesome karma; greed, hatred, and delusion are the unwholesome causes. Since these unwholesome causes are not eliminated, the fruit cannot cease.

Because the intention of the Noble Ones is first to extinguish the unwholesome causes, the "Chapter on Repentance" (Kṣamāpanā) comes first. Happiness is the fruit of the wholesome; repentance and praise are its causes.

Since through repenting of offenses and praising the Noble Ones, evil is extinguished and the wholesome arises, the "Chapter on Praise" (Stuti) follows at the end. This is also an instance of mutual illustration.

Repentance is of three kinds: that performed through ritual procedure (*vidhi*), that which takes signs as its mark, and that which is non-arising (*anutpāda*). Non-arising is the primary [repentance], while the other two serve as its aids;
therefore, it can cause greed, anger, and delusion to be extinguished. These three afflictions have both general and specific aspects;

now, understanding these general and specific aspects, one dwells within a single thought-moment and suddenly illuminates their non-arising. When this is combined with the aid of ritual repentance, there is no evil that is not extinguished. This is praised.
The three aspects refer to praising the *zhàngliù* (six-foot) body, the *zūntè* (extraordinary) body, and the *fǎxìng* (dharma-nature).

Now, we specifically praise the *zūntè* body, which above corresponds to the dharma-nature and below manifests as the *zhàngliù* body. These three are identical to the one, and this one is identical to the three;

they are neither vertical nor horizontal, being inconceivable. Praising the Buddha in this way encompasses all virtues. Together with the preceding repentance, this serves as the cause for the eternal bliss [of Nirvana]. Based upon this...
Regarding the sequence of the chapters: first, one employs repentance and cleansing to purify the three karmas, and then pays homage and praises the Three Bodies.
If the power of the merit from praising the Buddha is used to support the repentance so that the three obstructions are extinguished, this sequence is also logically established;
thus, it is said that these are mentioned interchangeably. △ Second, clarifying the doctrine and essence that can be accomplished.
This supreme function is used to adorn and manifest the essence of the resultant wisdom that is fully equipped.

The resultant essence of the Buddha is the essence of the mind of sentient beings; the Buddha reveals two kinds of supreme functions—repentance and praise—and when sentient beings practice them, they achieve the cessation of evil and the generation of wholesome functions.
Adorned by these functions, one manifests the Dharma as identical to the resultant wisdom of the Buddha.
The Essential Nature (xìngtǐ). △ Third, it clarifies that the five meanings are fully present:

the manifestation of the essence is called "Gold" (jīn); the completeness of the attributes is called "Fruit" (guǒ); the perfection of power is called "Radiance" (guāng); and the benefit of others is called "Teaching" (jiào).

This passage follows from above, meaning that the practitioner’s wisdom is complete, the essence is manifested, and since the essence is manifested, it is named "Gold" (jīn). As for the essential nature...
The wisdom that manifests the fruit is designated as being identical to its essence; this wisdom is called the "Power of the Radiant Array of the Fruit.

Because one’s own practice has reached completion and is capable of bringing great benefit, it is termed "Luminous Benefit. Regarding the matter of benefiting others, there is nothing superior to the establishment of the teachings.

The three characters beginning with "Gold" correspond individually to the essence and so forth; taken together, these three constitute the name. Since the five [senses] are thus induced, they should likewise respond to the five.
Now, by showing one set of five, you have already included two sets of five. △ Second, explaining that the two chapters mutually possess each other’s content:

The Chapter on Repentance (Chān-pǐn) eliminates evil but does not fail to produce goodness; the Chapter on Praise (Zàn-pǐn) produces goodness but does not fail to eliminate evil. Thus, each chapter speaks of only one side.
As it is said, the fault of not cultivating roots of goodness is precisely the cultivation of goodness within repentance;
and the virtue of being able to detach from defiled attachment is precisely the eradication of evil within praise. For now, these have been explained according to their predominant aspects.
△ Second, the section on the Chapter on Emptiness, one passage.

The "Chapter on Emptiness" provides dual guidance: it shows that if one cannot realize emptiness, evil will not be eradicated through repentance; and it shows that if one cannot realize emptiness, good will not be purified through praise.
The text states, "All-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) is the root," which is precisely this meaning.

This chapter provides a comprehensive discourse on emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the provisional (*prajñapti*), and the middle (*madhyama*), which sweeps away the three delusions and establishes the ultimate emptiness that leads to the dual functions of repentance and praise.
If one does not illuminate the non-arising of the three delusions, then even if one repents, the root of evil will not be eliminated;
it may temporarily subside but will arise again. Therefore, it is said that "evil is not eradicated" if one does not illuminate the non-attainment of the three truths (*triratna*).

Even if one were to praise [the Buddha], it would not manifest the merit of the purity of nature; rather, it would still become a cause for outflows (*āsrava*). Therefore, it is said that "wholesomeness is not pure.
Now, by means of the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā-jñāna*), which is without arising and without attainment, repentance and praise can adorn the resultant wisdom (*phala-jñāna*).

Thus, the wisdom of emptiness mentioned in the introductory chapter (*nidāna-parivarta*) serves as the basis for repentance and praise. However, those of sharp faculties do not practice [this] in the preceding two chapters.

Since the "Repentance for Birth" (*shēngchàn*) already accords with the praise of the Sovereign Extraordinary Form (*zūntè*), how could it deviate from the wisdom of emptiness (*kōnghuì*)? Yet, because those of dull faculties (*dùnzhě*) remain obscure [to this truth], it is specifically taught here.
Thus, this chapter states: "For the sake of those with dull faculties, he gives rise to a heart of great compassion. △ Third, the various texts below this clarify [the meaning].

From the "Chapter on the Four Kings" onwards, protecting the sutra so that it may be widely disseminated is the cultivation of goodness; averting calamities so that they may depart is the eradication of evil.

Since the "Chapter on Ghosts and Spirits" states that all [beings] are great bodhisattvas and the like, we know that both the protection of the sutra and the averting of calamities [are performed by them].

The powers are all partial attainments of the essence of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*, which manifest the body of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama* and give rise to its functions of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*.
Therefore, one knows that the deities who have attained the efficacy of this sūtra further protect it;

thus, from the following passage on curing illnesses, saving fish, and feeding tigers, it is clear that these are all the meritorious power and function of this sūtra for generating goodness and extinguishing evil.
The Four Kings said: "We have heard this sutra and our physical strength has increased; our minds have become more diligent, courageous, and sharp, and we are endowed with all majestic virtues.
Furthermore, when a human king burns incense to make offerings while reciting this sutra, it transforms into a fragrant canopy that radiates golden light, illuminating this world and other realms.
All of this is due to the majestic spiritual power of this sutra. △ Third, the summary and conclusion of the text.
Because these various texts are subsumed [here], it is said that its function consists in extinguishing evil and generating good;
the meaning of this is evident. △ Fifth, the Evaluation of the Teaching’s Characteristics: If one discusses the sequence of their arising, one first seeks the name to grasp the essence;

based on the essence, one establishes the thesis; once the thesis is established, there is function; and through function, the teaching is set forth. This is the sequential order for the formulation of the five chapters.

If one is to investigate these five meanings, one must clarify the general and specific names. The "general" refers to the three dharmas of essence, doctrine, and function; the "specific" indicates each of these three dharmas individually.

Regarding the current classification of the teaching’s characteristics (*jiaoxiang*), there are two parts: first, the heading. The preceding section on the general and specific [classifications] concerns the temporal periods and flavors (*rasa*) in which they are subsumed. [The text] now has two sections: the first is the heading.
Fifth, regarding the classification of the teachings (*panjiao xiang*):
the preceding four chapters have all treated the words of the Sage addressed to those below as collectively being "teachings" (*jiao*).

Now, by means of the five flavors, the four treasuries (*sì zàng*), and the four teachings (*sì jiào*), their specific characteristics are clarified so that those who peruse them may distinguish them according to their categories. △ Second.

The second part [of the commentary] has two sections. First, the refutation of others' divergent interpretations, which has three parts. First, the refutation of the ancient masters’ judgment that this belongs to the indeterminate teachings. First, the citation of their position:
The ancients maintained that this sutra is not a teaching for the convergence of the Three Vehicles, nor is it a teaching of praise or censure, nor is it a teaching of signlessness (*animitta*).
It does not list the assembly of co-hearers and is not situated within the sequence of the five periods; rather, it is a partial, indeterminate teaching concerning eternal abiding.
The *Saṃnipāta* [Sūtra] corresponds to the *Lotus Sūtra*; "praise and censure" corresponds to the *Vaipulya*; and "formlessness" corresponds to the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Since it is none of these three, one may infer from the absence of a list of the assembly of listeners that it does not belong to the sequential order of the five periods.

Furthermore, because it suddenly discusses the "Eternal" (the *nitya*) before reaching the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is therefore judged to belong to the "partial and indefinite" teaching (*bipān*). "Partial" means being biased or eccentric.
I recently remarked that the location referred to—the chamber of Xinzhi—is a remote place;

furthermore, the five periods established by the ancients for the classification of the teachings differ from those of today. They designated the *Avataṃsaka* as "Sudden" and established the other five periods as all being "Gradual":
first, the Teaching with Characteristics, referring to the four Āgamas; second, the Teaching without Characteristics, referring to the various Prajñāpāramitā sūtras; third...

The teaching of praise and censure refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* and other Vaipulya sutras; the teaching that all virtues converge in the same destination refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;

and the teaching of the five eternal abidings refers to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. As for the teaching of occasional and indeterminate intent, it is not subsumed under either the gradual or the sudden. **II.

Refuting [the Five-Period Theory]** First, refuting the claim that [the teachings] are not arranged according to the sequence of five periods. This has three parts: first, citing their established doctrine.

This interpretation is not correct; for if those who heard the teaching together were not listed in the sequential order, then the listing of the assembly of those who heard it together should indeed constitute the sequential order.
△ Second, citing the case of Aṅgulimāla.
The Aṅgulimāla Sūtra lists those who heard the teaching together with the other sūtras without difference; its praise and censure accord with the intent of the Vimalakīrti.
Why does the commentator not include it in the sequential order?
That sūtra’s general introduction does not fail to list the assembly; Aṅgulimāla disparages the Śrāvaka vehicle to clarify the Mahāyāna.
Daoyan agrees with Vimalakīrti, and the masters of the treatises agree with the present sutra in classifying it as a "partial" and "indeterminate" teaching.
△ Third, examining the establishment of the sequence:
if both the inclusion and exclusion of the assembly are not sequential, then both the inclusion and exclusion of the assembly should likewise be [considered sequential].
[The sequence is as follows] (and so forth).

Since the author of the treatise has already determined that Aṅgulimāla is out of order, it is known through inference that he is not listed because he did not hear [the teaching] together with the others;
thus, he is placed out of order. If this is so, what prevents the present sutra from being in its proper sequence despite not listing those who heard it together? △ Second, the refutation.
Regarding the "non-exclusive indeterminate" (apratiniyata-anaikāntika), first I shall establish its meaning.

If one were to say that while it was not yet appropriate to clarify permanence, the clarification of permanence constitutes the non-exclusive indeterminate, then according to the ancient judgment of the five periods (*pañca-kāla*), it is only in the fifth period, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, that the eternal abiding (*nityatva*) is discussed; the preceding four periods would all be devoid of it.
This sutra constantly transcends the sequence [of the Tripitaka] to pre-emptively clarify that the "limited" (prādeśika) designation for the lifespan is established first.
△ Second, citing the Vaipulya to refute [the limited view]:
The *Dhāraṇī* says: "In the three places of Rājagṛha, Vārāṇasī, and the Jeta Grove, he bestows predictions upon the śrāvakas."

Furthermore, why is it that the three [vehicles] which were not yet to be unified have been unified, thereby establishing a sequence; and why is it that the permanence which was not yet to be clarified has been clarified?
Why is this not fixed? "Dhāraṇī" refers to the Vaipulya Dhāraṇī Sūtra, which is precisely the fourth assembly, the Lotus Sūtra.
The three vehicles are exemplified in the fifth [chapter], the Discourse on Nirvāṇa, as being permanent.

Since the assembly of the Vaipulya sūtras already establishes the sequence of the three vehicles, why is the discourse on permanence in this present sūtra not fixed? This is because it is a text from the latter portion of the Vaipulya;
thus, it is able to refer back to the three stages and bestow the prediction of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas at the Lotus Sūtra. △ Third, refutation by citing various sūtras.

Furthermore, while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Prajñāpāramitā*, the *Vimalakīrti*, and the Vaipulya sutras all discuss the permanence [of the Buddha-nature] in a sequential manner, why does this sutra clarify permanence as existing uniquely and indeterminately?

The ancients’ classification of the teachings failed to realize that different names convey the same principle; thus, they conflated the Dharmadhātu of the *Avataṃsaka* with the reality of the Vaipulya.

If the Prajñāpāramitā of Characteristics, the Mother of Buddhas, the One Vehicle of the Lotus Sūtra, and so forth, were not identical to the eternal body of *nirvāṇa* and the immutable essence of the vajra,
how could phenomena subject to arising and ceasing and lacking permanence constitute the True Aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) and the One Vehicle?
Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states that the Dharma-body is unconditioned and does not fall into any numerical categories, and the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of it as "eternal."
In the *Śrīmaladevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and elsewhere, it is further stated that [the Buddha] "abides eternally and does not perish.
Since such various sūtras already occupy their respective positions in the sequence, why is this sūtra alone categorized as a "partial teaching" (*p'ien-fang*)?

This is precisely to show that the present sūtra proclaims permanence and is not an indefinite teaching, while incidentally demonstrating that all other sūtras likewise expound eternal abiding. △ Second, refuting one master’s judgment that [this sūtra] belongs to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Part One: The Narration.

Furthermore, another master says that this sutra and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* belong to the same fourth period, because their meanings regarding "mountains, weights, oceans, drops, and dust motes" are identical.

He means that the parable of the lifespan in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*—which uses the dust motes of the world-systems—is equal in intent to that of the present sutra; thus, he implies that both sutras had not yet appeared [at the time of his writing].
All quantities are impermanent. △ Second, the refutation:
This interpretation is not correct. The New Edition states: "Śāriputra, the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding body is bound by form;
there is no such thing as śarīra (relics). How could mountains and seas obscure its golden light, or how could grains of sand conceal its precious abode?"
This master failed to understand the discourse on permanence in these two sutras and merely clung to the notion of numerical quantity;

he did not realize that in this sutra—the *Dīrgha-āgama* (specifically the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-sūtra*)—it is extensively explained that because the Brahmin Śariputra desired to be reborn in heaven, he requested the Buddha’s relics, whereupon the Prince of the Licchavis [the Buddha] extensively discoursed on how the Buddha’s body is a permanently abiding essence and possesses no relics. This demonstrates that within the responsive form (*nirmāṇakāya*), there is precisely the Dharma-body.
The body is neither long nor short; by verifying this chapter, one understands that the totality of phenomena arises in accordance with what is appropriate, being able to be both long and short.
Eighty is "short" and a *śaila* (mountain-weight) is "long"; "short" represents the physical body, while "long" represents the retributive wisdom-body (*vipāka-kāya*).

The ancients did not see the new edition which clarifies that the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* is that which is realized, while the golden *saṃbhogakāya* and constant wisdom are that which realizes it—the light.
However, [the teachings] limited to the *saṃbhoga-kāya*—measured by the weight of Mount Sumeru or the drops of the ocean—belong to the category of impermanence;

they merely obscure the permanent *dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*, which are like golden light. Second, regarding those who do not understand the *Lotus Sūtra*: the two gates of "Original" (*hon*) and "Trace" (*saku*) expounded in that section both reveal the permanent body.
Why? Because within the Trace Gate, it says: "The characteristics of the world are eternally abiding at the site of enlightenment."
Having understood this, it is stated in the Original Gate (Honmon) that the Tathāgata clearly perceives the characteristics of the triple world as being neither identical nor different;

these are all the essence of the Middle Way, the eternally abiding *dharmakāya* that has been realized. Using the jewel at the topknot of the treasure island as a metaphor, since the realized *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding, how could the wisdom of the recompense (*saṃbhogajñāna*) that realizes it, and the applications of its emanated functions, not likewise be so?
In the *Anityatā-sūtra*, it is stated that the particles of the entire world (*dharmadhātu-rajas*) constitute the number of kalpas for the past original formation of the eon (*vivartakalpa*).
If one discusses the future, the scriptural text explicitly states that [the Buddha] is eternally abiding and imperishable.

Is this not because this master [Huiyuan] obscures the Three Bodies—compared to the "Jewel Place"—by using the kalpas of the world’s particles as the measure of his attainment of Buddhahood in the distant past? △ Third, the refutation of the True Dharma (Satyadharma) school’s judgment regarding the three periods.
The first month of the second year provides the introduction.
The Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha stated that this sutra was preached during the ninety days following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and preceding the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
He cited the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which says: "The Buddha told Pāpīyas: 'Three months from now, I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Upon hearing this, Śraddhālakṣaṇa...

Therefore, we know that he should enter parinirvāṇa at eighty. △ Second, the refutation of the two [objections]. First, the refutation by taking away [the opponent's premise]: The statement regarding the proclamation of entering nirvāṇa is common to all sūtras;

how could it refer exclusively to the occasion three months prior when he informed Pāpīyas? At that time, Śraddhālakṣaṇa harbored doubts. This section is divided into three parts; first, the general [refutation].
To refute this, the meaning is likewise not so; the intent of proclaiming the extinction was not solely to inform Māra that it was fixed for three months.
△ Second, citing the sutras.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that the Tathāgata will soon enter parinirvāṇa, and the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-dhyāna-sūtra* likewise says he will enter parinirvāṇa.
△ Third, the conclusion and refutation:
The proclamation of extinction in various sutras is not limited to a single instance; why must it necessarily be ninety days?
△ Second, the refutation by concession (yōng-pò). Part one:

Conceding the point and then scrutinizing it. Even if we concede that the three months belong to the fourth season and the remaining time belongs to the fifth season—so as to concede this because the declarations of extinction in various sutras remain consistent [with the view that] if one knows [the end of life] before the three months, it is fixed at eight [months].

For these ten reasons, we must allow that [the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*] may indeed belong within the three-month period; yet even if the months and years are permitted, one must examine the sequence and flavor of the sections to judge the teachings according to their general order.
Within the preliminary division, there is a fixed sequence, whereas the subsequent division is not fixed.

For instance, the present "Chapter on Emptiness" appears after the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and the *Dhāraṇī* chapter appears after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Although the latter is not fixed, it must be subsumed under the former.
Even if this sutra were preached during the three-month period, it would belong either to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* or to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*;
this follows the ancients who divided and assigned the two sutras—the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*—to the fourth and fifth periods respectively.
△ Second, verifying that [this claim] lacks a basis.

If it belongs to the fourth period, since the *Lotus Sūtra* has already abandoned the provisional means (*upāya*), how could one further permit the three vehicles to perform repentance together within this [text]?

If it belongs to the fifth period, how can it again be said to exist during the preceding three months? Thus, there is no basis for either position, and it is not subsumed under either of the two pillars [of the periods]. (And so forth.)
The "Text for the Common Repentance of the Three Vehicles" is extracted from the *New Scripture*. Practitioners of the three vehicles each seek to realize their respective fruits;

they all rely upon this scripture to cultivate repentance. Since the *Lotus Sūtra* abolishes provisional teachings and even discards the unique expedient means of the Separate Teaching (*bhedavāda*), how could it maintain the expedient of a common repentance for the three vehicles?

This would constitute a regression that is not in accordance with the *Lotus Sūtra*. Furthermore, as this scripture was preached prior to the three-month period [of the *Lotus Sūtra*], it is established as such.
Advancing is not Nirvana; at the two central pillars, the compass and square have no place to apply. △ Second, clarifying the present correct judgment has two parts:
first, determining by means of textual meaning; second, first, distinguishing from other times.

Now that these are no longer the same as the old [teachings], how are they to be classified? If one posits them as "signless" (animitta), then there is a difference in time; if one posits them as "converging with the three," then there is a distinction in flavor.

If one posits them as signless while acknowledging a difference in time, this excludes those that are not Prajñāpāramitā; it refers to the specific time, place, and assembly when those particular sections were taught.
Although many [sutras] share the same name of *Prajñā*, since this one is specifically established under the title *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama*, it differs from what was taught at that time.

The "convergence of the three" refers to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*; that sutra abolishes the provisional teachings so that they all return to the One Vehicle, being purely the single *amṛta* (clarified butter).
Since this [text] preserves diverse interests, it belongs to the stage of *ghṛta* (fresh butter); hence it is said that "the flavor is distinct. △ Second, determining its specific category.
Regarding the first of these two [points], the text is established by means of the scriptural passage. First, it cites a passage from the Vaipulya sūtras.
According to the text below, it says: "I have heard that in the past, in a secluded place, there was a bhikṣu who recited such a Vaipulya Mahāyāna sūtra.
Since it specifically mentions "Vaipulya," how could this not be a matter of the text?
△ Second, citing the texts on the Three Vehicles:
The teachings of the Vaipulya (fangděng) apply universally to the three vehicles. The new edition states:

"Those who wish to be born among humans or devas, those who wish to attain the four fruits, the pratyekabuddhas, or those who wish to attain Buddhahood—all should perform repentance to eliminate karmic obstructions and abide securely within the Vaipulya. The meaning of this is beyond doubt.

The designation "Vaipulya" (fangděng) is established with two intended meanings. If, as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, it says that just as cream is produced from curd, so too does the Vaipulya emerge from the *Sūtra*—then this refers specifically to the teachings of the third period, which are called Vaipulya;

these are intended for the capacities of those of the three vehicles across the four teachings. However, when the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* refers to the "Vaipulya," it names the perfect principle (*yuanlǐ*) directly.
This is not a designation for the category of teachings that universally encompass all capacities during the third period.

Since there might be those who suspect that the passage from the *Vaipulya* cited at the beginning is named after its underlying principle—similar to the *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* and other such texts—I have cited the passage on the repentance of the Three Vehicles to establish that this title is definitively derived from the category of teachings themselves. Therefore, the conclusion states: "Its meaning is beyond doubt."
△ Second, defining the two [categories] according to their meaning. First, it is clarified that the Fangdeng (Vaipulya) section is fundamentally not restricted [to a specific teaching].
Yet, an objector says: "The new edition states that 'the Dharma-realm has no different vehicles,' which harms the principle of universal applicability.
However, this point does not obstruct the intent that the Fangdeng, as the *manzi* (full letters), encompasses both the common and the distinct, as well as the common and the perfect.

Because our current position establishes that the Vaipulya teachings pervade the three vehicles, we have cited the passage from the new version [of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*] stating there is no difference between vehicles to challenge the claim that our position fails to establish such pervasion across the three vehicles; thus, it is said that this undermines the meaning of "pervasion.

However, in the subsequent explanation of this objection, it is stated that the Dharma-realm has no different vehicles; this means that both the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddhayāna*) and the Perfect Teaching (*samyaksambuddhayāna*) take the Dharma-realm as their basis.

Because it serves as the ultimate refuge, it is itself designated as the "Vehicle Without Difference" (Avaiṣamika-yāna). Since the "Perfectly Full" (Pūrṇa-akṣara) teachings of the Vaipulya already encompass both vehicles, what obstacle could there be?
△ Second, explaining the passage on the listing of the assembly: it may refer to the future.

The critic raises doubt because the assembly of fellow listeners (*saha-śruta*) is not listed; they ask why the Hu text contains so much more, and why it should stop at only four fascicles or seven scrolls, suggesting perhaps that its text has not yet been fully translated.

Regarding the initial failure to list the assembly of fellow listeners, others have doubted whether this scripture belongs to the third category of the Vaipulya (Vaipulya-sūtra). However, our Master has judged it to belong to the third category, the Vaipulya.

For this reason, the Great Master pointed toward India, where the text was still extant in great abundance— not merely the four fascicles translated by Paramārtha, nor the seven fascicles by Paramārtha himself—
but when Yijing of the Tang dynasty retranslated this scripture, naming it the *Suvarṇaprabhāsottama-sūtra*,
there appeared a listing of the assembly that perfectly corresponded to the Sanskrit manuscript indicated by the Great Master, as if in a hidden resonance.

Furthermore, the judgment of other masters that this [text] belongs to the "partial teachings" (piān fāng) is clearly erroneous, as evidenced by the talismanic seal. II. Judging by the flavor of the teaching (jiào wèi):

If one evaluates the meaning according to the five flavors of the milk products, it is subsumed under the third, "clarified butter" (shēng sū). If one evaluates the meaning according to the four baskets (sì zàng), it is subsumed under the "Miscellaneous Basket" (zá zàng).

If one evaluates the meaning according to the four teachings (sì jiào), it is subsumed under the "Shared Teaching" (tōng jiào). Within the Shared Teaching, it is understood that it carries elements of the "Distinct Teaching" (bié jiào).
This clarifies the perfection [of the teaching].

Because it is examined and verified against others and further based on the meaning of the texts, it is said that such deliberation involves the classification and subsumption by means of the five flavors, the four treasuries, and the four teachings.
First, regarding the five flavors, since the text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* already uses "fresh butter" (mṛdv-ājya) [to represent the second flavor]...
This is analogous to the Vaipulya [sūtras]; the present sūtra clearly contains both the text and the meaning of the Vaipulya.

Therefore, it must be subsumed under the third flavor. As for the subsequent four collections (*piṭaka*), they are the Śrāvaka-piṭaka, the Bodhisattva-piṭaka, the Miscellaneous collection (*Kṣudraka-piṭaka*), and the Buddha-piṭaka.

These are named after the persons [who practice them] to designate the aggregates of the Dharma; the term "Śrāvaka-piṭaka" signifies that it is purely Hinayāna, while the "Bodhisattva-[piṭaka]" signifies Mahāyāna.
The *Buddhapiṭaka* (Buddha-treasury) exclusively explains the *Mahāsaṃyukta-piṭaka* (Great Miscellaneous Treasury), which also contains both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings.

Since this present sutra permits the three vehicles to perform repentance together, it is able to subsume the Śrāvakas, Bodhisattvas, and the Buddha-dharma; therefore, it belongs to the *Saṃyukta-piṭaka*.

Regarding the latter four teachings, the names of the five flavors and the four treasuries are still identical to those of other systems of the four teachings for judging scriptures; however, only the present [system] is unique.

The essence of this sutra used here reveals that illusion is itself emptiness; it is entirely not the crude method of analyzing phenomena (*dharmaparyāya*) found in the Tripitaka, nor is it the uncommon Dharma of the Distinct or Complete Teachings shared by the three vehicles in their collective repentance.
It is precisely the Dharma of non-arising and non-extinction received in common by the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

Because bodhisattvas of sharp faculties therein know the permanent and penetrate the nature, it is called the "Shared Teaching with a trace of the Distinct" (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana-saṃgṛhīta-viśeṣa-prakāśana*).

Yuan asked: "If it is the case that those Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) who receive the 'reception' (shoujie) only realize it is not empty upon reaching the stage of the Sages, why is it that in the explanation of the title and the commentary on the scriptural text, you speak solely in terms of both beginning and end being perfect?

If this were so, then the interpretation of the text and the classification of the teachings would become as utterly disparate as Hu and Yue. Answer: "The capacities of those in the Shared Teaching are diverse; it is not the case that they only receive the reception [at the final stage]."

To understand that the *Abhūta-āvaraṇa-śāstra* (Treatise on the Non-empty Canopy) applies to the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*), one must possess three meanings: first, both cause and effect are common; second, the cause is common while the effect is not;
third, the distinct [teaching] is common while the perfect [teaching] is not. Regarding the first meaning:

it refers to those dull-witted bodhisattvas who perceive only emptiness and, from beginning to end, do not know the distinct principles of the two teachings; therefore, it is said that "both cause and effect are common. As for the next meaning: one perceives...
From the stages above the Grounds (*bhūmi*), one deeply contemplates emptiness and is able to perceive that which is not empty.

Because this Bodhisattva first relies on the principle of universal penetration (*yītōng*) to achieve the true cause, and subsequently relies on the principle of particularity to advance toward the fruit of Buddhahood, it is said that "the cause is universally penetrating, but the fruit is not.
Regarding the third meaning: within the stages of Dry Wisdom (*gānhuì*) and the Nature Ground (*xìngdì*), one hears of the emptiness of the essence of phenomena (*tǐfǎkōng*), yet not only...
Being empty of the twenty-five states of existence, one is likewise empty of the emptiness of *nirvāṇa*.
Although such a person relies on the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*) to discuss emptiness and open their mind, they realize that the essence of this emptiness is the Middle Way.

Thus, through the contemplations of the internal and external ordinary beings of the Distinct and Complete Teachings (*viśeṣa-yāna* and *abhisambodhi-yāna*), which are identical to those of the Two Vehicles, they pass through the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*) and the subsequent stages up to the tenth.
The stage immediately becomes the Buddha of the eight aspects at the first ground (*bhūmi*) and the first dwelling (*vihāra*) of the Distinct and Perfect [teachings];

this is the meaning of the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect teachings being mutually inclusive. Since one already knows that it is not empty upon reaching the first ground, one does not receive the designation of "being received" (*pratigṛhīta*).
For this reason, although this sutra is categorized as belonging to the Shared Teaching based on the common repentance of the Three Vehicles, there is no contradiction.
The explanation of the title and the interpretation of the scriptural text clarify that the beginning and end of these three dharmas are perfectly sublime;

this is precisely the third meaning of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*). Furthermore, one should know that since this sutra permits the three vehicles to repent together, the locus of their repentance accords with their respective faith and understanding—whether it be emptiness or non-emptiness, or gradual or non-gradual—and thus fully encompasses the first two [meanings] of the Shared Teaching.

The Great Master [Zhiyi] specifically set aside the inferior for the sake of establishing the perfect understanding and practice of practitioners of the present day, speaking exclusively of the Perfect [Teaching].
Those who have heard and seen this should reflect upon and cultivate it according to this intent.

Pillar. *Zhēn* (pronounced zhēn; to pour out, to take). *Yíjì* (a white pheasant, *hùjiān* rhyme;
resembling a partridge with a tail four or five feet long). *Jìngtǐng* (*tǐng* pronounced tǐng; straight and upright). *Rèng* (pronounced réng, fourth tone;
